Senses.Explanation: The Inscription on Trusting the Mind is a named verse attributed in Chan records to the Third Patriarch Sengcan; masters do not merely list it but quote its lines as encounter material, interrogate its claims, and sometimes turn its own wording against it. Juelang Daosheng cites its demands to stop views and avoid preference while instructing students to look for themselves. Yongjue Yuanxian quotes its opening and then objects that saying 'only dislike choosing' already chooses and that saying 'only do not hate or love' already enters the stated contrast. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises its line about the extremely small and the great, then asks whether his whisk's swallowing and releasing the world comes from the forgotten realm or outside it. Wansong Xingxiu uses its opening lines as the old wording tested by Fayan's question, and Yongming Yanshou cites another passage to argue that the six sense-objects need not be treated as hostile. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that merely citing this inscription and the Song of Realizing the Way can become borrowed understanding rather than actual realization.

Senses.Explanation: Juzhi’s One Finger names Juzhi’s recurrent public gesture and the case involving Tianlong, Juzhi, and the attendant boy. The Lamp Record supplies the narrative behind the label: Tianlong showed Juzhi one raised finger; thereafter Juzhi raised one finger to visiting monks; when a boy copied him, Juzhi cut off the boy's finger, called him back, and raised his own finger. Later records place ‘Juzhi's one finger’ beside Xuefeng's rolling ball, Yunmen's looking-and-‘look!,’ Muzhou's ‘ready-made,’ Deshan's staff, and Linji's shout as a named response associated with Yuanwu Keqin. Verses call it ‘one-finger Chan,’ say it was used throughout Juzhi's life, and repeatedly ask or comment on where he was accurate. The entry reports the gesture, its narrative, and its later case-label use; the texts do not supply a further gloss for what the finger denotes.

Senses.Explanation: Qiannu's soul leaves her body. In Chan records this phrase is the title and shorthand of a public case built around Wuzu Fayan's question: Qiannu's soul departed—which one is real? Wumen preserves the question and warns against running about wildly in his comment. Fojian Huiqin repeatedly presses Cishou Huaishen with the case until the record says an obstruction opened. Fuyan Ya discusses it with a lay official and warns him not to fasten onto Qiannu. Xueguan Zhiyin keeps the case open through its own alternatives: whether she is karmic consciousness or mind-born, and whether one or two; his answer says there is no need to display form and shadow. Chaozong Tongren answers the real-one question with two strikes and a warning against eloping. Baishan Dekai answers a layperson's version with ‘where money was lost in the river, dredge in the river.’ The tale-name has become a compact, repeatedly interviewed case formula. The entry reports the questions and answers without selecting a real Qiannu for them.

Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the rank “absolute within the relative” (偏中正) names the absolute or upright disclosed within the relative or differentiated, reversing the nesting of “relative within the absolute” while remaining paired with it in explanations and verse sequences. Caoshan Benji glosses the rank as leaving affairs and entering principle. The Eyes of Humans and Devas transmits the same affairs-to-principle gloss in its Five Ranks account. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives the rank a sea-cloud, sacred-peak, returning-traveler, and mirror image. Langting Ting pairs it with a yellow bird carrying spring news. Juelang Daosheng associates it with a western circle and lesser yin, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies the same shout as this rank when it is silent right where it occurs. Tianran Hanshi reports Dongshan's old-woman-and-mirror stanza and answers it with another mirror verse; the varied images illustrate rather than define the relation.

Senses.Explanation: The side position is the differentiated member of Caodong positional language: it is where forms, speech, and responsive activity are located in contrast with the straight position. Caoshan Benji identifies it with the realm in which myriad forms appear, then turns that classification into an interview test when a monastic questioner claims to come from the side position. Linquan Conglun preserves the refusal in his appraisal. Yongjue Yuanxian classifies merit and royal-son sequences as matters on this side while warning against mechanically mapping separate schemes together. Baiyu and Dahui Zonggao both expose a limit: diagrams and verbal explanations can themselves remain side-position talk. The term therefore names a relational position inside these attested schemes; it is not a general synonym for error, inferiority, or one physical side.

Senses.Explanation: Layman Fu is an invoked pre-lineage figure defined by his deployment in Chan records. Yuanwu Keqin raises the public case in which Emperor Wu invites Layman Fu to lecture on the Diamond Scripture; Fu strikes the desk and leaves the seat, and Zhigong says that the lecture is finished. Guishan Gumei raises another Emperor Wu case in which Fu arrives wearing a Buddhist robe, a Daoist cap, and Confucian shoes; questioned in turn about a monastic, Daoist, or Confucian identity, Fu points respectively to the cap, shoes, and robe (披衲 / 頂冠 / 靸履). The same Blue Cliff Record passage identifies him as living at Yunhuang Mountain, planting two trees called the Twin Grove, and calling himself the future Layman Shanhui. Later masters quote and test him rather than merely preserve biography. Pin Jixiang raises Fu's full verse: 'Night after night I sleep embracing Buddha; morning after morning I rise together with him. Sitting and rising we constantly follow each other; in speech and silence we dwell together. Not separated by the slightest hair, we are like body and shadow. If you wish to know where Buddha goes, it is only this voice' (夜夜抱佛眠，朝朝還共起，起坐鎮相隨，語默同居止，些毫不相離，如身影相似，欲識佛去處，只者語聲是). Fatai criticizes the verse's final line. Foyan Qingyuan's citation of Fu's Heart-King Inscription—salt's taste in water and blue pigment in color—appears in Baiyang Fashun's awakening account. Yina Jie inscribes Fu's portrait as neither Confucian, Daoist, nor Chan. A Chan old-case collection explicitly attributes to Fu the verse, 'Empty-handed, holding a hoe; walking on foot, riding a water buffalo; a person crosses over a bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not' (空手把鋤頭，步行騎水牛，人從槗上過，槗流水不流). Doushuai Congyue says Fu only knew washing while holding a bridge pillar and releasing a boat. Zhongfeng Mingben discusses Fu's voice saying, and Tianyin Yuanxiu raises and questions the lecture case. Thus the Zen Fu is lecturer-who-strikes-and-leaves, mixed-attire interlocutor, quoted author, verse speaker, portrait subject, and target of later public criticism.

Senses.Explanation: To transmit precepts is to confer a stated rule-set in an ordination event, often named in ceremony headings, public addresses, and institutional biographies. Konggu Daocheng and Meixi Du give hall addresses explicitly occasioned by transmitting precepts; the latter includes public questions about keeping and breaking them. Zhuanyu Guanheng's preface names a three-hall procedure for the event. Other records preserve verse dedications, household conferral, and repeated monastery appointments to open the hall and transmit precepts. These are observable ceremonies and responsibilities, not a loose synonym for teaching.

Senses.Explanation: To transmit the robe is to hand over the inherited physical robe in a lineage-succession account. Chan histories use the transfer as evidence, chronology, entrustment, dispute, and criticism, while one later ordination record uses the same graphs for distributing robes to recipients. The fullest direct account is Hongren's answer after giving Huineng the inherited robe. He says, 'When Bodhidharma first arrived, people did not yet trust; therefore the robe was transmitted to make clear that the teaching had been obtained. Now confidence is mature, the robe has become a source of contention; it stops with you and will not be transmitted again' (昔達磨初至，人未知信，故傳衣以明得法。今信心已熟，衣乃爭端，止於汝身，不復傳也). This account both states the robe's recorded evidentiary function and the reason given for ending its transmission. Other histories narrate that the time to transmit the robe arrived, that Hongren gave Huineng the robe and told him to guard what was entrusted, and that the transfer occurred secretly at night. Later records use the event as chronology, lineage claim, question, and criticism: one asks what is entrusted after Caoxi because 'from this point the robe and bowl were not transmitted' (自此不傳衣鉢), while Fuyan Baozong's address lists 'Huineng transmitting the robe through six generations, seeking that small advantage' (盧公六代傳衣，圖他小利). The collocation 'transmit the robe and entrust the teaching' (傳衣付法) occurs 29 times in 25 storage files representing 24 independent works, 'transmit robe and bowl' (傳衣鉢) 31 times in 26, and 'not transmit the robe' (不傳衣) 16 times in 15.

Senses.Explanation: This recurring recorder formula introduces a question by an unidentified monastic and hands the next turn to a named respondent. It can open a famous case, introduce another question in an ongoing record, or appear with modifiers such as “there was,” “again,” and “at the time.” The stored passages range from questions about a dog’s buddha-nature, the central meaning of the teaching, the ancestral teacher’s coming from the west, a singular matter, the price of rice, what the respondent is doing in the street, and the gate of absence of division. The first graph identifies the questioning participant as a monastic and the second marks the question event. Because none of the ten questioners is personally named after full passage and parallel review, the entry does not assign them masters’ names merely from the respondent or section owner. The four previously orphaned respondents are Oxhead Zhiwei, Helin Xuansu, Budai Qici, and Tianyi Yihuai; they answer the questions but do not utter the recorder formula.

Senses.Explanation: Fill hunger can name an actual meal, but Chan records repeatedly use it to test substitutes that look or sound useful while failing to feed. Baoning Renyong places a heat-mirage filling hunger beside plum-grove thirst relief among false expedients. Liaotang Weiyi also preserves the literal bodily baseline: Shakyamuni eats hemp and wheat to fill hunger during six years in the snow mountains. The Yongzheng Emperor explicitly calls grasping the pointing finger as the moon a painted cake used to fill hunger and says this is how teaching misleads people. The headword therefore retains its literal bodily standard: does the offered substitute actually feed?

SearchAliases: at the gate of light and shadow
Zen at the gate of light and shadow
Senses.Explanation: The gate of light and shadow is the records' visible threshold contrasted with the matter inside the house: people mistake its coarse, shallow business for what is within (光影門頭戶底麤淺底事，將作屋裏事). Elsewhere Xueguan Zhiyin says students "recognize only the gate of light and shadow as themselves" (惟認光影門頭當作自己). The phrase also enters verse as a place not to stop: "do not halt your steps at the gate of light and shadow" (光影門頭休駐足). Hongzhi supplies a notable counter-deployment: "a person who settles the matter at the gate of light and shadow will do" (光影門頭了事底漢即得), then immediately asks how one proceeds before guest and host divide and before an image is formed. Zen thus bends ordinary light, shadow, and doorway language into a recurring label for the visible or reflected threshold that records contrast with the inside of the house, oneself, and the not-yet-formed image.

Senses.Explanation: To enter settled absorption is to settle into an absorbed, composed state from which someone may later emerge. Sanghanandi sits in settled absorption for twenty-one days and then rises; the reviewed unnamed woman in the famous public case remains in settled absorption when Manjusri cannot bring her out. Zhirong asks Zhihuang whether he enters with mind or without mind. When Zhihuang says that during settled absorption he sees neither a present nor an absent mind, Zhirong replies that constant settled absorption should have no further entry or exit. Mazu Daoyi classifies observing emptiness and entering settled absorption as contrivance. Baizhang Huaihai says not to take settled absorption and enter settled absorption, just as one should not take Chan and think about Chan or take buddha and seek buddha. An unnamed monk asks Liuhe Xiangji Zi what an unnamed monk in settled absorption is, and Xiangji answers that the four seas are originally limpid. Yongming Yanshou criticizes merely leaving thought to enter settled absorption while rejecting objects to seek truth. These named challenges do not erase the visible state and its entry-and-emergence grammar; they are where the Chan record repeatedly tests it.

Senses.Explanation: To enter a Zen interview chamber for a recorded question, examination, or report: to enter for a chamber interview. The headword occurs 2,365 times in 313 allowlisted texts across both senses. Productive interview forms include "entered the chamber and asked" (入室問, 31), "entered the chamber and presented his understanding" (入室陳解, 3), "chamber-entering disciples" (入室弟子, 44), and "during a chamber interview" (入室次, 204). Huqiu Shaolong enters and is questioned by Yuanwu Keqin. Kaixian Shanxian enters to present his understanding, followed by Deshan Yuan asking how he understands. Tianyi Yihuai is tested during a chamber interview. A lineage notice counts 139 "chamber-entering disciples" and says each became a lineage master in one region. A later case describes Ciming Chuyuan placing a sword, sandals, and a basin in the chamber and saying "look, look" whenever someone entered; those who hesitated by the sword were shouted out. Zen bends ordinary room entry into controlled access to an institutional interview setting and into the status label “chamber-entering disciple.” It does not by itself guarantee approval, succession, or a particular result.

Senses.Note: Two independent allowlisted witnesses establish ordinary room entry through distinct following actions: sitting upright and dying, and fetching a named book. This remains separate so death-room and retrieval movements are not misread as interviews.

Senses.Explanation: An inner-room disciple is a student admitted to the lineage elder's closest instructional relation and recognized as such in rules, biographies, and lineage records. The Chan Pure Rules names special hospitality for lineage relatives and inner-room disciples. Lamp records count Nanyue Huairang's six such disciples and immediately narrate his individual acknowledgments of what each had attained. A later chronology records a lay follower vowing to become an inner-room disciple in life after life, showing the title as a claimed relationship as well as a compiler's classification.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan records it is a stock description of a recorded teacher becoming involved in words, teaching, or an encounter for others. One passage expressly calls the interlocked condition 'gain within no-gain and no-gain within gain' entering mud and water, then pairs it with 'ride the thief's horse and pursue the thief's band.' Before an assembly Guanghui Yuanlian says that he does not avoid others' scrutiny and enters mud and water 'for you people'; Songyuan Chongyue's record places the phrase as his answer in a numbered question-and-answer sequence. A historical contrast says that at Magadha the edge was already exposed and before Shaoshi Peak Bodhidharma 'entered mud and water.' The Zen deviation is this repeated use of ordinary muddy immersion for the teaching-seat act of entering entangling speech and encounters for an audience; the texts also criticize particular instances, so the phrase is not praise by definition.

Senses.Explanation: To enter the sea and count its sand is to undertake an immense enumeration that cannot deliver the thing sought. Huanglong Huinan pairs the image with reciting phrases and recognizing reflected light; Tian'an Sheng quotes the complaint that studying names and forms became sand-counting and counting another's treasure. Guxue Zhe applies it to extensive pilgrimage, while Chaozong Tongren lists classificatory schemes and interpretation as unable to reach the matter. Yuan'an Feng says a mistaken vision leaves later people counting sea-sand. Chan usage targets exhaustive accumulation that remains external to the immediate case.

Senses.Explanation: Inner succession is the inward side of the royal-line analogy used in Five-Ranks discourse. Jiufeng Daoqian defines it as knowing how to take responsibility within, distinguishes it from outer succession in the minister’s position, and still places the royal seed beyond both taking responsibility and carrying a burden. In Jiufeng Daoqian’s exchange, a questioner asks whether outward succession is the minister’s position and inward succession the royal seed. Jiufeng accepts the setup, then defines outer and inner succession separately before refusing to equate inner succession with the royal seed itself. The Records Pointing at the Moon and the Compendium of the Five Lamps preserve that same explicit definition, while the Complete Collection and Strict Lineage repeat the case in separate works. Hongzhi Zhengjue uses ‘inner succession arriving home’ opposite ‘branching off and borrowing the road’ in a public address. Yongjue Yuanxian distinguishes royal-prince Five Ranks as internally divided into inner and outer succession. The corpus therefore gives a technical relation, not a generic synonym for transmission.

Senses.Explanation: To present in full is to bring the whole matter forward without leaving a remainder; the phrase appears in questions, answers, and appraisals of complete presentation. Literally, to raise or present in full. Yunmen Wenyan supplies the decisive contrast: seeing no single form is only half-presentation, and even then one must know the occasion of full presentation . Shengyin Chongkai pairs presentation across past and present with the ancestral master's true command . Juelang Dasheng joins the flower at Vulture Peak and snow at Shaoshi with separate transmission personally shown and the true command fully presented . Yuanwu Keqin raises the command in full and publicly asks how it can be unfolded. Liao'an Qingyu says that the entrustment at Vulture Peak is precisely here and tells the assembly to take up one fully presented saying ; Shending Yunwai Ze similarly says that if one can present it whole with bare hands, ease is assured . Zen bends the ordinary sense of completeness toward teaching-seat language: a saying, command, or lineage entrustment is brought forward without remainder and submitted to the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: The whole dynamic or full pivotal function: the complete working of a trigger or pivot. The graphs join ‘whole or complete’ (全) to ‘trigger, pivot, or dynamic’ (機). The compound has 948 occurrences in 244 allowlisted texts. It is especially visible in ‘the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用). Yuanwu Keqin says this ‘whole dynamic and great function is manifest wherever one touches’ (全機大用觸處見成); elsewhere his record says ‘as the grass bends and the wind moves, the whole dynamic alone is exposed’ (草偃風行全機獨露), then asks what one says without relying on any thing or phrase. Yuanwu also speaks of the whole dynamic ‘alone functioning’ (全機獨用). Chaozong Tongren pairs a wisdom-sword cutting bonds with the whole dynamic ‘thoroughly freed’ (全機透脫), then immediately glosses being freed as a sick person finally sweating. The Blue Cliff Record uses the term both in Yuanwu's case pointer ‘the whole dynamic is displayed everywhere’ (全機隨處齊彰) and in his comment that several actions are all ‘places of the whole dynamic and great function’ (全機大用處). Gongchen Daoxian uses the compound predicatively: ‘if I deploy the whole dynamic, where will you search?’ (我若全機，汝向甚麼處摸索). The records thus bend an ordinary word for the complete working of a mechanism into language for undivided operation at the teaching seat.

Senses.Explanation: The whole body stands exposed means that the complete thing is already openly displayed, even where the person facing it fails to recognize it. Wuwai Wunian Yuanxin gives the contrast in one exchange: face-to-face it is not recognized, yet its whole body stands openly exposed. Miyun Wuyun likewise places the phrase in broad daylight under a clear sky after refusing both talk and silence as resting places. The exposed whole is not restricted to a human body. Ruibai Mingxue uses one jewel whose full body is present through its colored reflections; Puan Yinsu uses one broken grain of ordinary Luling rice; Jifei Ruyi answers from within the ocean-seal’s light. These images make exposure observable through what is present rather than through a hidden explanation. Failure to recognize it and differences among reflected colors do not make the whole absent. Body, jewel, grain, and luminous field are distinct images carrying one recurrent predicate: the complete referent is out in the open. They are not four separate dictionary senses.

Senses.Explanation: A double case is a second liability added by the attempted answer or escape: the response does not clear the first encounter but supplies another count against the utterer. When the questioner tries to excuse an answer by saying he has not entered the hall, Shoushan calls it a double case. After an old adept greets Muzhou with a shout, Muzhou turns his hand sideways and rules “a double case.” When the questioner says the fallen eyebrows do not fall, Yunfeng rules that this creates a double case.

Senses.Explanation: An eighty-year-old man entering the examination hall undertakes a consequential public test at an age when it cannot be dismissed as children’s play. Chan masters use the couplet to mark the gravity of a case, an address, or the claim to decide the matter for oneself. Dahui Zonggao caps Deshan’s bowl case with the old man in the examination hall and says it is no child’s game. Yinyuan Longqi compares the matter directly to the same late examination. Tianyin Yuanxiu uses the line in verse after “the dead person comes back to life.” Shending Yikui warns his assembly with the couplet if the preceding military images remain unclear.

Senses.Explanation: Thrown wide open describes an unobstructed opening, often enacted at a gate or in an address that claims nothing is being withheld. Yinyuan Longqi, Zhufeng Zhenxu, and Linye Tongqi speak at literal monastery gates, making the door image visible. Yuanwu Keqin, Baichi Xingyuan, and Yun’e Xi use the same image for public disclosure or entrustment. Feiyin Tongrong supplies the limit: although it is wide open, the listener must recognize it personally and turn.

Senses.Explanation: A public case is a recorded encounter or saying set before students as an authoritative test object. Zhongfeng Mingben explicitly compares it to a government office's case documents and says that a lineage teacher raises one to decide an unsettled student's understanding. Sanjiao Laoren says patriarchs established such records and left them for the monasteries. Wumen Huikai uses old public cases as tiles for knocking on the gate; Yuanwu Keqin says later people gave this name to the old teachers' occasion-matched pointers. Later records warn against dissecting every old case for a fixed route, renew an old case in present interview, and call an immediately present encounter a ready-made case. The legal comparison explains the authority and adjudicative force of the Chan record-object without reducing it to a secular lawsuit.

SearchAliases: at the gates of the six faculties
at the gateways of the six faculties
Senses.Explanation: The phrase locates activity at the six sensory gateways—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—where seeing, hearing, sensing, and thought meet their objects. Chan speakers point to these ‘gate-fronts’ as the immediate site of obstruction, light, responsiveness, or turning back, rather than as six architectural doors. The phrase occurs 116 times in 84 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says, "there is a phrase at the staff-head, beneath the straw sandals, three thousand miles away, and at the gates of the six faculties; if recognized at the gates of the six faculties, there is no need to seek separately three thousand miles away" (有一句子在六根門頭，向六根門頭薦得). Yuanwu describes the six faculty-gates as "clean-naked and bare" and then says the audience will not "turn the light around and look back" (六根門頭淨裸裸赤灑灑，只是不肯回光返照). Huangbo's record speaks of scraping and clearing at the gates of the six faculties until not a hair of greed or craving remains untreated (於六根門頭刮削併當，貪愛有纖毫治不去). Later addresses say a "natural ancient buddha" constantly "shines light and shakes the earth at the gates of the six faculties" (六根門頭放光動地), while Ying'an describes them simply as "bare" throughout the twelve double-hours. These are observable predicates and locations assigned by the texts; the entry does not substitute a general theory of sensation.

Senses.Explanation: To have a discerning eye: to be able to recognize, distinguish, or judge what an encounter puts forward. Danxia Tianran asks whether the person who fed a traveler has such an eye, and Muzhou Daoming asks the same about a donor after an unnamed participant returns from a meal. Fayan Wenyi explicitly tells an unnamed participant that his earlier question shows a discerning eye, then asks why he did not cover the exchange before the public assembly. Jiashan Shanhui gives the negative boundary: someone who depends on buddha-and-patriarch sayings as a model has not yet acquired the eye. Fayun Faxiu promises the eye if listeners can identify the color of the wind. Yuanwu Keqin asks those with the eye to judge whether Xuedou or the Buddha has exposed the other. Tiantong Hongzhi says an eye-equipped Chan participant will recognize and assent to his sequence of circle figures; Sanshan Lai says such a discerning guide departs as soon as the matter is raised. Mingjue Cong uses the forehead-eye expansion when he says the teaching seat should make each person discerning and impartial underfoot. Chan bends ordinary possession of sight into a public capacity that named speakers confer, question, demand, and test; it is not a physical-eye diagnosis and not automatic approval of every claim.

Senses.Explanation: To be complete, fully endowed, or lacking nothing. Xuansha says, “each person is fully endowed; each person is manifest” (人人具足，人人成現). Another address ranges across monastics and laypeople, women and men, wise and foolish, noble and low, saying all are fully endowed “without the least lacking” (悉皆具足，曾無欠少). Hongzhi pairs “fully endowed from the beginning” (本來具足) with “not a hair's breadth lacking, not a hair's breadth in excess.” A later text warns that merely accepting “fully endowed from the beginning, no need to seek outside” can become empty talk. In the ordination compound “full precepts” (具足戒), the same completeness word modifies the precepts: biographies record receiving or being given the full precepts. Predicate and attributive placement express the same completeness, not different lexical referents.

Senses.Explanation: The full ordination precepts are the rule-set received when a novice or other recipient is fully ordained. Patriarchal biographies narrate shaving a recipient and then conferring the full precepts. Later lamp biographies date a person's reception of them as a concrete institutional transition. Poshan Haiming records a nun coming to receive the full precepts and addresses the obligations and encumbrances surrounding that event. Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, arrival within integration (兼中到) is the fifth named relation. Dongshan’s verse places it outside the opposition of existence and nonexistence; later records repeatedly describe distinctions as exhausted or integrated. Dongshan Liangjie begins the fifth-rank verse by saying it falls into neither existence nor nonexistence. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives it a dawn verse, while an unnamed monastic asks Fenyang Shanzhao for it and receives images of a weaving jade woman and a drumming stone man. Langting Ting uses a returning cuckoo, Juelang Daosheng offers a later black-white diagram, Yongjue Yuanxian says affairs and principle are both gone, and Ruibai Mingxue applies it to a shout after holy and ordinary, subject and object, and existence and nonexistence are exhausted. These remain attributed illustrations of one rank.

Senses.Explanation: To turn the light back and reflect is an instruction or reflexive action directing illumination back upon oneself or one's stated understanding. The records also criticize people who use the four graphs as a label for quiet withdrawal, so the phrase is not defined as secluded quiet. Zibo Zhenke tells someone caught by disputation to turn the light back and reflect. Guishan Lingyou tells Yangshan Huiji to do so independently and immediately asks him to present his actual understanding, then tests each reply. Yuanwu Keqin says his listeners refuse to turn the light back and reflect before raising encounter records. Longqing Qingxian directs the action to one's own heels in a hall address. Zhongfeng Mingben elsewhere explicitly interrogates the four graphs and rejects calling secluded quiet by this name; the phrase therefore remains an attested reflexive instruction, not a quietist program.

Senses.Explanation: Knowing hot and cold for oneself is the recurrent predicate of the drinking-water comparison: the person concerned, not another reporter, knows the temperature. Literally, one knows cold and warmth for oneself, usually in the comparison “like a person drinking water, knowing hot and cold for himself” . Huiming uses it after Huineng's instruction to report that he now has an entry; Huangbo joins it to conduct in each movement, dwelling, and instant; and other teachers pair it with looking for oneself rather than seeking from another. The phrase also becomes an object of interrogation: Longmen Foyan grants that hot and cold can be known, then asks what the one who knows for himself is. Daodu pairs “knowing hot and cold for oneself” with “handling slow and urgent matters for oneself” and says the matter cannot be spoken out even when both parties exert themselves. The Chan bend is this sensory commonplace's use as a first-person report, an answer about the Way, and a question about the knower; the texts preserve the water comparison and these recorded deployments.

Senses.Explanation: The paired phrase names ordinary feelings and holy views together as a two-sided obstruction or contrast. Caoshan Benji calls them the “golden lock on the dark road” and says one must mutually interchange (凡情聖見是金銷玄路，直須回互). Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang says there is no need to remove the pair before cold fills the whole sky and heat fills it. Chaozong Tongren calls ordinary feelings and holy views the road of birth and death, then contrasts exhausting the feelings of holy and ordinary with the road out of birth and death, while warning that this remains reciprocal treatment. Yongjue Yuanxian repeats the golden-lock formula and says earlier sages used the teaching to winnow it away. These deployments treat both poles as a coupled conceptual formation, not as praise of the holy half.

Senses.Explanation: A point of emergence is an opening by which a person, line, or proposed answer is not trapped in the position posed by an exchange. The record marks the constraint physically: Lingyun Baoyin says a line must have such a point, because lacking one is like a black ox lying in dead water. Yuanwu Keqin says that a sentence has a point of emergence and that either answer—“it is destroyed” or “it is not destroyed”—can have one, so the term does not name one approved conclusion. Asked whether there is a point of emergence when the spirit platform is not established, Huaguang Fan says yes; asked what it is, he answers only “Emerge” (如何是出身處。出). When Baoen Huaiyue is asked for the student's point of emergence, he replies, “What is binding you?” and, after the student says he cannot emerge, asks, “Whose fault is that?” Yunmen Wenyan answers the buddhas' point-of-emergence question with “East Mountain walks on water”. Yungai Zhiben answers the student's version with “Xuefeng was originally a man from Lingnan”, exploiting the ordinary geographical sense of where someone comes from inside the public question.

Senses.Explanation: The discriminating mind is the mind described as raising divisions among encountered things, positions, or qualities; Chan records define, criticize, and contrast this operation. The Mirror Record says that when discrimination arises, perceived objects appear, and calls that arising ignorance. Huanyou Chuan says a discriminating mind starts when people take what appears before them as outside their own share. Baizhang Huaihai's exchange asks how an undivided knowing could cut the mind that sees and discriminates, then continues until both sword and knowing are unavailable. Other records contrast discriminating and undiscriminating minds without turning the latter into a prescribed exercise.

Senses.Explanation: An emphatic warning governing an action or error: literally 'urgently avoid,' hence 'strictly avoid,' 'take care not to,' or 'beware of.' The object supplied by the record must be translated rather than replaced by a general spiritual warning. Daowu says, 'where knowledge does not reach, strictly avoid speaking of it' (智不到處，切忌道著); Daoqian answers a question about words that display the Way with 'strictly avoid choosing' (切忌揀擇); Tianyin tells the assembly 'strictly avoid conjecturing' (切忌卜度). Other high-seat warnings preserve concrete allusions: 'the sword has long gone; strictly avoid marking the boat' (劍去久矣，切忌刻舟), and 'if you are not a guest of the Dragon Gate, beware being branded on the forehead' (不是龍門客，切忌遭點額). Its Chan deployment is a direct warning embedded in interviews and public addresses, not a commentator's private aside.

SearchAliases: before and after are cut off
before and after limits cut off
Senses.Explanation: The records repeatedly place the phrase in the formula 'when not one thought arises, the before-and-after limits are cut off' (一念不生，前後際斷), and biographies use it for a recorded event occurring at words or while raising a question. Chan usage does not make that condition a final verdict: Dahui quotes people who obtain bodily and mental extinction, the before-and-after limits cut off, resting and ceasing, and take it as ultimate, then says that this 'fine condition' obstructs them. Another lamp record says of the same event that the person had 'died and could not come alive'; a public interview answers 'what about when the before-and-after limits are cut off?' with 'raise thirty blows,' followed by an actual strike. The Zen deviation is therefore the phrase's use as both a named event and something masters publicly test and criticize; this entry does not turn it into the roadmap's unattested 'timeless gap.'

Senses.Explanation: An instant is a very short interval. Yongzheng Emperor says that it is swift as a finger-snap. Wuyi Yuanlai compares three elapsed years to the interval of an instant, while Zhongfeng Mingben says there is no instant without birth and change or cessation. Yongming Yanshou uses flowing water to describe the previous instant ceasing and the next arising. Chijue Daochong gives a finer inherited reckoning whose source-visible count reads literally ‘six-thousand-five’ instants in one finger-snap, followed by 900 arisings and cessations in one instant; no parallel or apparatus variant resolves whether the first written number is meant as 6,005, a colloquially shortened 6,500, or a textual error. Lingao Benyu instead begins from one thought containing ninety instants and likewise gives 900 arisings and cessations within each instant. Those differently framed calculations confirm extreme brevity but do not establish a single modern duration. Yang Jie says the Source-Mirror's treasure is gained without even an instant's exertion. Ziyang Zhenren contrasts becoming buddha in an instant with wandering for myriad ages. These named speakers repeatedly bend the tiny time-unit into a sharp interval for change, attainment, or contrast, without turning the interval into a person, title, or separate lexical object.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula "outside the eon." The Chan corpus uses it as a productive modifier and location in sayings and verse: "spring light beyond the eon" (the beyond-the-eon expression春光), "the spring beyond the eon returns and the ten thousand things wither" (the beyond-the-eon expression春回萬物枯), and "the true lineage beyond the eon" (the beyond-the-eon expression真宗). It is paired explicitly with the time before buddhas and patriarchs were born: "before buddhas and patriarchs were born, outside the empty eon" (佛祖未生空the beyond-the-eon expression). It also enters public address as a demand to "take responsibility beyond the eon" (於the beyond-the-eon expression承當), contrasted in the same question with meeting now (而今相見, "meeting at present"). The corpus thus bends chronological language into a recurrent Chan register for the sayings, activity, spring, and lineage it places outside or before measured epochs.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula “Stir a thought and at once deviate” functions as a compact verdict, but the records immediately deny that mere nonmovement or dead-water stillness resolves it. Literally, “stir a thought and at once deviate.” The phrase's Zen-specific deployment is a compact verdict and answer, frequently paired with “form an intention and at once err” , but the corpus explicitly refuses to turn its negative wording into mere mental stillness. Huangbo says, “it is just this; stir a thought and at once deviate” , then compares what he has described to measureless space. Linji pairs “form an intention and at once err” with the headword and immediately continues with the person who understands not being apart from what is before the eyes . Shimen Cizhao quotes the pair and adds: “not intending and not moving, one is doing business in dead water” . Huanglong Huinan gives the parallel correction: “not intending and not moving is no different from wood and earth; a traveling monk must obtain a turning phrase” . In direct questions, Tianyin answers “What is the body of things?” with the phrase, while Linye Qi answers “How, finally, should one head toward it?” with it and answers the follow-up “what about when thought does not move?” with “the eyebrows are above the eyes” . The record thus bends an ordinary warning about a wayward thought into a portable Chan verdict while its own corrections exclude “do not think” as a complete gloss.

Senses.Explanation: The compound marks a test carried through to exposure: to see someone or something through. Zhaozhou Congshen returns from testing the old woman on the road to Mount Wutai and declares that he has seen her through. Xuedou Chongxian and Wansong Xingxiu use the completed formula as a capping verdict. Dahui Zonggao turns it reflexively, telling an interlocutor that the old monk has been seen through by him before striking when he hesitates. Another transmitted version gives Zhaozhou's declaration that he saw the woman through. Wumen Huikai reverses the testing relation by saying the two hermits instead saw Zhaozhou through, and elsewhere preserves Zhaozhou's declaration in the Wutai-woman case. The tester can thus be tested in turn; the verb denotes successful exposure claimed within the encounter, not an infallible external judgment.

Senses.Explanation: To examine and discriminate is to test an interlocutor, a claim, or an answer in a public interview and distinguish what survives the exchange. Tianru Weize says that after examination and discrimination are clear and the matter is firmly grasped, activity in the dusty net is unobstructed. Hengchuan Xinggong rebukes Zhen Dianxiong's claim that he could examine masters everywhere; Xutang Zhiyu says, “I too cannot examine and discriminate you,” and Baichi Yuanshuo asks where the capacity formerly used for examining masters has gone. The term names an active interview function rather than the whole question-and-answer encounter.

Senses.Explanation: The verdict “toil, yet no result” (勞而無功) is applied in Chan records to fruitless searching, speaking, contrivance, and failed responses. Verses and addresses use the same four graphs where exertion is expressly followed by failure to accomplish; the phrase judges the outcome of the labor, not labor as such.

Senses.Explanation: To summon the thief who ruins the house is to make a move that invites its own undoing. Chan critics apply the household image when a participant’s question, accommodation, or display gives the other party the opening that defeats it. Yangshan Huiji applies it to Huangbo’s exchange with Linji. Foxin Bencai places it beside leveling high and low. Lüyu Jiao applies it to the Buddha questioning two pig-carriers. Chijue Daochong says Yinshan summons the thief by answering Dongshan until he yields a confession.

Senses.Explanation: Open and unobstructed in all ten directions is a recurrent verdict for unrestricted reach, contrasted with blocked movement, partial response, or a closed eye. Fushan Fayuan contrasts an eye sealed without leakage with one for which the whole earth opens and all ten directions are unobstructed. Yuan'an Liao asks how anyone overwhelmed by ordinary oppositions could claim such free passage. Hongzhi Zhengjue joins the phrase to openness without reliance. Later hall speakers apply it to response, illumination, and the mutually unobstructed field of things, preserving a public verdict rather than naming a private state.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes the Ten Oxen in these Chan records. Its wording is "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and its associated pictures. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, the identified teacher interrupts the recorded questioner asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?" (牛在甚麼處). The deviation from an ordinary count of cattle is documentary: "the Ten Oxen" (十牛) functions as the proper name of a Chan verse-and-picture series, circulated, recited, questioned, and criticized inside the record.

Senses.Explanation: A thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions names the proliferating variety of words, gates, cases, and appearances. Masters test both errors: being lost in the differences and erasing the distinct uses that must still be handled. Kuoan criticizes treating the patriarchs’ myriad differences as arbitrary and asks how their expedient gates can be digested. Dahui says that knowing the myriad differences are one kind leaves a person exposed to attack from every side. Yunmen says pursuing words and explanations produces myriad differences and only greater distance from the matter. Xueyan pairs myriad differences with being threaded through by one principle.

Senses.Explanation: The thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion are tested through questions about the true or principal eye. The “thousand hands and eyes,” attested 242 times in 108 allowlisted texts, is the invoked form of Great Compassion, or Guanyin. Chushi Fanqi’s image record identifies it directly: “Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes are Guanyin’s responsive transformation-body” (大悲千手眼者，觀音大士應化之身也). In the Chan record the figure is repeatedly placed inside public interviews asking which is the “true eye.” Daowu asks, “Among Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes, which is the true eye?” and receives “like a person at night reaching behind for a pillow” (如人夜間背手摸枕子); the Magu–Linji encounter turns the same question into grabbing, demanding an immediate answer, and changing seats. A later teacher raises the whisk and says, “This is Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes” (此是大悲千手眼).

Senses.Explanation: Not transmitted by a thousand sages marks the ‘upward road’ or matter that no succession of sages can hand over as received information. In interviews it provokes the questioner to ask what that matter is or why it is not transmitted; answers redirect the question toward going, seeing, trusting, or acting for oneself. Later masters also quote the formula in their own addresses, so each occurrence belongs to its immediate utterer rather than to an anonymous traditional voice.

Senses.Explanation: To strike once, normally with the staff named immediately before it. In formal addresses the single blow is an audible and visible event followed by a question, declaration, shout, or descent from the seat. The records narrate Wuzhun Shifan striking once after telling the assembly to hear the staff speak, and Dahui Zonggao striking once before asking whether they hear. A stage direction narrates Zhean Jingfan raising the staff, calling it the fine finger, striking once, and then calling the sound the fine note. The narrators place the same one-blow action by Yuanwu Keqin, Hongjue Min, Jinshan Tanying, and Dahui Zonggao at a turn in their formal addresses; these masters perform the action but do not utter the headword.

Senses.Explanation: Nanquan cuts the cat names the canonical monastery dispute and the decisive action at its center. Nanquan cuts the cat is the name of the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat, Nanquan demands a word, and the assembly does not answer. Later masters question, verse, criticize, and pair the case with Guizong cutting the snake, including explicit precept challenges but no single recorded explanation of Nanquan's intention. The wording functions as a case name, the object of public questions, and the subject of later verses and comments. In Miyun Yuanwu's recorded public interview, a question states that killing living beings is a major precept (殺生是大戒) and asks why Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake; Miyun tells the questioner to repent (汝當懺悔去). In a sermon for a newly completed animal-release pond, Guxue Zhe quotes the rule to rescue animals being killed and asks how the cat and snake could have been saved. Guangfu Weishang asks Jueyin, “What is the import of Nanquan cutting the cat?” (南泉斬貓兒，意旨如何); Jueyin answers, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui Zonggao reports and rejects two labels students apply to the paired cutting cases. Wuming Huijing names the cat and snake cases while discussing coarse conduct, and Shanyi Chun places the pair in a teaching-seat statement about cases and precedent. The entry preserves these attested precept challenges, questions, comments, and refusals and does not provide an unrecorded intention for Nanquan.

Senses.Explanation: To calculate and guess; speculative reckoning. The graphs join ‘divine or forecast’ (卜) to ‘measure or estimate’ (度). The compound has 778 occurrences in 227 allowlisted storage files. Its recurrent coordinations locate the act in thinking, affective cognition, the root of thought, and mental weighing without creating additional senses. Dahui Zonggao says, in a list, ‘do not reckon under the root of thought; do not give a phrase; do not remain silent for a long time’ (不得向意根下卜度，不得下語，不得良久). His memorial inscription says, ‘Chan, Chan: do not use thinking and conjectural calculation; it does not concern written words and speech’ (禪禪不用思量卜度，非干文字語言). Yuanwu Keqin asks in the Blue Cliff Record whether the cited matter can be reckoned by affective cognition (以情識卜度得麼). Baoguo Zhao warns the assembly not to conjecture inside cognition because that becomes inverted imagining (莫向意識裏卜度，却成妄想顛倒). Shaoshan Daoxin gives the compact public-interview verdict: ‘if you conjecture, you lose body and life’ (卜度則喪身失命). Zen bends an ordinary term for divinatory estimation into a recurrent name for the mental guessing explicitly rejected at the teaching seat. Yongjue Yuanxian says that conjecturing within discriminating consciousness leaves only a vaguely perceived clod; Shending Yunwai Ze groups conjecture and discursive thought with outward seeking and self-binding. Both confirm the same act of speculative assessment.

Senses.Explanation: Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story. The name occurs 90 times in 52 allowlisted texts. In his Book of Serenity commentary, Wansong Xingxiu retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by telling Touzi Datong, “I bring you the uncut jade and ask you to carve and polish it”; when Touzi Datong refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Danxia Zichun's verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it? … Bian He had knowledge; the king of Chu rejected him” (卞和有智楚王嫌). Zen therefore deploys Bian He as the named bearer of unrecognized jade in answers, student self-comparison, verses, and case commentary. These records, not a general literary biography, define the entry.

Senses.Explanation: The term names the recorded act by Tianyi Yihuai, Nanyue Huairang, and other identified teachers of approving or certifying a person's understanding; the entries keep that act distinct from assigning succession. Literally, "seal" (印) and "approve or permit" (可): "approve and certify," attested 761 times in 173 allowlisted texts. Lamp and lineage records use the verb for recorded acts of approval. After a student opens to understanding at Tianyi Yihuai's assembly, Tianyi "approves him, saying: this is my house's thousand-mile colt" (印可曰，此吾家千里駒也). Another account says Nanyue Huairang approved six room-entering disciples individually and told them, "you six people together verify my body; each accords with one part" (汝等六人，同證吾身，各契其一). Narrative forms include "all received approval" (皆蒙印可) and "received approval" (蒙印可). These passages record approval, the approving teacher's words where preserved, and who received it; they do not make every occurrence a single theory of what was certified.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records load the ordinary printing block into a criticism of sayings and conduct reproduced from fixed models. One record asks, 'what is block-stamped?' and answers: people who grope along walls, have no genuine understanding of their own, and rely entirely on ancient sayings as a staff. Another defines 'printing-block Chan' as reading the records of Yuanwu, Dahui, and Zhongfeng and turning out something resembling them. The widespread paired formula says that teachers or learned sayings are 'stamped from a printing block and released from a mold,' then contrasts this with responding as circumstances arise. The Zen deviation is this printing-shop language for publicly criticized, model-bound Chan speech; the term does not merely mean generic sameness.

Senses.Explanation: This very mind is this very buddha: a recorded saying, question, quoted case, and the first member of a recurring contrast with 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). In the exact wording (即心即佛), the first 'this very' (即) identifies mind, and the second identifies buddha. In the record of Huineng and Fahai, Fahai asks for an explanation of 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛願垂指喻); Huineng answers by pairing 'the preceding thought not arising is this mind' (前念不生即心) with 'the following thought not ceasing is this buddha' (後念不滅即佛), then 'forming every characteristic is this mind' (成一切相即心) with 'leaving every characteristic is this buddha' (離一切相即佛). In Mazu's recorded exchange, when asked why he says it, he answers, 'to stop a small child crying' (為止小兒啼); when asked what happens after the crying stops, he says, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). Damei Fachang is later quoted saying that Mazu told him 'this mind is this buddha' and that, whatever Mazu now says about 'not mind, not buddha,' he retains the former words. Later masters also ask 'How is it when this mind is this buddha?' (即心即佛時如何) and place the phrase beside 'not mind, not buddha' and 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing' (不是心不是佛不是物). Chushi Fanqi pairs the phrase with ‘not mind, not buddha’ before dismissing both with a marketplace saying. Danxia Dangui calls the negative formula a note on the positive one. In Chaozong Tongren's hall, an unnamed monk asks how both can stand and Chaozong tells him to keep running between two ends. These witnesses preserve one quoted formulation while showing three sharply different public deployments.

Senses.Explanation: The formula identifies this very mind with Buddha, yet the records present that identification as an answer, an instruction, and wording whose implications speakers continue to test. Mazu Daoyi answers Damei Fachang’s question “what is Buddha?” with “this very mind is Buddha” (即心是佛). Sikong Benjing pairs seeking Buddha with “this very mind is Buddha” and seeking the way with “no-mind is the way,” then explains that Buddha is awakened through mind and mind is made manifest by Buddha. Huangbo Xiyun says no particle of teaching is obtainable apart from the one mind and immediately states the formula, criticizing a second mind raised upon mind to seek Buddha outside. Daodu describes hearing the phrase, trusting it, and allowing no other direction. In Dahui Zonggao’s retelling, Damei retains “here I have only this very mind is Buddha” against Mazu’s later wording. Dahui himself states “this very mind is Buddha; there is no other Buddha,” reverses it as Buddha being mind, and continues by denying that mind belongs to spatial positions or Buddha to temporal positions. Thus the formula can answer, identify, awaken confidence, and be defended against a competing formulation; its force depends on the speaking turn rather than the bare identity syntax alone.

Senses.Explanation: The Accord of Difference and Sameness is the title of Shitou Xiqian’s verse, identified as a composed work, quoted by its opening and closing lines, and discussed by later masters. The title combines participation or joining , sameness , and accord or tally . In the Chan corpus it is the proper name of Shitou Xiqian's verse. The Transmission of the Lamp says that Shitou wrote it, calls its language deep, and prints the work under his name. Its opening says that the mind of the great Indian immortal is intimately transmitted east and west ; its closing tells the person investigating the mystery to meet the source on hearing words and not waste the daylight . Fayan Wenyi later invokes the title in hall discourse, calls it a piece of wording, and quotes its opening. The Joint Essentials of the Lamps connects Shitou's composition with his reading that the sage has no self and nothing is not himself . Zen bends the phrase into a lineage-specific bibliographic name: these records use it not for a general agreement but for Shitou's transmitted Chan poem and for quotations from that poem.

Senses.Explanation: To visit and question a lineage figure is not merely to ask for information. In these records the headword names the student's entry into a face-to-face encounter: Tanran and Huairang arrive and immediately ask the meaning of the ancestor's coming from the west, while Juzhi answers every visiting student's inquiry by raising one finger. Biographical uses also measure a student's career by whom he consulted, or pointedly say that he asked nobody. The word therefore marks public, answerable contact in which a student exposes his question.

Senses.Explanation: To visit and consult a true teacher is the itinerant act of going to someone able to expose and settle the matter in direct encounter. The Bloodstream Treatise says that one who has not clarified must consult such a person to settle the root of birth and death, while denying the title to anyone who has not seen directly. A lamp address describes itinerants arriving at a community, setting down bowl and flask, and then meeting that person. Later masters include consultation among leaving home, traveling on foot, entering retreat, and raising a saying, but also ask listeners to identify the single present action running through all of them.

Senses.Explanation: To join, attend, or report to the communal hall. Biographical records use the expression for formal admission: people seeking to join the hall might wait for months, while a favored visitor is admitted that same day; Wuzu orders Yuanwu to join the hall immediately, after which Yuanwu enters the attendants' quarters. In encounter records the imperative 'go to the hall' regularly closes or dismisses an exchange. Wuju says it after striking two visitors, and Wenshu Siye shouts it to a former butcher, who then goes down to the hall. In commentary on the rhinoceros-fan case, an unnamed monk tells the entire assembly to go to the hall, and Yuanwu explicitly says that the unnamed monk has seized the authority of the host. The institutional and imperative uses share the same hall-directed action.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names sustained investigation of Chan rather than merely learning information about it. Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that investigating Chan requires an iron person whose mind is decided on taking it up, calls the great matter of life and death its crucial point, and compares its aim of awakening with livelihood's aim of wealth. Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes people who speak of investigating Chan only with their mouths and turn encounter records into conversation material. Xueguan Zhiyin insists on determined effort rather than merely staring toward the school’s signboard. Dahui Zonggao retrospectively calls his own years before breakthrough investigation of Chan; Konggu Daocheng joins it to strenuous personal effort. An unnamed lay questioner asks Yongjue Yuanxian where investigating Chan gains force. Together these uses denote committed inquiry directed toward resolving the great matter, while warning that verbal cleverness does not constitute that inquiry.

Senses.Explanation: To investigate the particular word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out from a recorded exchange. Frozen-corpus concordance: 195 exact hits in 81 storage files representing 81 independent works. Poshan Haiming identifies what remains unresolved in a scripture or public case as one's personally investigated saying. Zhongfeng Mingben supplies the actual question, 'Why did Zhaozhou say the word no?', and directs the listener to investigate that wording and raise great doubt. Zhanran Yuancheng says to investigate one's own selected saying in earnest, while Ruibai Mingxue says to place it before one and keep it continually in mind. Other witnesses explicitly police the action: Zhuanyu Heng criticizes seeking the wording in books and other people's mouths and asks whether those who perform it differ from those who do not; Zongbao Daodu says earlier patriarchs did not teach people to investigate sayings and presents the instruction as a later response to proliferating calculations; Gumei You says not to speculate over public cases or search in scriptures. Zen bends recorded public speech into the selected object of investigation, while the same records challenge where the wording is sought, what the action is taken to accomplish, and whether it should be reified.

Senses.Explanation: A visit to a named instructor or assembly in order to ask questions and request instruction. It occurs 243 times in 121 allowlisted texts and includes both institutional attendance and the encounter itself. Zhicheng leaves Shenxiu, travels to Shaoyang, and "joins the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請); Shuangfeng Gu's biography says that at Shishuang he merely followed the assembly and "no longer visited and inquired" (更不參請). The monastic regulations place "traveling from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請) under a heading that lists departure from one's teacher, seeking a respected elder, requesting lodging, first reporting to the guest office, and next registering at the hall office. Huanyuan Fuyu "bent his knees to visit and inquire" (屈膝參請), after which Lingyin Tai addressed his understanding. Tianning's monastic and lay followers visited and inquired morning and evening while Huqiu Shaolong answered them without weariness (晨夕參請，師與唱酬無倦). The recorded actions are visits, institutional participation, questions, and responses in Chinese Chan texts.
Senses.Note: Productive constructions mark the same range: "join the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請, 27 occurrences), "enter the room to visit and inquire" (入室參請, 2), "travel from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請, 6), and headings for "circumstances of visiting and inquiry" (參請因緣, 2). Fayan can ask what scripture someone reads "apart from visiting and inquiry" (於參請外), placing it among the ordinary activities of a visitor's life. The Blue Cliff Record contrasts a superintendent's not having "visited and inquired or entered the room" (不曾參請入室) with Fayan subsequently asking why he does not come enter the room. The overlap between travel, residence in an assembly, and direct exchange is native to the term, so these are kept as deployments of one sense.

Senses.Explanation: Inquiry must be genuine and awakening must be genuine is a paired Chan demand for actuality on both sides. The surviving deployments oppose verbal or secondhand approximation to personally verified inquiry and awakening. Three independent records preserve the paired demand in admonitory speech. Their surrounding clauses insist that neither talking about inquiry nor claiming awakening substitutes for the real event.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1414.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Liao’an Qingyu (了菴清欲禪師語錄): Exact actor: Liao’an Qingyu. Liao’an Qingyu utters the phrase while adjudicating the complete raised Deshan encounter.

Senses.Explanation: A mouth like a basin of blood is the speech-organ pictured as a huge blood-filled opening, commonly paired with teeth like a forest of swords. Chan records apply the pair to formidable verbal performance, yet repeatedly add that such a mouth can still merely flaunt verbal sharpness or fall short at the decisive exchange. Lan’an Dingxu joins the sword-teeth and blood-basin mouth, then calls their display an empty show of verbal sharpness and force. Tian’an Sheng places the same mouth among the equipment of a clear-eyed person who judges dragons and snakes. Baiyu says that even someone with this mouth and lightning-like activity has not yet smelled the host’s foot-sweat. A questioner asks Dahui Zonggao what happens if such a person refuses Dahui’s answer; Dahui replies that this would show the person has an eye. Yuanwu Keqin uses the pair for true teachers in his own record, while Xutang Zhiyu is publicly asked whether his own saying passes such a mouth. Liao’an Qingyu says that even Deshan’s sword-teeth and blood-basin mouth would retreat before the action in the raised case.

Senses.Explanation: The Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies is the title of a compiled record of earlier masters and their encounters. The title stands on the work’s own volume heading, while later letters, biographies, and textual studies cite it as a book that can be opened, read, purchased, and used as evidence. Mizang Daokai describes an immediate surge on opening it. Hanyue Fazang’s chronology reports that he sought out its volumes and wept over awakening encounters and exchanges between teachers and students. A Complete Five Lamps biography says Yelü Chucai repeatedly brought material learned from it to Sheng’an Cheng. Zen bends no individual word inside this title; its distinctive work is documentary. The collection carries attributed voices into later encounters, where readers cite, test, contest, and reuse them.

Senses.Explanation: In public questioning, this formula pivots from the point just discussed to a particular countercase: ‘as for this case, what then?’ Literally, "just as for" . Across Chan discourse and case commentary it is a grammatical pivot: the construction provisionally leaves the preceding statement in place, selects a concrete case or condition, and reopens questioning. Yuanwu moves from a claim about a world that is entirely a diamond eye to "just as for... how do you observe it?" , and elsewhere from passing beyond form and sound to "just as for... how is a message conveyed?" . Lamp commentary uses it to press whether Vajra-Equality saw the obstructing demon king, to turn from a general claim to Mazu's exact words, and even to compare the issue with having eaten and walking down the east or west corridor. The imperial birthday addresses likewise move from ceremonial description to "just as for the people of the Way in the forest... how is the line raised?" . There is no special lexical departure from the ordinary connective; its Chan value is the repeatedly attested dialogue structure of concession or setup followed by a pointed case-question.

Senses.Explanation: One can know propriety is a line from a traditional primer sequence that Chan speakers quote, splice, and deploy as an interview reply or learned-speech cap. Its literal claim concerns recognizing proper conduct; its corpus job comes from the exact exchange or recitation around it. Jianfu Chenggu performs a mock qin gesture and recites the primer chain through 'one can know propriety.' Chushi Fanqi inserts the phrase between the two halves of Shakyamuni's birth declaration. Jinian Jingxian glosses a verse line by line with the primer and ends on the phrase. Dahui Zonggao recites it after classical and primer lines, then asks how Baofeng compares with Confucius and caps the address with a line about speaking poetry to one who understands. These are observable reuses of school wording, not a hidden technical definition.

Senses.Explanation: A conforming or pat phrase: an answer that fits a ready verbal pattern. Frozen-corpus concordance: 143 exact hits in 96 storage files representing 93 independent works. Its defining proverb says, ‘One conforming phrase ties up a donkey for ten thousand ages.’ Yuanwu Keqin uses the label as an immediate verdict on an answer and warns, ‘Take care against conforming phrases.’ Yunwai Ze lists stock replies—including ‘when the sky is clear the sun comes out’ and ‘when it rains the ground is wet’—as dead sayings delivered as conforming phrases; elsewhere he describes people using such phrases when questioned. Yuanwu says his own teaching seat does not make conforming phrases or look-alike phrases. Later commentary can dispute the verdict: Yushan Shangsi says that treating Yunmen Wenyan’s ‘the body exposed in the golden wind’ as a conforming phrase fails to recognize it.

Senses.Explanation: To live and die together is to share the same exposure in a Chan encounter: the exact named speaker calls for someone who will stand with him through the case rather than remain a spectator. Dahui Zonggao asks whether anyone will live and die together with him, then calls that person out to meet his staff. Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise asks for a patch-robed monk who will do so after raising Fengxue’s opposed alternatives. These are public challenges, not descriptions of two people sharing dates of birth and death. Yuanwu Keqin applies the phrase to the cited named speaker who enters the same cauldron and furnace as the person being freed, and elsewhere to going through the fire sermon with the buddhas of the three times. Yunwai Xingze uses it in a memorial address but immediately refuses to let the phrase pass without a further test. An unnamed monk asks Fushan Dexuan directly what living and dying together is; Fushan turns the question back on whether the explicit unnamed questioner may be called Buddha. The sources repeatedly mark shared exposure, accompaniment, or matched commitment under a live test. They do not make the phrase a promise of literal simultaneous death, nor do they supply one abstract theory behind every case.

Senses.Explanation: Sticking out the tongue is a narrated bodily response of surprise, acknowledgement, or reaction within an encounter. The Chan record repeatedly makes this visible gesture part of public encounters, but does not give it one invariant emotional gloss. Huangbo involuntarily sticks out his tongue (不覺吐舌, “without realizing it, stuck out his tongue”) on hearing that Baizhang was deaf for three days after Mazu's shout. Elsewhere a visitor sticks out his tongue and says, “truly a dragon-elephant”; an unnamed monastic leaves with his tongue out after a rebuke; and a later monk says that Huangbo Xiyun's gesture shows he has been caught out. Masters also deliberately use the action as an answer: Nanyuan sticks out his tongue when asked for “one word,” and Zhongqing opens his mouth and sticks out his tongue when asked what his appearance as abbot is for. Thus the ordinary bodily gesture is bent into an answer or demonstrative act in the teaching hall as well as remaining a recorded reaction; the texts themselves decide its local force, and this entry does not assign one motive to every occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a singular “road upward” repeatedly posed as beyond transmitted formulas. Panshan Baoji places it after both mind-is-Buddha and not-mind-not-Buddha and says the thousand sages do not transmit it, while students exhaust themselves like apes grasping reflections. An unnamed monk asks Dongyan Kexiu what the road is, and Dongyan answers by raising his robe collar. Ciming Chuyuan's variation says the thousand sages do not make it so. Other unnamed monks ask Xuedou Daorong, Bianlong, and Foyan Qingyuan about the road and receive sharply different replies: numerical nonsense, “beneath your feet,” and a refusal to frame it as upward or downward. The stable lexical item is the challenged road; the divergent answers prevent converting it into one explanatory teaching. Juelang Daosheng later distinguishes the road as separately honored after a three-sentence classification, adding an institutional deployment rather than another copy of Panshan’s line.

Senses.Explanation: Toward or facing (向), above or further up (上), and matter or affair (事): the further matter beyond what has already been reached or named. It runs in a recurrent dialogue. A monk asks whether there is still an upward matter (向上還有事也無／還有向上事也無); the respondent says yes; the monk asks, 'What is the upward matter?' (如何是向上事); and the respondent gives an answer such as 'break the mirror and come; I will meet you' (打破鏡來，與汝相見), 'a person from Silla does not wrap his head' (新羅人不褁頭), or 'downward the text runs long' (向下文長). It also appears in 'knows that there is an upward matter' (知有向上事, 72 occurrences) and its negation. One line says that Xuefeng had words only after he knew there was an upward matter (雪峯知有向上事始有語話分). The expression can be dismissed with 'What upward matter are you talking about?' (說甚麼向上事). The corpus also attaches 'upward' to named limits: 'the matter upward from buddha' (佛向上事, 169 occurrences) and 'upward from Vairocana' (毘盧向上). It is paired with 'the last word' (末後句) in the statement that one must also know the upward matter and the last word (更須知有向上事末後句始得). Related forms include 'the upward road' (向上一路, 1,082), 'the upward move' (向上一著, 303), 'the upward aperture' (向上一竅, 292), 'the upward pivot' (向上關捩子, 62), 'the upward person' (向上人, 253), and 'the upward vehicle of the lineage' (向上宗乘, 491). Yuanwu Keqin states directly that an upward person must know the upward matter, providing an independent own-record witness for the same relational formulation. In a case later raised by Yunmen Wenyan, Dongshan Liangjie says one must know the matter beyond buddha, and an unnamed monk separately asks what that matter is.

Senses.Explanation: The further mechanism (向上機) prevents an answer—or even the claim to have gone beyond answers—from becoming a final resting place. Tonghui Gui contrasts an initial mechanism with a further mechanism not yet trodden, making 'beyond' another public test rather than a hidden teaching. Mingjue Cong and Zhean Jingfan display it through ordinary sounds, actions, and conduct, so it is not confined to an abstract formula. Yuanwu Keqin calls its expanded form 'raising a sound to stop an echo'; Pin Jixiang calls it a rotten hemp rope; Panshan Liaozong says that even blocking passage between ordinary and sacred is still not it. The records deploy the term and then turn it against anyone who settles on the term.

Senses.Explanation: In Caodong technical discourse, lord and minister name a relational configuration used to explain upright and inclined positions and their interaction. Caoshan Benji maps lord to the upright position and minister to the inclined, then names minister-facing-lord, lord-regarding-minister, and lord-and-minister accord. A later Caoshan quotation repeats that mapping. Juelang Daosheng equates arriving within both with lord and minister according. Yinqian identifies the Caodong house through their accord. Langting Ting disputes the later classification of Caoshan's answers as five lord-and-minister positions. Shixi Xinyue sets the five positions beside Linji's three mysteries and three essentials. Shaoyuan says the five positions are all penetrated when host and guest accord. These uses establish a technical relational family while preserving disagreement about its historical systematization.

Senses.Explanation: Minshu raises Lü Dongbin as the sword-bearing immortal who tries to strike Huanglong with a flying sword but is instead transformed and awakened by him; Minshu then quotes Lü abandoning his gourd and lute, no longer refining mercury into gold, and recognizing that his earlier effort was wasted after seeing Huanglong. Xisou Shaotan titles a verse ‘Lü Dongbin meets Huanglong,’ says that even long life finally decays, and describes Huanglong as covering or protecting Lü. Wuwen Daocan says that Lü walks freely only after personally seeing Huanglong. These three named speakers make Lü Huanglong's immortal visitor in this dictionary. Wumen Huikai's portrait names sword-bearing Lü Dongbin, has him bare the blade and wield commands of killing and giving life, and ends by naming him the True Person Pure Yang. At a formal installation, Yunshan Yanju Shen strikes his staff and says that he breaks Lü Dongbin's elixir cauldron to pieces. Qiaoyin Wuyi's portrait retains Lü's Daoist clothing, boxed sword, Penglai setting, and wine. These named raisers and portrait writers define the Zen figure through the Huanglong encounter and its later sword, longevity, cauldron, clothing, and changed-bearing scenes, not through an imported immortal's biography or a single inferred lesson.

Senses.Explanation: To revile buddhas and curse patriarchs is a named act of verbal attack on the tradition’s highest figures; records use it as conduct, answer, prediction, appraisal, and self-description. Yangqi Fanghui uses a close rebuke-graph variant in a hall saying. Zhenjing Kewen applies the exact expression to Deshan; Yulin Tongxiu imagines withdrawing to a solitary peak to do it; and Guishan Lingyou predicts that Deshan will live on a solitary peak and do it. Later public questions receive it as an answer, Baoning Renyong includes it among acts that make a great buddha-work, and Zhenjing both questions what fault lies in Deshan’s conduct and says he himself will go do it. Approval, criticism, prediction, and quotation change stance, not the named act.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 適來哭，如今為甚却笑？師云：適來哭，如今笑
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Essential Compendium of the United Lamp (聯燈會要): Baizhang Huaihai. The full-case proof distinguishes this actor from nearby respondents, questioners, and section subjects.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 適來哭，如今為甚却笑？師云：適來哭，如今笑

Senses.Explanation: An audible ‘ha-ha’ laugh is assigned to the person who laughs, often closing or turning a public encounter. It is sometimes followed by speech and sometimes serves as the whole turn. The exact phrase occurs 1,829 times in 305 files representing 300 independent works. The records preserve its range without assigning one fixed motive to it. Baizhang Huaihai laughs after a colleague asks why he had just cried and answers only, “Earlier I cried; now I laugh” . Zhaozhou Congshen laughs during an exchange and then repeats Hanshan's cry, “Heaven! Heaven!” . Jinniu Heshang dances with the rice tub, laughs loudly, and calls the assembly to eat . After an unnamed member of Baizhang's assembly reports returning to eat when he heard the meal drum, Baizhang laughs. Xiangshan Yunliang laughs after a pause and asks, “Laugh at what?” . Yuanwu Keqin laughs and then calls his own address speech about a dream where there is no dream and an affair where none exists. Dahui Zonggao laughs after an unnamed questioner answers by saying farewell and immediately tests the next entrant about that response. Zen preserves the laugh as a public-interview speaker-turn and teaching-seat action rather than reducing it to an editorial report about emotion.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 汝向枝上斫。其能斷命根乎。
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X80/X80n1565.xml). Five Lamps Compendium (五燈會元): Dahui Zonggao owns the exact headword-related wording quoted in this entry.

Senses.Explanation: The life-root is something cut off or held fast in encounter language, while a separate technical use names the vital faculty among listed faculties. A life-root is the hold that Chan records locate and describe as cut, broken, or gathered up. The phrase occurs 829 times in 226 allowlisted texts. Luyuan spreads his hand and says that the life-roots of all the old masters and senior monks are 'all here' (天下老和尚．諸上座命根。總在這裏). Jiaozhong Huian Miguang supplies the corpus's clearest physical comparison: one cut at a tree's root severs its life-root, whereas chopping its branches does not (如人斫樹，根下一刀，則命根斷矣。汝向枝上斫，其能斷命根乎). Ying'an Tanhua's record says that when a blind was rolled up, 'the lacquer bucket broke open and the life-root snapped on the spot' (豁然漆桶破，命根嚗地斷). Wuyi Yuanlai postpones speech until the questioner's own life-root is severed (待闍黎命根斷即道). These predicates make the life-root a locatable and severable Chan expression, distinct from the enumerated vital faculty in the second sense; the entry makes no claim about an inward meaning beyond those recorded predicates.

Senses.Note: This sense is included because it is attested within the allowlisted record, not because a Buddhist glossary controls the Chan sense.
