Senses.Explanation: To receive it is to take a handed object into one's possession, often followed immediately by an action that answers the handover. Linji receives Longya's Chan board and strikes him; Manjusri receives Sudhana's sprig and displays it; Luopu receives a letter and sits without opening it. Guizong puts the received mud to use, and Xuefeng receives a bowl only to throw out its water. A ceremonial document, Xuefeng's carved wooden snake, and Hongzhi's robe confirm the same concrete transfer outside those recensions. Zen bends this ordinary result-verb through timing: the records attend to what the recipient does at the instant the object arrives.

Senses.Explanation: To cover one's ears while stealing a bell is to hide from oneself the noise that exposes one's own act. Muzhou Daoming says a pious-sounding account resembles covering the ears while stealing a bell. Yuan'an Feng joins it to 'clutching the stolen goods and crying injustice'; Hanyue Fazang calls his interlocutor an ear-covering bell thief and then strikes him. Yuanjie Ying forbids the move, while Konggu Daocheng applies it to people who imagine they have deceived others. Chan usage preserves the self-defeating concealment: the attempted evasion itself advertises what the named critic exposes.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X79/X79n1557.xml). Linked Lamps Compendium: Yunmen Wenyan raises Mazu Daoyi’s formula, praises it, and invites a question; an unnamed monk asks for the Deva school and Yunmen answers by ranking him last among the ninety-six kinds.

Senses.Explanation: The Deva school is a named Chan case-formula: masters ask what it is, answer with a turning word, or invoke Mazu Daoyi’s claim that every verbal expression belongs to it. It is not a historical survey label for an externalist sect. In Baling Haojian’s case an unnamed monk asks, “What is the Deva school?” and Baling answers, “Snow heaped in a silver bowl.” Yuanwu Keqin says people commonly mistake this for an externalist school and rejects that reading outright. Other case collections preserve the exchange among Baling’s three turning words and build verses on the answer. A second recurrent deployment raises Mazu Daoyi’s declaration, “Every verbal expression is the Deva school; take this as principal.” Jieyun Ju tests the declaration with his staff. Yunmen Wenyan praises it, invites the question, then answers the unnamed monk by placing him last among the ninety-six kinds. These are live case deployments of the same named school-formula, not descriptions of two institutions. The sources license the translation “Deva school” and show how the label is wielded. They do not license replacing Baling’s or Mazu’s words with a fixed teaching, and Yuanwu expressly blocks the externalist-sect gloss.

Senses.Explanation: To take up the lineage's matter and keep it actively before an assembly. Its recurrent objects are “this matter,” the ancestral seal, the school's essentials, the Buddha teaching, an upward move, or the authoritative command; the action is performed in addresses, case comment, and face-to-face presentation rather than describing private possession. Wuwen Can says that he came two thousand leagues to reside at a monastery solely to sustain this matter, then raises the whisk and says, “Look! Look!” Yuanwu Keqin pairs carrying the school with upholding the ancestral seal and says the ancients entered deep mountains to sustain the school's essentials. Baiyu Jingsi describes Mazu Daoyi's sickbed answer as an all-out presentation for others. Zhean Jingfan criticizes how the ancients handled the seventeen hundred cases, while Feiyin Tongrong raises his staff and presents one move face to face. Jiguang Huo contrasts upholding the authoritative command and blocking the vital crossing with following the waves and setting up guest and host. Hongzhi Zhengjue describes both participants in an exchange as each putting out a hand and bringing up the matter. Dahui Zonggao uses the verb both critically, for going once through an old saying and calling that freedom from words, and instructively, for bringing something up from time to time and amid walking, sitting, emotion, and responsive dealings. The Zen bend is the interpersonal and case-facing use: this ordinary act of calling attention becomes something done in the interview, received by Foyan Qingyuan from his late teacher, or repeatedly directed at a recorded saying, without naming a separate regimen.

Senses.Explanation: To have one’s eyes swapped out is a repeated warning that words, texts, sounds, or another person’s formulation can replace how one sees. Literally, "swap out the eyes" . In ordinary wording this would name a bodily exchange; Chan records use it as an accusation that a saying, written formulation, sight, sound, or teacher has displaced a person's own seeing. Miaoyun’s commentary says that the unnamed questioner who asks Xuansha about his own self has his eyes swapped out by Xuansha’s reply. Shiyu says altered wording and changed characters swap out people's eyes, and elsewhere says waterbirds, groves, bells, and gongs do it. Sanyi warns against letting the writing brush exchange black beans for one's eyes , then identifies bird-script, dragon-writing, paper, ink, and written characters as fit for ordinary circulation rather than Chan discussion. A case comment even judges the words "Where is the eminent monk?" themselves to have plainly swapped out the eyes. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore an adversarial verdict about seeing being commandeered; the texts apply it to both words and sensory displays, not to literal surgery.

Senses.Explanation: To cast aside cause and effect is a named and condemned error: treating conduct and consequence as though they can simply be denied. The Record of Gu Xue Zhe says that misconstruing the ancients’ situation-matched talk can lead people to cast aside cause and effect and invite calamity. The Record of Gu Ting places the error after laziness gives rise to wild thoughts, and the Complete Record of Juelang asks how cause and effect could be cast aside when speaking of individual and shared karma. Dahui’s formal discourse likewise warns that hearing emptiness and then denying cause and effect is an error. The two stored expression-by-negation controls define expression by negation but do not themselves contain the no-cause-and-no-effect formula; they therefore mark a comparison that must be made from exact speech frames, not a license to equate every negative formula with causal denial.

Senses.Explanation: The expression “part the grass and watch the wind” (撥草瞻風) combines movement through grass with observing the wind; Chan records use it for travelling seekers arriving to inspect a host’s manner and ask a question. Retained encounters introduce a visiting monk as having “parted the grass and watched the wind” before he requests instruction or meets the host. In addresses the phrase also names the approach of people coming from elsewhere. Grass and wind remain the visible travel image; the recurrent arrival-and-inquiry frame supplies the Chan-specific usage.

Senses.Explanation: Clapping the hands is a narrated audible gesture, often paired with laughter or used to close a comment. The gesture occurs 880 times in 253 files representing 249 independent works, commonly as a visible turn in a public exchange. It may stand alone (‘clapped three times’), accompany departure, a shout, or a blow, or join laughter: ‘clapped his hands and laughed loudly’ occurs 114 times in 69 files representing 67 works. The record does not assign one fixed attitude to it. Yangqi Fanghui claps and laughs before saying an answer is ‘not worth half a cent’; an unnamed monk claps once after shouting; Xiyuan claps three times when asked why he bathes without an attendant. Caoshan later explicitly calls the action ‘hand-clapping’ and distinguishes Xiyuan’s use from the same physical action elsewhere. In the Shuilao case, Shuilao rises after Mazu kicks him, claps and laughs, and speaks; later records repeatedly cite that sequence. Zen bends an ordinary gesture by making it an answer, rejoinder, appraisal, or recorded public-interview move, while the surrounding words—not the gesture alone—establish whether a given occurrence is laughter, challenge, celebration, or dismissal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 水中擇乳須是鵝王
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2004.xml). Book of Serenity: Wansong Xingxiu says that selecting milk from water requires the goose king, using the image for the exacting work of distinguishing the participants’ handling of a case.

Senses.Explanation: To select the milk is to distinguish what matters within a mixture whose parts are not obvious at a glance. Chan masters make it the goose king’s capacity: unlike ducks, it selects milk from water, and the image becomes a verdict on whether someone can tell the live point of an encounter from its similar-looking alternatives. Wansong Xingxiu states the image most explicitly: selecting milk from water requires the goose king. He applies it to the fine discrimination needed to read how the participants handle a case. Guishan Lingyou calls Yangshan’s raised ear of grain “the goose king selecting milk” after Yangshan refuses a choice among green, yellow, and neither. The act distinguishes the point without accepting the offered alternatives. Dahui repeatedly uses the formula as a verdict. He applies it to Yangshan’s apparently contradictory statements about awakening, to two identical-looking offerings treated differently, and to the precise shortfall in Baofu’s answer. The goose-versus-duck contrast does not make the phrase a claim about birds or a general compliment for intelligence. In these records it names discrimination demonstrated in a concrete exchange, and Dahui adds that it requires seeing with one’s own eyes.

Senses.Explanation: To hit the bench or platform-seat used during an address to the assembly. The strike is public teaching-hall conduct, not merely damage to furniture: it often supplies the last percussive event before leaving the seat, but it can also become a turn in an exchange. Yuanwu Keqin raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, then strikes the teaching seat and asks again. Foyin Qing makes the contrast explicit by asking whether they see the raised whisk and whether they hear the struck seat. Dahui Zonggao labels the raised whisk “form” and the seat-strike “sound.” Shishuang Chuyuan strikes once with his staff, asks whether the assembly understands, and cites the line “one strike, and what was known was forgotten.” Dayu Shouzhi answers a six-rung-reviewed unnamed questioner's question about buddha by striking once and saying it has already been forgotten. Songyuan Chongyue strikes once with the whisk and asks whether his listeners feel pain or an itch. The omitted or named instrument and the various questions change the deployment, not the physical action. The phrase has 686 matches in 141 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: In ordinary usage, ‘capture and release’ is a commander’s battlefield tactic: take the opponent, then let him go at will. Chan speakers bend that command pair toward control of an encounter, repeatedly coordinating it with rolling out and folding up or killing and giving life. That command register is the word's Zen bend. Literally, 'capture and release': 'capture' (擒) paired with 'let loose or release' (縱). The compound occurs 124 times in 82 files representing 81 independent works. Its most frequent fixed relations are 'capture and release, kill and bring to life' (擒縱殺活, 20 occurrences) and 'roll out and fold up, capture and release' (卷舒擒縱, 13 hits in 10 files representing 10 works). Yuanwu also records the reversed framing 'release and gather, capture and release' (放收擒縱) and says, 'capture and release are not another's; rolling out and folding up are with me' (擒縱非他。卷舒在我). In an assembly address he writes that only afterward does one 'release and gather, capture and release, and obtain great freedom' (放收擒縱得大解脫). Another address says, 'within killing there is bringing to life, capturing and releasing humans and gods; within bringing to life there is killing, weighing buddhas and ancestors' (殺中有活擒縱人天。活中有殺權衡佛祖). His Essentials states: 'able to capture and release, skilled in killing and bringing to life—great teachers do not fail to use these' (能擒縱，善殺活，得大解脫，知識無不用之). Later commemorative prose similarly says 'capture and release, killing and bringing to life, are all complete' (擒縱殺活皆全). The corpus thus deploys the pair as the cited speaker's coordinated command of the encounter, commonly placed in four-part action strings.

Senses.Explanation: A comic epithet for a one-sided person: a fellow carrying a board and seeing only one side. The stock line says that Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side, while Baiyu Jingsi states directly that each party sees one side and is precisely a board-carrying fellow (各見一邊，正是擔板漢). In a case Baiyu raises, Muezhou Daozong calls to an addressee and applies the name when the man turns; Xuedou Chongxian and Huanglong Huinan then debate its application, and Baiyu judges their opposed comments one-sided. The label extends beyond that case. Dongshan Meixi Du says that learning without awakening is overbearing pride, whereas awakening without learning is a board-carrying fellow (有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢). Zhe'an Jingfan applies it both to delight at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket, and elsewhere says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients only makes such a fellow before asking how the matter can be raised whole (只成擔板漢，此事如何舉得全). Yuanwu Keqin says that a board-carrying fellow often dies in the phrase (若是擔板漢，多向句中死却). Zen bends a comic physical image into a public epithet for the person whom a record presents as fixed on one side or trapped in wording; the entry reports those attested applications without generalizing beyond them.

Senses.Explanation: To carry the cangue and submit one’s own indictment is to incriminate oneself by the very answer or claim offered in defense. Senses.Explanation: To assume and bear responsibility, especially for the teaching or its succession. Yuanwu Keqin places successful shouldering beside accepting, heading toward, and carrying out; elsewhere he says only Shenguang was permitted to bear the subtle key of Shaolin. Guangzhi Quanwu calls for someone able to shoulder it with the whole body, and Xueqiao Yuanxin calls a person with strength to come forward and bear it on one shoulder. Jiufeng Daoqian explicitly defines inward accepting and shouldering as inner succession, then contrasts it with the person who has no accepting and no shouldering. These responsibility, authority, and succession frames make the omitted load institutional and figurative. They are a different referent from physically carrying cargo, even though the metaphor retains the bodily image.

SearchAliases: carry snow to fill a well
Senses.Explanation: Carrying snow to fill a well is a recurrent comparison for ineffective effort, applied to talk, question-and-answer, sitting Chan, and other undertakings. Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" : the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" , to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" , and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" . Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball . Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

Senses.Explanation: To aim the mind is to set it toward an anticipated understanding or result. Chan records warn that aiming can miss, but they also bind the alternatives: Huangbo Xiyun says aimed mind, non-aimed mind, and neither-non-aimed mind can each become a binding demon. The term therefore does not command thought suppression. Across 6 independent works, the stored clauses preserve the headword in complete local sentences rather than as an unanchored quotation. Zen uses the instant of forming an intention as the point at which immediacy is already missed; the warning concerns the movement as it starts. The gloss stays at the level supported by those deployments; it does not import a fixed religious resolution from outside the corpus.

SearchAliases: frame it in mind and miss
Senses.Explanation: The phrase “Frame it in mind and already miss” is paired with stirring thought, then corrected against inert nonmovement in repeated hall statements and interviews. Literally, "frame it in mind and already be off" . Chan records make this a compact warning and an answer: Huangbo places it after saying that mind is not to be sought with mind; another record answers "What is buddha?" with "frame it in mind and already miss; use mind and already go astray" . The fixed expansion "frame it in mind and already miss; stir a thought and already go astray" is also tested rather than left as a slogan. Two Dong'an notices add that neither framing nor stirring leaves one "working for a livelihood in dead water" , while neither framing nor stirring makes one no different from wood and clay . Fayyi answers a student's quotation of the formula by asking why someone who is always framing does not miss, and then calls the student's next move "already a miss" . Thus the Chan deviation is observable in the records' refusal to let either side—deliberation or inert non-deliberation—serve as the definition.

Senses.Note: In the Extended Record of Yongjue Yuanxian, Yongjue quotes "gathering the mind is called restraint" (攝心名戒), then challenges it point by point: "what thing is mind that it can be gathered? What thing is gathering that it can gather mind? Water does not wash water" (心是何物而可攝？攝又是何物而可攝心？水不洗水). Yongming Yanshou's Source-Mirror Record states that before reaching its stated gate, "saying right makes wrong; gathering the mind is still an error" (說是成非，攝心猶錯). Shiwu Qinggong's community verse retains the ordinary finite action by listing chanting and "gathering the mind to drive off sleep" (攝心除睡). Counted forms include "gathering the mind is called restraint" (攝心名戒, two occurrences in two texts), "gather the mind to drive off sleep" (攝心除睡, two in two), "the way of gathering the mind" (攝心之法, one), "place of gathering the mind" (攝心處, one), and "gather the mind and illuminate within" (攝心內照, three in three). The entry records the action and the texts' own challenges without resolving those challenges into an external system.

Senses.Explanation: Gathering the mind is the proposed finite action of collecting, drawing in, or holding in the mind. Chan records both give that action concrete work and challenge whether the wording has any stable basis: the tension belongs in the definition rather than being resolved into a system. The phrase occurs 137 times in 71 allowlisted texts. Asked to ‘show the way of gathering the mind’ (示攝心之法), Chaozong Tongren answers, ‘sit still for one stick of incense’ (靜坐一爐香), but immediately calls this ‘a fine saying’ and warns that it must not be misunderstood (好箇話頭，只是不得錯會). In a separate verse requested on the term, Chaozong says, ‘the myriad things are brightly clear—what thought and what consideration? If you intend to gather the mind, there is no basis to rely on. I now write these words for you; just this is the place of gathering the mind’ (萬法朗然，何思何慮？擬欲攝心，無本可據……只此便是攝心處).

Senses.Explanation: To drop the butcher’s knife names Guang’e’s decisive action in the Nirvana-assembly case, immediately followed by his claim to stand among the thousand buddhas. Chan masters repeatedly raise that action while disagreeing about what may be claimed from it. Dahui Zonggao presents the knife-dropping as an abrupt turn and contrasts it with manufactured quiet. Baichi Xingyuan answers a direct question about the formula by saying an iron man is required. Hanxiu Qian asks what Guang’e saw when he dropped the knife. Juelang Daosheng prescribes thirty blows when a layman asks how to reproduce Guang’e’s act, and refuses the bare declaration “I am Buddha.” Chushi Fanqi calls the famous claim already inept. The stable referent is the public case action; approval is not stable. The phrase is not generalized into “ceasing violence causes awakening.” These witnesses invoke one butcher case and openly conflict over its force, so the entry records the turn without supplying a moral mechanism or automatic result.

Senses.Explanation: An imperative: 'put it down' or 'set it down,' with the final graph marking the command. The records use it for things held in the hands and for what a questioner says cannot be brought. When an unnamed monk raises his sitting cloth and asks for an answer, the named record subject says, 'Put it down,' then says 'withdraw' when the unnamed monk starts to spread it. In the Yan Yang–Zhaozhou case, Yan Yang asks what to do when not one thing is brought; Zhaozhou says, 'Put it down.' When Yan Yang asks what there is to put down, Zhaozhou replies, 'If you cannot put it down, carry it away.' A second recorded exchange has Shakyamuni tell the Black-Clan Brahmin three times to put things down: first each flower, then, after both hands are empty, the six external objects, six internal faculties, and six intervening discriminations. Another exchange draws the text's own contrast: scattered thoughts are answered with 'put it down,' while not producing a single thought is answered with 'raise it up.' The phrase is an instruction within these specific exchanges; the entry preserves the imperative and its stated objects.

Senses.Explanation: In a public encounter, to open the way and allow movement instead of blocking or holding fast. The recurrent contrast is with “hold fast” or “hold in place,” and the records make the difference visible through their own images. Tianzhang Yuanshan says that holding fast freezes dripping water and stops the rivers, while releasing brings warm sun, mild wind, and mountains and streams competing in beauty; he then asks which is good. Xuedou Chongxian says that under release rubble shines, while under restraint true gold loses color. Yinyuan Longqi opens a cloth bag, opens one road of release, and lets the assembly jump east and west before asking which is release and which is restraint. Tiantong Hongjue Min is asked for “a releasing saying” after the restraining side is set aside; he answers, “open in all directions.” Yuanwu Keqin asks whether releasing for people or holding them fast is good. Wumen Huikai says that holding fast and releasing each puts out one hand to raise the ancestral vehicle. Yongjue Yuanxian contrasts Boshan Wuyi, who only knew how to hold fast, with his own release on that day. The phrase has 1,169 occurrences in 247 files representing 242 independent works.

Senses.Explanation: To let one move pass is to allow or overlook one move in an encounter; Chan speakers repeatedly pair that allowance with falling into second place, turning game-like judgment into a compact public verdict. Zhongfeng Mingben uses the phrase plainly when he declines to press a visitor's offense. Yulin Tongxiu and Miyun Yuanwu give the fixed pair, while Poshan Haiming and Feiyin Tongrong quote it and immediately ask how the one is to be raised. The formula is a verdict rather than an automatic final answer. Juelang Daosheng allows the wind-and-banner line one move but assigns thirty blows to the mind-moving line; Miyun's separate addresses repeatedly turn the pair back into a question to the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: A warning that yielding a single move already leaves one in the secondary position. It functions as an inherited Qianfeng maxim and as a line later masters quote, recast, and interrogate. Zhenjing Kewen states the maxim at the opening of Mazu’s memorial hall. Miyun Yuanwu uses it to close his appraisal of the Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra episode. Yuezhou Qianfeng gives the inherited formula in a public address, after which Yunmen answers with a deliberately indirect travel report. Baichi Xingyuan quotes Miyun’s challenge about what it would mean to raise the first rather than fall into the second.

Senses.Explanation: To imitate the frown is to copy another person’s manner, with the famous beauty Xishi supplying the named original in one Zen reply. Yongjue Yuanxian says directly, “imitating the frown is not Xishi.” Other masters call their own verse or whisk demonstration the copied-frown expression, sometimes modestly and sometimes critically; the word therefore ranges from self-described imitation to a rebuke that the copy is not the original person.

Senses.Explanation: An exposed failure is a defect made visible in an answer, exchange, action, or speaker's handling of a case. In Chinese Chan records the compound is a recurrent verdict of failure on an exchange, statement, answer, or speaker. The allowlisted corpus has 594 hits in 193 texts. It records the constructions 'incur a failure' (納敗闕, 154 hits in 92 texts), 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕, 155 hits in 96 texts), and 'the place of the failure' (敗闕處, 47 hits in 32 texts). In one direct exchange an unnamed questioner asks, 'What failure do I have?' and receives the answer 'Wrong.' Elsewhere Dahui quotes Linji calling an old man's response 'a failure today,' then answers the question 'Where is his failure?' with 'The road is far and the night is long; stop carrying a torch, everyone, and blow it out while walking in the dark.' Yuan Cheng is asked how to have no failure and replies, 'Eat three meals.' A later comment can apply the verdict to both parties while also calling both adept: 'As failures, both are failures; as adepts, both are adepts.' These records leave the verdict attached to the cited exchange rather than supplying one universal defect that the word always names.
Senses.Note: The word carries a military register: 'rout' (敗) plus 'breach' (闕) becomes a verdict that an exchange has failed, as in 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕) and 'incur a failure' (納敗闕). All seven required definition formulas were searched; none produced a lexical definition. The entry therefore foregrounds the direct 'what failure?' exchange, the 'where is the failure?' retrospective, verdict uses, and the corpus's own two-party contrast. The rare 'no failure' construction (無敗闕) has one hit in one text. Exact actors are named on every retained occurrence except the source-anonymous questioning monk, whose reviewed exception record preserves all six attribution rungs.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this phrase as a lineage charter, a recurring interview question, and an object of explicit qualification about what “outside” and “separate” do not mean. The flower case places it beside not setting up words and entrustment to Mahakasyapa. Yuanwu repeats it in the four-part banner, while Yunmen asks why it is asserted when the canon is hardly wordless. Unnamed monastics ask Gushan and Shishuang what the transmitted matter or phrase is. Zhongfeng Mingben distinguishes speech and writing from what is separately transmitted, calls the latter Chan and another name for the one mind, and elsewhere denies that it is some additional teaching outside mind. The corpus thus supplies a transmission claim, not a warrant to erase its recorded verbal uses.

Senses.Explanation: A verdict that a supposedly hidden condition has already disclosed its distinctive pattern or signs. Speakers use it to expose traces in concealment, speech, writing, or an attempted challenge. Zhenjing Kewen answers “what about a turtle withdrawing its six limbs?” by saying that the pattern is already manifest. An unnamed monk tells the responding master that his verbal fall is unavoidable because the signs are already showing. Zhaozhou Congshen compares the national teacher’s repeated calls to writing in darkness: the characters do not form, yet their pattern is already evident. Mingzhao Deqian says that Xuansha’s three sheets of white paper cannot prevent the pattern from already showing. Yuanwu Keqin says that when cloud ribbons open and jade tablets unfold, their pattern is already manifest and should be recognized.

Senses.Explanation: To appraise and distinguish is to test, sort, or discriminate people, responses, or stated teaching positions. To appraise, sort out, or distinguish; noun constructions name the resulting appraisal or classificatory distinction. The term is attested 266 times in 126 allowlisted texts. Nanyue Jiqi Hongchu's unnamed questioner sets two episodes side by side and asks Nanyue to “please appraise and distinguish” them (兩段不同，試請料揀); Wuyi Yuanlai asks who can sort out a presented conjunction. The same appraisal vocabulary appears in Linji's “Four Selections” (四料揀). The Eye of Humans and Gods records Nanyuan Huiyong asking Fengxue Yanzhao, “the Four Selections—what do the selections select?” (四料揀，料揀何法), and compiler Huiyan Zhizhao begins another exposition with people of middle and lower capacity under that heading. Zhanran Yuancheng calls paired evaluative formulas “the old so-called selection sayings” (古所謂料揀語). The public act, resulting distinction, and named set remain one appraisal-and-selection family; noun and verb grammar alone do not create different lexical things.

Senses.Explanation: The parent image names verbal entanglement in Chan records, but this exact compound is very thin and occurs only in late framing prose. Gao Shitai's prefatory verse praises the record owner for effacing forms and cutting vine-tangle; a preface says that Linji's staff and shout cut all vine-tangle; a biographical preface pairs cutting vine-tangle with destroying thorn thickets. The Zen deviation comes from the established Chan use of creepers for entangling words, here made the object of cutting. Unlike more common longer forms that add an explicit verb of severing, the exact phrase is not attested in this concordance as a live-exchange command, so this entry does not present it as one.

Senses.Explanation: Cutting the cat names Nanquan’s canonical action and functions as a later benchmark for decisive conduct. This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 allowlisted texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”

Senses.Explanation: Cut off the head while seeking life is an impossible rescue: the very act taken to find life removes what must remain alive. Chan masters repeatedly oppose it to adding another head atop one’s own, placing both images on rejected sides of a verbal choice. Poshan applies the pair first to ‘mind/buddha’ wording and again to seeking a decision from oneself or another; Tianyin applies it to saying exertion is absent or present; and Fachang applies it to saying one understands or does not.

Senses.Explanation: Cut off the life-root is a violent Chan instruction and verdict for ending the operative root that keeps an attachment, understanding, or verbal move alive—not for killing a person. Juelang Daosheng says that even after passing beyond delusion, awakening, sights, and honored states, a remaining root must be cut here. Dahui Zonggao compares inadequate inquiry to chopping branches instead of delivering the one axe-stroke that severs the tree’s life-root. A verse on Zhaozhou’s “no” joins a sharp blade cutting the life-root with jumping clear of fox and dog packs. Across these uses the action is radical and terminal, but its object is the sustaining foothold exposed in the case.

Senses.Explanation: Cutting off the arm is the bodily action attributed to Huike and raised repeatedly as a named ancestral case. In the Chan record it overwhelmingly names the founding episode in which Shenguang, later named Huike, stands in the snow before Bodhidharma, cuts off his left arm, and places it before him. The lamp account has Bodhidharma say, 'you have now cut off your arm before me; your seeking may be accepted,' and then rename him Huike. Later records compress the episode into paired formulas—'standing in the snow and cutting off the arm,' 'cutting off the arm and pacifying the mind,' or 'face the wall for nine years / cut off the arm and pacify the mind'—and repeatedly reopen it as a public question. Ciming Chuyuan asks, 'what did the cutting off of the arm accomplish?' and strikes the staff before leaving the seat. Another is asked why one cuts off an arm to seek the Way if this house style is inherent in everyone; he replies, 'there are many mistaken understandings.' Still another says, 'why cut off an arm and seek elsewhere?' The Chan-specific bend is that Huike's bodily act becomes compact lineage and interview language, quoted, challenged, and criticized across later records. These later uses do not authorize this entry to declare the act a required sacrifice or explain its intention beyond what the accounts say.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes every day is a good day in these Chan records. Its wording is "every day is a good day." Yunmen tells the assembly, "I do not ask you about before the fifteenth day; bring me a phrase about after the fifteenth." When the assembly gives no answer, he answers for them: "every day is a good day." The corpus thereafter quotes it as Yunmen's answer, pairs it with "every year is a good year," challenges it in questions, rebukes the recorded questioner who offers it, and expands it in later teaching-seat verse. Its specifically Chan deployment is therefore as Yunmen's public answer and a line later masters openly quote, test, contradict, and comment on; the record supplies no mystical paraphrase for "good."

Senses.Explanation: The transient-guest quarters are the monastery's office and lodging for newly arrived or short-stay monks, supplied with beds and provisions and governed by arrival rules. The Pure Rules orders the guest prefect to keep the quarters' bedding, lamps, firewood, and charcoal ready and to treat new arrivals warmly. Other regulations direct a transient guest to ask where the quarters are, unload there, and meet the guest prefect. Lamp biographies use the same institution in arrival narratives: monks meet or fight there, and the rules for new arrivals determine whether they remain. References to the transient-guest hall and its three-day stay retain the same institutional referent.

Senses.PreferredTarget: become clear about mind and see nature
AlternateTargets: make the mind clear and see its nature
understand mind and see nature directly
Senses.Note: Critical deployments are equally explicit and must remain part of the article. Yongjue Yuanxian places “clarifying mind and seeing nature” beside three other formulas and calls it “putting grit in the eye” (明心見性是眼中著屑). A six-rung-reviewed unnamed attendant asks Yongzheng Emperor for instruction; Yongzheng compares the request to lighting a lamp under water, then asks, “how can mind be clarified? How can nature be seen?” (心如何可明？性如何可見). Poshan Haiming reports someone declaring the formula correct and responds, “what shape is mind? What thing is nature?” (心是何形？性是何物). The exact question “what is clarifying mind and seeing nature?” (如何是明心見性) occurs three times in three texts; “how to clarify mind and see nature” (如何明心見性) occurs twice in two. The entry preserves affirmative and critical deployments without making any single appraisal universal.

Senses.Explanation: A fixed pair naming two claimed recognitions: becoming clear about mind and seeing nature. The records use it as an answer, a road, a requested explanation, a direct question, and a target of criticism; they do not give the formula one uniform appraisal. Yongzheng Emperor's verse unpacks the pair through wordplay: “one who clarifies clarifies the mind; one who sees sees its body; seeing nature clarifies the mind-body; clarifying mind sees the nature-principle” (明者明其心，見者見其體；見性明心體，明心見性理). In a raised case, Zhaozhou Congshen answers “what is the road without error?” with “clarifying mind and seeing nature is the road without error” (明心見性是不錯底路). A six-rung-reviewed unnamed questioner asks Konggu Daocheng what clarifying mind and seeing nature is; Konggu answers, “I do not know” (如何是明心見性？不識). The phrase occurs 146 times in 84 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: The records use light and dark as a coordinated pair in visual conditions, questions, verses, and instructions; their attested relations include distinction, intermingling, reciprocity, and pairing. The graphs themselves mean “light or bright” and “dark.” The record uses the pair for visual conditions and as a coordinated pair in questions, verses, and instructions. Caoshan says, "mountains, rivers, and the great earth: light and dark are each distinct" (山河大地，明暗自殊). Another verse says, "light and dark intermingle—the pivot of killing and bringing to life" (明暗相參殺活機). A transmission verse says, "light and dark do not concern one another; each divides one half" (明暗不相干，彼此分一半). Frequent coordination with "form and emptiness" (明暗色空, 256 occurrences) places both pairs among the things named in the scene.

Senses.Explanation: Moonlight and reed flowers form a pale scene in which boundaries can look erased. Chan masters use that resemblance, then repeatedly refuse to let resemblance harden into identity: the same pair can be said to share one color, not resemble each other, or remain a place from which one must get out. Zhuanyu Guanheng calls moonlight and reed flowers one fresh color while saying there are not two sides. Huanyou Zhengchuan makes the pair nod inside his answer on the five ranks. Yushan Shangsi warns that merely invoking it enters an old groove. Xueyan Zuqin says moon, reeds, and egret are alike, then asks how many people cannot leave that ground and values his own exposition at less than half a coin. Foyan Qingyuan puts moon and reeds beside red smartweed; Binya Jian sets them on the two banks after dismissing fixed acceptance and rejection.

Senses.Explanation: Dahui directly defines dull sinking by contrast: forgetting and falling into a dark cave is called dull sinking, while deliberate mental succession is called agitation. Literally, dim or dull sinking . Dahui supplies the corpus's clearest direct description: forgetting or blanking out falls into the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain, and the teachings call this dull sinking; he contrasts it with deliberate attention, whose thought-consciousness flies about and is called agitation. Other records label dull sinking “not good” beside “binding thought strays from the real” and pair it repeatedly with agitation as the two named conditions found in the Chan hall. The Chan record also bends the inherited fault-category against simple rejection: Gaofeng says the four graphs “dull sinking and agitation” are themselves buddha-nature, Daodu calls the pair one's place for establishing life, and Dahui tells Lü Juren that whether dull-sunk or agitated, it is still only Lü Juren. The deviation lies in this combination of exact diagnosis, fixed pairing, and masters' refusal to locate the named condition outside the person who reports it.

Senses.Explanation: A reduplicated description: brightly evident (昭昭) and keenly numinous or responsive (靈靈), hence "bright and numinous." It occurs 240 times in 101 allowlisted texts. Chinese Chan records frequently use the phrase while rejecting its identification with one's true self. One address asks, "if you recognize the bright and numinous as your reality, why does it no longer remain bright and numinous when you are asleep?" (汝若認昭昭靈靈是汝真實，為甚麼瞌睡時又不成昭昭靈靈). The same address gives a direct account: the bright and numinous arises because colors, sounds, scents, and other things before one are distinguished; without those things it is like "turtle fur and rabbit horns" (昭昭靈靈，祇因前塵色聲香等法而有分別；若無前塵，同於龜毛兔角). Another record states that the fault lies in taking the presently bright and numinous as correct, since it "arises dependent on encountered objects" (昭昭靈靈乃是緣境而有). These are the corpus's explicit predicates, not an entry-level theory of consciousness.

Senses.Explanation: The expression asks what an indicated object, person, place, or phrase is. Mazu asks about the wild ducks, ‘what is this?’, and Baizhang answers ‘wild ducks’ (是什麼？野鴨子). Foyan Qingyuan points to a raised whisk and asks ‘what is it—can you hear?’ (是什麼，還聞麼), while Yunmen repeatedly summons his attendant, receives ‘yes,’ and asks ‘what is it?’ (是什麼). With a following noun, the interrogative asks ‘what person?’ (是什麼人) or ‘what thing?’ (是什麼物). The records repeatedly attach the question to a visible object, named person, or live exchange without supplying one dictionary answer for every case.

Senses.Explanation: Say more or go on to say marks additional speech after something has already been said. In commentary it can instead report that Xuedou, Tianyin, or Wansong adds further words. These are grammatical viewpoints on one continuation of speech, not different senses; whether the added words succeed remains open to the surrounding response.

Senses.Explanation: In public interviews it rejects a proposed connection between Cuifeng Chongxian's words and the matter asked about: after an unnamed monk identifies Cuifeng Chongxian with an earlier house, the answer is "what connection does that have?" (有什麼交涉). The phrase also appears in prose criticism. The Blue Cliff Record says that treating Mazu's left and right eyes as the sun-face and moon-face has "what connection?" and that such readers have missed the old matter. Elsewhere Juehua Puzhao asks, "if lips, voice, and appearances are taken as oneself, what connection does that have?" (若以唇吻聲色以為自己，有什麼交涉). In another exchange, an unnamed monk himself uses the question after the answer "the graph 'by means of'" (以字), and receives "the graph 'eight'" (八字), a spoken play on similar-sounding graph names. Zen bends an ordinary request for relevance into a compact interview verdict: the reply or explanation offered has not connected with the exchange.

Senses.Explanation: What has that to do with it? is a spoken Chan rejection of a proposed connection. The records place the question after a quotation, classification, or offered formulation and use it to deny that the proposal reaches the matter under examination. Sanshan Denglai rejects both commentary on an old exchange and inert long-bench sitting with the same question. Baiyu Jingsi dismisses a polished account of mind and teaching before setting his staff against it. Yuan'an Liao uses the question twice against stock answers offered for the study-eye and the grounded statement. Hengchuan Rugong applies it first to verbal presentation itself and later to the old moon-viewing exchange, where the masters' displayed answers are said to have nothing to do with the moon.

Senses.Explanation: Wooden figures appear as insensible constructed bodies that walk, sing, or answer only in the records’ impossible images and contrasts. The wooden figure is an ordinarily inert human-shaped figure that Chan records repeatedly make act: it beckons, answers, speaks, dances, embroiders, and claps a board in the clouds. The recurrent bend is the impossible agent, often paired with the barren woman, rather than a separate named person. Hongzhi Zhengjue pairs the wooden figure beckoning with the barren woman nodding. Dengzhou Zhongdu states the contrast most sharply: the wooden figure always replies, while one with nature cannot speak. Cian Shoujing says that through the scorching summer retreat the wooden figure's dirty flow does not cease. Ruibai Mingxue makes the wooden figure embroider a flowered cap at midnight while the barren woman breaks a mirror at dawn. Wuyi Yuanlai says the wooden figure rising to dance is not extraordinary, and Qingshan Shoulong answers a question about an auspicious sign with the wooden figure clapping a board in the clouds. Wuyin Zijing makes a wooden figure divine an auspicious sign at the turn of the year. Tian'an Sheng separately uses 'carved wooden man' as a disparaging person-epithet; that different referent does not prove the stock figure's physical construction; the many human actions remain predicates of that figure, not additional senses.

Senses.Explanation: The wooden buddha is a materially wooden image in Danxia Tianran’s burning case and in the fixed contrast that a wooden buddha does not pass through fire. Literally a "buddha" (佛) made of "wood" (木): a "wooden buddha," attested 663 times in 181 allowlisted texts. The principal recorded case says Danxia, encountering severe cold at Huilin Temple, took a wooden buddha and burned it. When the superintendent rebuked him, Danxia stirred the ashes and said he was looking for relics. The superintendent replied, "How could a wooden buddha have relics?" Danxia said, "Since it has no relics, bring two more honored ones to burn" (木佛何有舍利，既無舍利，更請兩尊來燒). The phrase also appears in the fixed line "a wooden buddha does not pass through fire" (木佛不度火), alongside a clay buddha not passing through water and a gold buddha not passing through a furnace.

Senses.Explanation: The wood-rooster is an impossible verse-image whose recorded predicates make it crow at midnight, carry an egg, sweat, announce dawn, and act where no sound is heard; one comparison also says a gaunt person looked like it. The corpus gives no manufacturing predicate and does not narrate the inherited cock-training story, so the relation of the wood modifier remains unresolved rather than being asserted as construction material. In the transmitted public case, an unnamed questioner asks Fengxue Yanzhao, “The ancient tune has no tone or rhyme; how can it be harmonized?” Fengxue replies, “The wooden rooster crows at midnight; the straw dog barks at dawn” (木雞啼子夜，芻狗吠天明). Later masters repeat the line as answers to such questions as “What is the precise meaning?” and explicitly say, “where the wooden rooster crows there is no sound” (木雞啼處無聲). Other records make it announce dawn, run carrying an egg, or sweat in summer. The Chan deviation is this use of an inert crafted bird as a recurring public-interview answer and impossible-event agent, often paired with the straw dog; the entry records the uses without resolving them into a hidden teaching.

In the Continuation of the Lamp Record, Lianhuafeng Xiang answers “A sound” when asked about Yunmen's wooden horse neighing. Shiyu Mingfang brings it back neighing in wind, Ruibai Mingxue places its summer cold beside a stone ox's winter warmth, and Tianzhu Chonghui uses its neigh in a public answer about the lineage matter. The corpus often pairs it with a mud ox or stone ox, but these pairings do not turn it into a different object. Nor does the contrast license an imported explanation about no-mind: the entry records these exact predicates and settings without deciding what hidden lesson they signify. The headword occurs 801 times in 217 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: Not yet; not there yet: in the Chan corpus this is especially frequent as a teaching-seat verdict on a reply, shout, verse, or claimed understanding. The exact words (未在) also retain their ordinary temporal force. Zhaozhou Congshen says, 'Not there yet; say more' (未在更道). Gufeng Xiu tells Wanshan Zhengning, 'You have got it, but you are still not there yet' (你也得，只是未在). Fushi Tongxian likewise says, 'Not there yet; say more,' while Tianyin Yuanxiu uses the phrase to reject an attempted deception. Guangxiao Huijue says, 'Even if you reached a thousand years, you still would not yet be old' (直至千歲也未在). Thus the corpus deploys one phrase both as an evaluative reply and in ordinary statements of something not yet reached or completed.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB182.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wanru (萬如禪師語錄): Wanru Tongwei is the exact speaker. Wanru Tongwei speaks from the hall, says earlier figures had not yet passed the final barrier, and asks whether anyone present has passed it.

Senses.Explanation: This is the final formidable barrier or severe checkpoint in a sequence of testing, something speakers say must be reached, passed through, or personally arrived at even after an earlier understanding. ‘Final’ marks its position and (牢) marks its formidable resistance; neither word by itself supplies the whole expression. The records speak of passing through or penetrating it, and use it as a severe last check. Yuan'an, after listing a series of named cases, calls "this whole tangle" (者一落索) the final locked barrier and criticizes estimating it through cognitive calculation. Juelang says even someone who has understood "this affair" but has "not passed through the final locked barrier" (未透末後牢關) can still mistake a shadow for a head. Yulin asks, "how many people have passed the final locked barrier?" (末後牢關幾人透得). Other formulations say it is "not measurable by humans or gods" (人天莫測) and "not understood by a thousand sages" (千聖不曉).

Senses.Explanation: Originally complete is a strong sufficiency claim that Chan records immediately turn into questions about transmission, awakening, manifestation, and whether anyone will shoulder what is already theirs. Zhongfeng Mingben says every class of being is originally complete, then asks what single transmission transmits. Mi'an Xianjie's memorial prose makes failure to realize the originally complete way urgent, while the Yongzheng Emperor presents ancestral transmission as evidence for the claim. Zhe'an Jingfan says the robe points to everyone's originally complete affair but people refuse to shoulder it. The Lamp record says wisdom-light is originally complete yet obscured by delusive thought; the Record Pointing at the Moon says original quiescence cannot manifest itself and depends on discernment.

Senses.Explanation: Originally, there is not a single thing is a received verse-line whose exhaustive denial is repeatedly transmitted, varied, challenged, and placed beside counter-statements. The received Zongbao Platform Sutra gives the line in Huineng’s verse, while other collections transmit different surrounding lines. The older Dunhuang wording lacks this exact headword, so the entry limits its claim to the received line and later transmissions. Dongshan Liangjie says that even stating it directly does not earn the robe and bowl. Huangbo Xiyun answers a question about no-thing by denying even “no,” Yulin Tongxiu sets the line beside Changqing’s exposed solitary body, and Zhongfeng criticizes conceptual interpretation of it. These tests block treating the line as a self-explaining theory.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J10/J10nA158.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun (密雲禪師語錄): Miyun Yuanwu, in the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Miyun (密雲禪師語錄), urges the assembly to recognize the original face, asks what it is, and follows the question with a shout.

Senses.Explanation: The “original face” is the face a person is challenged to recognize or investigate before acquired distinctions settle the answer. The records repeatedly preserve Huineng’s question to Ming: when not thinking good and not thinking evil, “what is your original face?” (不思善不思惡，正恁麼時，如何是上座本來面目). Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes that question and the instruction to turn the light back upon one’s own original face. Guanyin Congxian deliberately removes the four words “original face” from Huineng’s demand and asks whether the alteration still belongs to Huineng’s lineage. Dahui Zonggao pairs the phrase with one’s home-ground scenery and says that the original face itself has never been deluded or awakened, locating delusion and awakening in a person’s momentary thought. Yulin Tongxiu tells the emperor to investigate the phrase in activity as well as stillness. Zhuanyu Guanheng equates the six sense-fields, when recollected without discrimination, with one’s own original face. Miyun Yuanwu urges recognition of it amid ordinary bending and looking up, then answers his own renewed question with a shout and a spatial saying. Yushan Shangsi makes his staff leap into a hall, knock down the person of no rank, and smash the original face in a deliberately extravagant hall address. Across these uses the phrase is a question, an object of investigation and recognition, an explicit equation, and a target of corrective wordplay; no single verbal reply is made its universal definition.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan interview and instruction, the compound names the matter proper to the person rather than an item borrowed from authoritative predecessors. Zhaozhou Congshen says a lineage teacher must receive people with it, while an unnamed monk’s question about it is answered by pointing the matter back to the questioner. Baichi Yuanshuo places inquiry, eating, bodily functions, and ordinary activity within one’s own matter but still demands that it be stated directly. Danxia Dangui warns that merely speaking of it has already made it extraneous, and Xiuyelin defines it as where one’s own root-destiny comes to rest. Bai Juyi challenges a scripture-reciting monk about a cleric’s own matter. Yuanwu Keqin says that even cloudless clarity in it cannot simply be let pass. Nanquan Puyuan likewise demands it directly without pointing east or west. Across these uses, the phrase marks what cannot be outsourced or replaced by discursive display, while remaining a demand made in concrete encounters rather than an imported abstract teaching.

Senses.Explanation: The saying, question, or public case singled out as a person's main subject of inquiry. The possessives and verbal predicates in later Chinese Chan records make this local use concrete. Jiexian tells a hall leader to know each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; another passage says that not knowing it leaves the leader without a way to act. Zhanran Yuancheng tells people to place the selected saying before their eyes, Konggu Daocheng says to raise it, and Langting Jingting warns Qianyun that he has dropped one line of it behind his head. The compound can take 'public case' or 'word, saying, conversational thread' after it, and can itself be said to be broken through. Yongzheng asks, 'What is primary investigation?' and gives one particular example: if one trusts the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate who is recollecting buddha. Wuyi Yuanlai says that the Chan house relies on primary investigation and that when it breaks through it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. These predicates describe the assigned subject and the act of investigating it without turning the term into a named system.

Senses.Explanation: One's own case-phrase is the particular unresolved point in a saying or case that the student cannot yet get through and keeps immediately at hand. Poshan Haiming defines it from the obstruction itself: whatever remains unclear and unpenetrated in a teaching or public case is precisely the personal case-phrase. That definition keeps the term tied to a person's actual unresolved point rather than to a generic list of cases. The other records show how concrete that possession becomes. Zhanran Yuancheng and Ruibai Mingxue say to set it before oneself, comparing its continuous presence to leaning against Mount Sumeru, a hen holding an egg, or a cat watching a mouse. Konggu Daocheng links raising it with the movement of doubt, and Wuyi Yuanlai says to raise one phrase and press through the mass of doubt. Zen bends the 'phrase' into the student's live obstruction: it travels through ordinary activity and is tested by whether the unresolved point actually breaks open.

Yinyuan Longqi places it before parental birth and before yin and yang divide. Yun’e Xi repeatedly asks where it lands for beings, patriarchs, buddhas, the assembly, and himself. Baichi Xingyuan says recognizing it is the whole demand of the directly pointing school. Dahui Zonggao makes the boundary sharp: knowing its landing place can hold Jinli at the encounter, but taking karmic consciousness itself for this source is an outward-running mistake. Lianfeng Su likewise makes awakening to it the demand of genuine inquiry. The graphs retain the flavor of a natal allotment, but the selected Zen records bend them away from a horoscope entry and into a public demand to locate the source and standing of one’s own life. The entry does not decide that demand for the reader.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use “original landscape” for what is disclosed as one's own, often pairing it with the original face and contrasting its presence with seeking outside, clinging to purity, or remaining blocked by distinctions. Yuanwu Keqin and Dahui Zonggao place the expression beside the original face and say it is present through ordinary modes of activity or belongs to each person. Mi'an Xianjie says it suddenly appears when inquiry reaches the end of explanations, while Tianyin Yuanxiu says paired categories such as illumination and function appear upon this landscape. Jie'an Wujin's verse says it was never sought outside and is not absent in walking, sitting, or lying down. Zhongfeng Mingben provocatively says dullness and distraction are wholly this landscape, but immediately warns that merely accepting that formulation is another error. Sanyi Mingyu likewise denies that settling into undifferentiated purity is the original landscape.

Senses.Explanation: One's nature as it is from the outset. Chan records repeatedly use 'see one's own original nature' beside 'recognize one's own original mind.' The Platform Record makes seeing it the distinction between remaining outside the gate and entering, and describes it as not arising or extinguishing. The Mirror Record says that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct. These are the texts' recorded descriptions; the English should preserve the plain noun phrase rather than substitute a later explanatory system. The omitted collocation "original nature empty" (本性空) occurs forty times in thirty texts, but it has more than one syntax. Twenty-seven occurrences in twenty-five texts belong to the fixed line, "understand body and mind, original nature empty; how would this person differ from buddha?" (了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別). A later Chan address raises that line and immediately comments, "the buddha-body is neither real nor empty; buddha-as-appearance is not appearance" (佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻). The Source-Mirror Record gives a separate explicit definition: "as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean" (本性空者，即是自性清淨心；本性即自性；空，即清淨義).

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula “Fundamentally, not one thing” occurs as assertion, verse line, and interview question; the records place it beside what can be presented, displayed, or investigated. Literally, ‘fundamentally, not one thing.’ The exact shorter phrase occurs 34 times in 30 allowlisted texts. Yangshan's record predicates it of one's own mind-source and contrasts immediate recognition there with gradual certification through myriad deeds. Yinyuan Longqi says there is fundamentally not one thing to present. Yulin Tongxiu places three heads, six arms, a thousand hands, and a thousand eyes beside the statement that fundamentally there is not one thing, while also saying the myriad forms run crosswise. In a public exchange, Miyin is asked what the student investigates if fundamentally there is not one thing and answers, ‘take yourself out.’ Huineng's longer ‘originally, not one thing’ is a close morphological family form, preserved as family evidence rather than counted as the exact headword. The shorter phrase is thus a predicate, verse line, and publicly tested proposition, not an imported metaphysical definition.

SearchAliases: complete in itself from the origin
Senses.Explanation: It appears in the Platform Record's list of Huineng's statements on the nature: "who expected the nature to be from the start pure … from the start complete … able to produce the myriad things?" (何期自性本自清淨；何期自性本自具足；何期自性能生萬法). The corpus also turns the wording into a direct question: "what is complete from the start?" The recorded answer is, "because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete" (因無一物可得，所以說具足). A prose criticism asks, "complete from the start—who picks it up or puts it down?" (本自具足，阿誰拈起放下). Other records set the phrase against outside acquisition: living beings are complete from the start and "do not depend on seeking outside" (不假外求). The Zen deployment therefore joins the phrase to the nature, direct questioning, the impossibility of picking it up or putting it down, and explicit refusal of outside acquisition; this entry reports those statements without converting them into a system of cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: The compound occurs 381 times in 145 allowed texts as a verdict on a person, answer, explanation, or speech, and as a verb for making such material up. A late direct naming statement criticizes assigning difficult cases to newcomers without matching the person and the case: after comparing it to fitting a square timber into a round hole and losing people's time, Jiexian says, 'To call it fabricated—is that not fitting?' (謂之杜撰，不亦宜乎). A playful assembly exchange separates the graphs as a surname and personal name: the staff says, 'My surname is Du, given name Zhuan'; asked why it is called 'fabricated,' it answers, 'If the elder did not fabricate, how could he spend all day talking about Zhang and Li?' (長老若不杜撰，如何終日與人說張說李). Dahui uses the word self-deprecatingly when he says, 'I have not read Guo Xiang's explanation or the various commentators' explanations; I only rely on my own fabrication to explain your silence' (我也不曾看郭象解并諸家注解，只據我杜撰說破爾這默然). The stock rebuke 'fabricated elder' (杜撰長老) occurs 68 times in 53 texts, often in the fuller comparison 'fabricated elders are like hemp and millet'—that is, extremely numerous (杜撰長老如麻似粟). 'Fabricated Chan fellow' (杜撰禪和) likewise appears as a verdict on a respondent, while 'fabricated conjectural talk' (杜撰臆說) names speech. These are grammatical deployments of one shared judgment; the texts do not establish a distinct sense from the proper name Du Mo, whose 18 hits refer to a person or to being silent.

Senses.Explanation: East Mountain walks on water is Yunmen’s compact saying, repeatedly cited, questioned, and commented upon as a named case. Yunmen Wenyan's fixed answer to ‘What is the buddhas' place of emergence?’ is ‘East Mountain walks on water’ (如何是諸佛出身處。師曰。東山水上行). The phrase occurs 290 times in 131 allowlisted texts. Later masters keep this impossible-looking sentence in public circulation as a named case-saying rather than using it as an ordinary report about a mountain. Yuanwu Keqin repeats Yunmen's exchange and gives a different answer to the same question: ‘The fragrant wind comes from the south; the halls give rise to a slight coolness.’ Xiatang Huiyuan is asked directly for the saying's import and answers, ‘The thirty-first day of the first month; no need to choose a date.’ Chaozong receives the same question in a hall exchange. Juebao Qing quotes Yunmen and then makes the sentence the opening line of his own verse. Tianran Shi titles a verse with Yunmen's saying and closes it by saying that the conversational thread has been transmitted to the present. The corpus therefore establishes what the phrase is and how it is used, but supplies no stable decoding of how or why the mountain walks.

Senses.Explanation: A dragon sings in the dead tree is an impossible sound-and-life image repeatedly paired with eyes in a skull and explicitly treated as vivid but not yet finished. Langting Shiyun places it among festival wonders in the marketplace; Sanyi Mingyu verses it beside eyes in a skull on an ancient road. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives the decisive control: the dead-tree dragon-song still carries joy, just as skull eyes still carry awareness. The same formula circulates in Zhaozhou commentary, the Blue Cliff Record, and the Five Lamps, where dead-tree dragon-song brings spring to the whole earth. These uses retain one image while varying its appraisal.

Senses.Explanation: Dry Chan is one label whose appraisal changes with context. Poshan, Wanshou, Guangshou, and Shiyu use it critically for limited sitting, guarding stillness, or speechless withdrawal. Wuzhun reports Cheng adopting it as a self-name while mocking that adoption, whereas Xutang deploys it for Bodhidharma-style wall-facing in contrast with public office. The entry therefore records the label and its attested appraisals rather than treating every occurrence as inert cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: Outside the ordinary frame of categories, grading, or established standards. Chan records apply the descriptor to sayings, phrases, actions, workings, people, and house styles, but they do not make it automatic praise. Baiyu Si contrasts phrases addressed to middle and lower capacities with handling “outside the frame” that establishes no grade of capacity. Tianyi Yihuai says a formulation is not yet a saying outside the usual frame, then contrasts it with explaining meaning by relying on scripture. Qingxu Xiujing applies the descriptor to Zhaozhou Congshen's “cypress tree in the front garden” answer. Mengtang Tan'e characterizes Yunmen Wenyan's house as solitary and steep and upheld outside the ordinary frame. Juelang Daosheng is directly asked for a phrase outside the frame and answers, “the staff-tip points out a thousand lovely peaks; before Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for good news.” Yuan'an Feng rejects Yaoshan Weiyan's own claim to possess workings outside the frame, judging that it reveals what it tries to hide. The headword occurs 1,203 times across 263 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: A phrase outside the standard is a public-interview utterance class placed beyond ordinary or established standards. Yuanwu’s pointer says that if one can distinguish such a phrase, ‘raise one and understand three’; later in the same collection he says one must know the phrase outside the standard so that, when public cases and words are raised, one knows their place. An unnamed questioner can ask directly, ‘what is a phrase outside the standard?’ and receive the answer, ‘the staff-tip points out a thousand peaks; before the Five-Phoenix Tower, listen for fine news.’ Other speakers coordinate it with ‘the upward pivot,’ contrast it with ‘the basic-function mechanism,’ or attribute it to Yunmen while saying that Yunmen and the Buddha each displayed their own style but had not yet accorded with the basis. One later discourse dismisses ‘the phrase outside the standard’ as a worn-out straw sandal alongside ‘the upward pivot’ as rotten hemp rope. Zen usage therefore bends the ordinary ‘outside the norm’ modifier into a technical phrase-class that masters request, distinguish, perform, compare with other phrase and mechanism classes, and appraise in public interviews.

SearchAliases: the bottom drops out of the bucket
Senses.Explanation: A bucket loses its bottom in the middle of use: contents spill, the vessel no longer holds, and the event can be seen. Chan records reuse that concrete collapse as a comparison after a blow or a phrase, as a direct answer to ‘What is buddha?’, and as an image whose literal kitchen occurrence remains visible. Its comparison form 'like the bucket-bottom falls out' (如桶底脫) occurs 38 times, including 26 exact endings in 'resembling the bucket-bottom falling out' (桶底脫相似). Xuefeng reports that after Deshan struck him, 'at that time I was as if the bucket-bottom had fallen out' (我當時如桶底脫相似); Yantou immediately challenges what Xuefeng brought in through the gate. Yuanwu uses the same comparison after 'under one phrase' (一言之下) and elsewhere joins the literal image to 'the mechanisms are exhausted' (桶底脫機關盡). The phrase is also recorded as a direct answer: asked 'What is buddha?' (如何是佛), Shoushan Huaizhi says, 'the bucket-bottom falls out' (桶底脫). A separate kitchen encounter uses the words literally: while noodles are cooking, the bucket-bottom suddenly falls out, the assembly cries that it is a pity, and the cited speaker says, 'the bucket-bottom falling out should itself be cause for joy—why are you distressed?' (桶底脫自合歡喜), before agreeing that the lost bucket of noodles is regrettable. The physical event and its simile therefore share one graph-level sense while appearing in an answer, recollection, comment, and kitchen exchange.

The root-and-branches idiom becomes a Chan verdict on replacing direct responsibility with scriptures, phrases, learning, or a sought awakening. Extensive Record of Chan Master Hongzhi (宏智禪師廣錄): The Extensive Record of Chan Master Hongzhi (宏智禪師廣錄), in Hongzhi Zhengjue's own hall-address section. Hongzhi says that things arise through the convergence of conditions, that shadow arises from form and echo from sound, and that the whole array of phenomena becomes densely arrayed.

Senses.Explanation: The whole array of phenomena: a collective for the countless forms or appearances presented together, from landscape and moonlight to ordinary and holy beings. ‘Densely arrayed’ (森羅) describes their spread, and ‘the ten thousand forms’ (萬象) supplies the members. The expression occurs 685 times in 213 allowlisted texts; its reversed form, ‘the ten thousand forms arrayed’ (萬象森羅), occurs 730 times in 231. Fayan Wenyi answers ‘What is the second moon?’ with the headword, then answers ‘What is the first moon?’ with the reversed order. Xuedou Faning compares the hundred rivers reaching their limit in the sea with the whole array reaching its limit in empty space. Lingyun Baoyin places the moon amid it, Kongsou Yin calls empty space illness and the array medicine, and Shangfeng Bencai extends Vimalakirti's illness through a staff, the entire array, and ordinary and holy beings. Changlu Yingfu first describes encircling rivers and mountains and halls rising into the sky, then gathers that visible multiplicity under the expression. Hongzhi Zhengjue says forms arise from converging conditions and become densely arrayed. Its Chan deployment is not a hidden entity behind those things, but the records' use of an ordinary totalizing collective as an answer, comparison, question, and speaking subject in public discourse.

Senses.Explanation: Karma is action and the consequences carried with it; these Chan sources both affirm that causal register and preserve sharply framed language of being without karma. The Blue Cliff Record quotes past-life wrongdoing producing a present consequence, and Xuzhou Sheng’s record says fixed karma is difficult to escape and invokes hell directly. The Shaoshi Six Gates supplies the deliberately contrary formula that a buddha is a person without karma, cause, or effect. The stored definitions of expression by negation explain how negating language removes what is being rejected, but they do not by themselves prove that every no-cause formula has the same force. The fox-case anchor and Chaozong’s question about illness arising from karma show further Chan handling of causation. The evidence therefore supports a real tension inside the corpus; it does not support collapsing karma into conceptual entanglement alone or assigning unstored claims to additional masters.

Senses.Explanation: To speak across and upright is to speak at length in every direction or manner. Chan records use the paired verbs to characterize extensive discourse, sometimes adding contrary or compliant speech, and then appraise what such speech does not reach. Huangbo Xiyun says Niutou spoke every which way but still did not know the upward hinge. Chijue Daochong describes Shakyamuni speaking every which way through hundreds of assemblies and still not reaching the matter. Wuyi Yuanlai repeats the phrase for Shakyamuni and for his own present address, adding contrary and compliant speech. Tianyi Yihuai says an unnamed questioning monk may speak every which way yet still lack the eye at the crown. These uses characterize discourse range; they do not establish a separate thing for each direction.

Senses.Explanation: The responsive action displayed in an encounter: conduct that meets a changing occasion rather than merely following dead rules. Records say that Dahui exhausted or displayed all his responsive operation before Wuzu, that Wumen Huikai's and Yuelin Shiguan's responsive operation 'matched closely,' and that a portrait praise had Linji's responsive operation without indiscriminately carrying out staff-blows and shouts. Appraisals call it cutting, like thunder and lightning, or say it runs like thunder; instructional prose pairs living responsive operation with changing circumstances and contrasts it with dead rules. The compound also expands as 'great responsive operation' and joins recurrent predicates such as display, exhaust, match, be lively, run crosswise and lengthwise, or be fully raised. These are corpus descriptions of observable encounter conduct; the pivot or occasion graph (機) does not by itself name a student's graded capacity, and the records assign no single hidden purpose to the actions.

Senses.Explanation: The sharp edge of an encounter is the quick, pointed capacity displayed when speakers meet in questioning and response. Records call it swift, steep, lightning-like, exchanged, or brought into contact with another's. The term can praise acuity, but criticism of merely rapid performance shows that speed alone does not establish success. It names the responsive edge being displayed or assessed, not a guaranteed result.

Senses.Explanation: The saying redirects “what does buddha-nature mean?” toward the occasion now at hand. In Zen records it regularly launches an immediate test: a whisk is raised, a platform struck, the questioner asks for the present occasion, or the named headword utterer leaves the seat. Dahui Zonggao follows the formula with “when the occasion arrives, its principle displays itself,” then asks whether the assembly sees the whisk and hears the platform. Miyun Yuanwu likewise raises the whisk and demands the present occasion. HuiGuo answers the questioner’s request for the occasion by leaving the seat. In Baizhang Huaihai’s account of Guishan at the fire, the formula marks awakening as the arrival of conditions, like suddenly recalling what was already one’s own. In Monk Yushan’s whisk session, an unnamed monk uses the formula to frame a public question; Yushan answers that everyone has a share in looking up to it.

Senses.Explanation: The isolated four graphs say, 'stop (歇)—that is (即) awakening (菩提),' but the corpus's recurring full quotation supplies the omitted subject: 'the crazed mind does not stop; when it stops, that is awakening' (狂心不歇，歇即菩提). A historical compendium follows the phrase with its own explicit explanation, beginning 'as for “when it stops, that is awakening”' and describing what it calls awakening. Chan masters repeatedly take up the quoted line in hall discourse. One says that when dust-labor suddenly stops, 'when it stops, that is awakening,' then immediately asks the assembly, 'from where is it obtained?' Another says people run north, south, east, and west for years without a place to stop and asks, 'can you people stop?' The Zen deviation is the quotation's deployment as a public teaching-seat proposition and direct question. Restoring its attested subject avoids turning every kind of ceasing into the roadmap's broad 'ceasing itself is enlightenment.'

Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, coming from within the absolute (正中來) names a movement from the upright or correct position; Caoshan describes it as words within no-words, without setting up rank or falling to either side. Caoshan Benji explains the label through coming from the correct position and gives examples of speech within no-speech. Hongzhi Zhengjue's verse pictures a great fish shedding its shell and taking the bird path, while an unnamed monastic later asks Fenyang Shanzhao for the rank and receives the image of lotuses opening on dry ground. Langting Ting pairs the rank with partridge calls and opening flowers. Juelang Daosheng later explains it through a ruler at the highest point, Yongjue Yuanxian gives a midnight plum opening against snow, and Ruibai Mingxue classifies a shout free of names and words as this rank. These changing images and schemata illustrate one named relation rather than establish separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the relative within the absolute (正中偏) names differentiated appearance within the absolute or upright. Records identify it relationally and then test it through verses, images, and contrast with the absolute within the relative (偏中正). Caoshan Benji explains that the upright position is the empty realm and the partial position the realm of forms; he glosses the relative within the absolute (正中偏) as turning from principle toward affairs and elsewhere as the lord looking toward the minister. Hongzhi Zhengjue's Five Ranks verse gives the rank a night image in which a wooden boy strikes the moon's door and wakes a jade woman. The Mirror of Humans and Devas records an unnamed monastic asking Fenyang Shanzhao for this rank and preserves Fenyang's moon-and-cock response. Langting Ting gives it swallows murmuring between roof beams. Juelang Daosheng relates it to an eastern circle and lesser yang, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies his own shout as this rank once he has mounted the seat. Tianran Hanshi transmits an older night-and-moon verse whose historical author is not established in the available six-rung evidence and then offers his own matching verse, showing that no single image exhausts the relation.

Senses.Explanation: The expression “raise the proper command in full” (正令全提) brings the proper command fully forward; Chan records place it in martial, governmental, and hall-order language. The “proper command” is operative command language, while “fully raised” marks its complete presentation or exercise.

Senses.Explanation: The Caodong upright position is the relational term opposed to the inclined position. Caoshan Benji identifies it with the empty realm, originally without a thing, while the inclined position is the realm of forms.
