Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2004.xml). Wansong’s Commentary and Chanting on Tiantong Jue’s Verse-Comments on the Ancients: Record of the Congrong Hermitage (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄): Wansong Xingxiu, in (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄) (Wansong's Commentary in the Book of Serenity), identifies the original Lanke woodcutter account.

Senses.Explanation: The rotted axe handle is the records’ time-lapse allusion: a woodcutter watches an immortal chess game and returns after his handle has decayed. The Chan corpus does not usually retell that background in full; it repeatedly names its visible pieces. Fang'an Xian says that when the game ends no one knows where to go, leaving “the Lanke man” sorrowful in the empty mountain (局罷不知何處去，空山惆悵爛柯人). Yuan'an Feng repeats, “the Lanke woodcutter doubts there is a road” (爛柯樵子疑無路). Yongjue Yuanxian lists taking up “the Lanke axe” beside propping a broken-legged pot, while Zhongfeng Mingben says the axe handle has rotted and vanished but the game is not yet finished. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly says that an earlier verse already has the original account of the Lanke woodcutter (已有爛柯樵子本傳). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the rotted handle, woodcutter, unfinished game, and lost road as a compact allusion in case verse and formal speech. The outside story remains an inherited historical lead except where the Chan text names these elements directly.

Senses.Note: Mount Lanke occurs as a compound place-name in several allowlisted texts. One exact place witness is sufficient to establish the distinct referent; the entry makes no claim about the mountain's outside history.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1360.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan (瞎堂慧遠禪師廣錄): Xiatang Huiyuan, in (瞎堂慧遠禪師廣錄) (Extensive Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan), names rain on Mount Lanke.

Senses.Explanation: The same graph pair also forms the proper place-name Mount Lanke. Xiatang Huiyuan says that rain on Mount Lanke pours like a basin while Turtle Ridge's forehead sweats. This geographic referent is not the rotted axe handle or its woodcutter, even though the place-name inherits the same graphs; it therefore has its own sense.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records turn the time before one’s birth into a pointed interview location from which a person’s original face, identity, or decisive word is demanded. Xueyan Zuqin asks what it ultimately is before one’s parents gave birth. An identified lay questioner surnamed Wan turns his surname into a challenge about what he was called before that time. A verse attributed to Huineng answers with ‘originally not a single thing,’ while Tianyin Yuanxiu reports the phrase as a question repeatedly assigned for investigation. Other records keep the answers concrete and discordant: an unnamed monastic asks for the original face, Yushan Shangsi pairs before-birth with a stone mortar fried in oil and after-birth with a steelyard weight dipped in snow, and Zhe’an Jingfan says that recognizing the person in a crowd also reveals this original face. These witnesses support the recurring temporal challenge without promoting any one answer into its definition.

Zen before your father and mother were born
Senses.Explanation: The clause asks about the time before one's parents were born; the seven exact witnesses use it as a teaching contrast, a question, a measure of what is already complete, and a formulation of the face to be seen. Yuanwu Keqin sets 'before father and mother were born' (父母未生已前) against 'after father and mother were born' and the completed body. Gulin Qingmao says that before one's parents were born there was already a line for repaying beneficence (父母未生已前，便有報德酧恩一句). Taiyuan Fu asks Gushan where the nostrils were before one's parents were born (父母未生已前，鼻孔在什麼處). Chushi Fanqi asks how the time before one's parents were born compares with the current occasion (父母未生已前，何似這個時節). Cijue Puyin asks a respondent where he traveled before his parents were born and strikes him as he prepares to answer (父母未生已前，在甚麼處行履). Yinyuan Longqi says that, as for recommendation, it was already finished before one's parents were born (父母未生已前薦拔已竟). Konggu Daocheng links seeing the faces of the buddhas to seeing the face before one's parents were born (父母未生已前面目). The corpus thus bends the temporal clause into a recurring interview boundary and face-formulation; these witnesses do not supply one uniform answer.

Complete Record of Chan Master Juelangsheng of Tianjie (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄): The cited complete recorded-sayings collection (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄): after dismissing the questioning monk, Juelang Daosheng says that the final phrase first reaches the tight barrier and asks for the phrase that gets free of it and walks alone in every direction.

Senses.Explanation: A tight barrier or secured pass: a checkpoint represented as shut against passage and therefore as something to hold, close, break, or get through. In Luopu Yuanan's recorded formula, the last phrase first reaches this barrier, which shuts the critical crossing so that neither ordinary nor sage passes. Yuanwu Keqin repeats the same formula. The records also make the image operational: Puming holds the barrier shut through a ninety-day restriction period and then breaks it open; Baiyu Jingsi holds it with no inside or outside; Juelang Daosheng asks for the phrase that gets free of it. When an unnamed monk asks Tianyin Yuanxiu what the barrier is, Tianyin answers, "Break through it and come meet me." The Zen-loaded phrase is thus not merely a difficult obstacle: it names the deliberately secured final checkpoint that a named record speaker can hold fast and a respondent must break through.

Senses.Explanation: Herding an ox is an action and image, while Oxherding sequences are named picture-or-verse sets and remain a different object. The farm action of tending or herding an ox. In Chan records this action is repeatedly deployed as a comparison. When Mazu Daoyi asks Shigong Huizang what he is doing, Shigong answers that he is herding the ox; he says that whenever it enters the grass he seizes its nose and pulls it back (一回入草去，驀鼻拽將回), and Mazu replies that he truly knows how to herd it (子真牧牛). Baizhang Huaihai compares his handling of an addressee to an oxherd who holds a staff and prevents the animal from trespassing on crops (如牧牛人執杖視之，不令犯他苗稼). Yunqi Zhuhong's preface traces the expression to the comparison of watching an ox with a staff (譬如牧牛，執杖視之，不令縱逸，犯人苗稼), while Guting Shanjian explicitly says that its illustrated use compares the ox with the wild restlessness of human nature (夫謂牧牛者，譬人性之狂掉也). Yunyan Tianyou also attacks the inherited image: after the nose-rope breaks, his verse asks what excrement or wind remains to herd (牧甚屎屁). Zen bends the ordinary action into a publicly tested comparison, while the last witness shows that masters could also overturn it.

Senses.Note: Picture-and-verse and verse-only forms are variants of the same kind of titled sequence, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Oxherding pictures are illustrated and versified Chan sequences that arrange the ox-and-herder image into named stages; the corpus preserves more than one ten-picture order and also warns that diagrams can become stale goods. The Puming arrangement begins with the ox unherded, moves through initial restraint and habituation, and ends with both ox and herder forgotten. A second sequence runs from searching for the ox through finding traces, seeing and gaining it, returning home, forgetting ox and person, returning to the source, and entering the marketplace. Prefaces connect the pictures with older public ox-herding exchanges and invite readers to compare their own position. Yet Zhuhong's preface explicitly says that for someone who enters directly, the picture becomes stale merchandise and the verse surplus talk. Later prefaces likewise treat different arrangements and responses as material for examination, not an invariant prescription.

Senses.Explanation: Oxherding verses are an ordered Chan verse-sequence that stages seeking, finding, handling, losing, and moving beyond the ox. The label is not admitted from contents headings alone: complete sequences follow it in masters’ records, other masters write named harmonizations, and Yuetong publicly tests a request for such verses by saying that one must use one’s own. Jiguang Huo’s record prints the label directly before a staged sequence beginning with entering the hills to seek the ox and continuing through finding tracks, catching, tending, forgetting ox and person, returning to the source, and entering the marketplace. Shiyu Mingfang, Xiangtian Jinian Jingxian, and Fushi Tongxian each supply actual harmonized sequences rather than bare catalogue labels; their opening stage names and first lines are preserved beside the exact headword. The Brocade River lamp biography quotes an oxherding verse after saying its subject harmonized an earlier sequence. When Sanmu asks Yuetong for oxherding verses, Yuetong answers that one must use one’s own and then tests Sanmu’s attempted whisk gesture. The genre is therefore deployed inside an interview as well as transmitted in verse sections.

Senses.Explanation: A child who tends cattle: a herdboy, cowherd boy, or oxherd boy. The term occurs 334 times in 139 allowlisted texts, and Chan records concentrate its distinctive use in oxherding songs, pictures, public questions, and verse. In Puming's ten oxherding verses, the boy holds the grass rope without slack and works all day; later, when there is no ox anywhere, the boy is idle, claps, sings under the moon, and still returns to “one further barrier.” Fenyang Shanzhao's Herdboy Song says that the boy does not copy texts or read a single graph, yet unfolds countless scrolls and handles question and answer. Asked “what is the herdboy's song?” Xuefeng Yicun dances and leaves the teaching hall. Jiashan Lingquan Ziying answers “who is the person within Jiashan's scene?” with “the herdboy sings in the open fields; the woodcutter laughs deep in the clouds.” Dizang Shouen, Danxia Zichun, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Furong Daokai further place the boy in teaching-seat and portrait verse. Zen bends the ordinary cattle-tending child into a recurring actor in staged ox-and-herder sequences, direct interview answers, and teaching-seat songs; different stages of the same herdboy-and-ox deployment are not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: The rhinoceros, chiefly as the animal demanded back from Yanguan Qian's broken rhinoceros-fan case. Yanguan calls for the fan; when his attendant says it is broken, Yanguan demands, ‘Then bring me back the rhinoceros’ (扇子既破。還我犀牛兒來). Later speakers repeatedly raise, verse, answer, and dispute this exchange. Yinyuan Longqi says that once the fan is broken, its head and horns are fully displayed (犀牛扇既破。頭角已全彰). In Shiyu Mingfang's exchange, an unnamed monk claims that Yanguan wrongly called the fan a rhinoceros; Shiyu demands what else it should be called and sets a community fine if the questioner cannot say. Asked what the rhinoceros itself is like, Feiyin Tongrong answers, ‘Its head and horns stand high’ (頭角崢嶸). Baishan Dekai's verse puts down a rabbit-horn staff and picks up the rhinoceros fan; Xuefeng Huikong says that when the fan breaks, the rhinoceros remains; and Pin Jixiang depicts the rhinoceros falling into water when Yanguan uses the fan. The animal-name is thus repeatedly pulled out of its broken fan and handled as a public case-object. The texts do not supply one symbolic meaning for the rhinoceros.

Senses.Explanation: A monkey becomes a recurring answer and acted image in Chan records. Huangbo Xiyun answers a question about Chan, 'a monkey climbs a tree, its tail tumbling over its head' (猢猻上樹尾連顛). Deshan Yuanmi tethers the monkey to a pillar before the buddha appears and puts it into a cloth bag afterward; Poshan Haiming separately answers that a monkey enters a cloth bag. Doushuai Congyue makes two monkeys hang by four tails, while Zhu'an Shigui has a drum-beaten monkey run away when the drum breaks. The Chan-specific bend is this repeated placement of the animal in public answers, paired before-and-after sayings, and impossible stage-scenes; the entry does not assign a hidden meaning to those actions.

Senses.Explanation: The mysterious or profound purport: a hidden or difficult-to-reach gist that is asked about, sought, recognized, or awakened to. The records do not replace it with one stable explanatory proposition. An unnamed monk asks Guizong Zhichang what it is; after saying that no one can understand it and that directing oneself toward it departs from it, Guizong asks, "Who is seeking the mysterious purport?" Other questioners receive deliberately different replies from Zhaozhou Congshen and Zhangyi Daoqin. Jiashan Shanhui gives a reciprocal formulation in which the interlocutor's mysterious purport is Jiashan's tongue and Jiashan's is the interlocutor's tongue. A verse attributed to Sengcan warns that failing to recognize it makes quieting thoughts futile, while a lamp biography says Zhongshan Tancui greatly awakened to it. The Zen bend is the public question itself: this purport is repeatedly demanded from a named respondent, yet the recorded answers redirect the demand rather than reducing it to a portable statement.

Senses.Explanation: A named Caodong road or course: the first graph qualifies the road as dark, hidden, or mysterious, without establishing a physically dark roadway. The allowlisted corpus records 268 occurrences across 116 texts. Dongshan Liangjie himself names it as one of his Three Roads: ‘I have three roads for receiving people: bird course, hidden road, extending the hands’ (我有三路接人，鳥道玄路展手). The compound then moves through independently attributable teaching-seat uses rather than one fixed explanation. Fenyang Shanzhao asks his assembly, ‘What is the hidden road? Is there anyone who understands? Tell Fenyang’ (作麼生是玄路／與汾陽說看). Hongzhi Zhengjue says, ‘One step secretly shifted, the hidden road turns; the whole body released, the aeon-vessel is empty’ (一步密移玄路轉，全身放下劫壺空). Xisou Shaotan puts it at the grass tips—‘penetrate the hidden road’—while Xueguan Zhiyin says a spirit horse may gallop and a numinous crane soar, ‘crossing the hidden road freely, without touching the bird course’ (玄路縱橫，不觸鳥道). Touzi Yiqing says that even after host and guest and spoken question and answer have been established, raising the hidden road from the side is still only halfway (問答言陳，仍玄路旁提為唱／猶在半途). Shanfeng Xian turns it into teaching-hall action: ‘Holding the white staff crosswise, open the hidden road’ (橫拈白棒開玄路). The longer golden-lock family is locally explicit rather than a gloss of the bare road: Caoshan Benji says ordinary feelings and holy views are ‘the golden-lock hidden road’ and must be interchanged, while Yongjue Yuanxian calls exhaustion without the ability to turn the same compound. The Chan bend is therefore the conversion of a hidden or mysterious road into a named Caodong category that can receive, turn, be penetrated, be crossed, be opened, be appraised as halfway, and enter the golden-lock compound. None of those predicates makes it a physically dark roadway or licenses replacing every occurrence with ‘the Way.’

Senses.Explanation: The hidden barrier is a gate to be opened, penetrated, or locked, and it appears in interview questions and barrier imagery across the records. The expression occurs 593 times in 212 allowlisted texts. One penetrates, passes, strikes, breaks, or kicks it down. Speakers ask about ‘the higher hidden barrier,’ call for one who has passed it, and ask publicly how it is passed. One discourse warns that ‘clinging to the hidden barrier’ loses the larger function; another says those not through it often construe Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing merely as facing a wall. Zen bends the gate into a public-interview checkpoint, but no corpus-wide sentence defines fixed content behind it.

Senses.Explanation: Already present, complete, or ready at hand rather than newly produced. Named Chan speakers apply the word to each encountered matter, a public case, immediate use, scenery before the eyes, and everything disclosed in the present scene. Yuanwu Keqin pairs 'this very thing is ready' with 'this very thing is for use'; Ruibai Mingxue asks who lacks what is originally ready, while Hanxiu Xingyun pairs original completeness with everything already present. Chan bends an ordinary word for something ready-made by using it to challenge the search for a result elsewhere, yet the word itself does not tell the reader what the ready thing is in every passage.

Senses.Explanation: A public case that is already complete, present, or ready to hand. The expression is fully attested in Chinese Chan records as a case-term and an utterance. One address says, 'One who comes this way is a ready-made public case.' Another named record subject waits for the assembly to settle, says only that even a ready-made public case cannot be arranged, and steps down. A later record says that whenever an unnamed monk came, Muzhou said, 'Ready-made public case.' Teachers also ask directly what a ready-made public case is and answer with such lines as 'the eastern ravine's water flows into the western ravine; clouds rise on the southern mountain and the northern mountain.' Yuanwu says that before the ready-made public case is spoken its pattern is already manifest, and when its root is raised it leaks through layer after layer. The expression is also followed by 'there is no need to investigate' in fourteen matches across fourteen files. These Chinese uses supply both the literal compound and its deployment as an actual public-case expression.

Senses.Explanation: A coordinate pair naming “principle” and “affairs, events, or matters.” Chan records ask how principle and affairs are unobstructed, say that both sides have been penetrated or are fully provided, and require them to be clearly distinguished. The Mirror Record gives one explicit account of their relation: “This principle is the principle that completes affairs; this affair is the affair that displays principle.” Ying’an says, “Penetrated on the side of principle and penetrated on the side of affairs: this is called principle and affairs fused through.” Other records speak of both being complete or ask directly, “What are principle and affairs?” The expression is translated as the coordinate pair stated by the texts rather than collapsed into one abstract category.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1420.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chushi Fanqi (楚石梵琦禪師語錄): Chushi Fanqi removes the single grass blade and asks where the jeweled towers and jade halls are.

Senses.Explanation: Jeweled towers and jade halls are the palace-image in Baiyun Shouduan's blade-of-grass saying: the palace appears on one grass blade, yet the same blade can cover it. Baiyun Shouduan frames both directions around whether one has truly sweated once. Qianyan Yuanzhang asks how a doubtful listener could make a grass blade into a great body, establish a monastery, or show the palace on it; Feiyin Tongrong recasts the same reversal as making a palace from grass. Later masters keep testing the proportion. Dahui Zonggao accepts the palace appearing on grass but warns against being deceived by its being covered; Yuejian makes the palace cheap as grass in one direction and grass costly as the palace in the other; Chushi Fanqi removes the grass and asks where the palace is; Lianfeng Su asks how grass and palace become one piece.

Public addresses also pair rubble with walls, light, radiance, or gold: “When released, rubble shines; when held fast, gold loses its colour” (放行也瓦礫生煇，把住也黃金失色) explicitly contrasts shining rubble with gold losing colour. The concrete material remains the referent in both literal and evaluative deployments.

Senses.Explanation: The formula says that birth and death is the great matter: the records make it an urgent reason to seek clarification, and several directly explain it as not knowing where birth comes from or where death goes. Dahui Zonggao calls not knowing one's coming the greatness of birth and not knowing one's destination the greatness of death, and names that condition with the formula. Tianru Weize gives the same paired explanation, while Xueyan Zuqin urges listeners to take it as a matter of unsurpassed weight and get it clear. Yuanwu Keqin describes declaring this great matter and one's own affair still unclear as the proper initial reason for approaching an established lineage instructor. Zhongfeng Mingben rebukes people who carry the words in their mouths while hunting a phrase from old paper. Dufeng Xingjian says neither saying nor knowing it is enough, and Shending Yunwai Ze says it cannot be finished through oral proof or acceptance in thought. The entry therefore records urgency, definition, and corrective use without treating repetition of the slogan as its resolution.

Senses.Explanation: Birth and death are the great matter; impermanence is swift is an urgency formula. In its two exact corpus deployments it interrupts postponement: Jinian Jingxian uses it to praise refusing tomorrow’s feast, while Gaofeng Qiaosong Yi recalls it when abandoning ordinary study over whether reading could escape birth and death. Jinian Jingxian asks whether the Wayfarer of Jingshan refused the next day’s feast precisely because he painfully kept the formula in mind, contrasting that refusal with accumulation and delay. Gaofeng Qiaosong Yi’s record places the formula in his own youthful question after seeing chrysanthemums wither and return: can reading avoid birth and death? The next sentence says he stopped his studies.

Senses.Explanation: The noun means other kinds or another class, and Chan records press it through direct questions and the fixed demand to move among other kinds. Its defining Zen deployment is the fixed expression "move among other kinds" (異類中行). Nanquan says people of the time must move among other kinds; challenged on "kind," he puts both hands on the ground. Another witness places the expression beside "although moving in an animal's conduct, one does not receive an animal's recompense" (雖行畜生行，不得畜生報). Cao Dong's record supplies the sharpest lexical boundary: the ancients provisionally borrowed the water buffalo as an "other kind"; it is an other kind in the matter, not an other kind in language (古人權借水牯牛為異類。秖是事上異類。非言語中異類). The entry records these answers and boundaries without deciding what spiritual condition they express.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names movement or conduct “among different kinds,” and Chan records make it a contested classification of how a person goes rather than a zoological destination. Nanquan Puyuan says that Chan monks “must move among different kinds” (須向異類中行), answers Guizong Zhichang’s animal-conduct objection, and elsewhere classifies Daowu Yuanzhi’s withdrawal from an exchange as “moving among different kinds” (他却是異類中行). Caoshan Benji repeats Nanquan’s classification while discussing forms of speech. Langting Ting distinguishes moving among different kinds without cutting off sound and form as the “following fall” (隨墮), alongside the kind-fall and honored-fall. Xieyun Ji uses the phrase of a cat in a playful letter, while Juelang Daosheng tells Huang that earlier people required moving among different kinds and contrasts this with being soaked dead in still water. The shared wording therefore covers named conduct, classification, question-and-answer, and later explanation; the records do not reduce these deployments to a single animal act.

Senses.Explanation: To draw a snake and add feet is to spoil a sufficient figure by adding what does not belong. Langting Jingting applies the phrase to describing an incomparable mind with an added moon image. Huanglong Huinan uses it for saying more than one's share requires; Shanfeng Xian calls his own further remark an added foot; Juelang Daosheng says the ancestral style never needed such additions. Yuan'an Feng playfully reverses the result—adding feet makes a dragon—while Danxia Dangui tags an old question as the needless addition. The shared Chan test is whether extra speech clarifies the live matter or merely decorates and distorts it.

SearchAliases: a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger
Senses.Explanation: A painted cake is repeatedly named as something that cannot feed: the records apply that bodily limit to words, talk, blows, and shouts that likewise fail to satisfy hunger. Literally a cake drawn or painted rather than edible. Chan records make it a stock verdict by completing the image: “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” . In the Xiangyan case, after he cannot answer Guishan's question and searches all the writings he has read for a reply, he sighs, “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” ; the record then has him burn those writings. Dahui's verse pairs it with another ineffective likeness: “how could a shimmering mirage ever stop thirst? When could a painted cake fill hunger?” . The verdict extends beyond writings. One discourse says “discussing the obscure and speaking of the marvelous is like using a painted cake to fill hunger” ; another asks whether wielding the staff and shouting differs from filling hunger with a painted cake . A verse explicitly places it beside “speaking of food never makes one full” . Thus the object keeps its literal non-feeding property while the corpus repeatedly applies it to quoted words, explanations, stock gestures, and other substitutes that it says do not fill hunger.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大慧忌日，拈香云：口似血盆呵佛祖，牙如劍樹罵諸方，而今死入阿鼻獄，看你如何孟八郎。若說佛法供養大眾，雪上加霜；若說世法供養大眾，擔水河頭賣。總不與麼，刺頭入膠盆，別有機關，也是胡孫伎倆。畢竟如何？衝開碧落松千尺，截斷紅塵水一溪。台州光孝入院，云：機輪轉處，作者猶迷；祖令當行，魔軍膽喪。設使言前薦得，畫餅充飢；句下精通，釘樁搖櫓。何如具大種智，有大信根，豁開心眼，洞徹威音，於一毫端現寶王剎，坐微塵裏轉大法輪，便見山林城市初無兩般，佛法世法打成一片。畢竟是什麼人分上事？莫怪渠儂多意氣，佗家曾踏上頭關。釋迦掩室於摩竭，欲隱彌露；淨名杜口於毗耶，葛藤不少。須菩提喝無說以顯道，巡人犯夜；釋梵絕聽而雨花，隨邪逐惡

Senses.Explanation: Right then and there: a temporal expression marking something as occurring without an intervening interval. Shanglan Shun's verse says accumulated ignorance disappears right then; the Five Lamps narrator says Zhitian awakens on the spot when shown the blowing-a-hair case. Huangbo Xiyun uses it for the time of becoming clear without retaining a mark of clarity, while Linji Yixuan uses it for being without further business after turning the light back and recognizing no difference from the patriarchs and buddhas. Huqiu Shaolong says that if listeners trust the presented mind-settling scene, the mind is settled right then. Wuyi Yuanlai attaches the expression to one thought not arising, Miyin to the ice-like disappearance of a raised repentance case, Xuedou Chongxian to a mirror distinguishing beautiful and ugly as soon as it is set up, and the Yongzheng Emperor to a selected saying and discriminating consciousness shattering on the spot. The Zen record prizes the compressed timing, but the word itself remains a temporal modifier: it does not by itself name a teaching, a prescribed exercise, or a distinct temporal entity.

Senses.Explanation: Meeting the occasion means answering or acting aptly at the live trigger-point of an encounter. The phrase can introduce a request—“with one phrase meeting the occasion, please speak the teaching” (一句當機請師說法)—or appraise an immediate response. Feiyin Tongrong strikes the staff and says, “freed through on the occasion; it is no other thing” (當機透脫，更非別物). Yuanwu's verse says that buddhas and patriarchs “value what is ready-made when meeting the occasion” (佛祖當機貴見成) and immediately calls for someone to come before the assembly and settle doubt. Thus the corpus bends a general word for apt timing toward the live occasion of encounter, question, answer, and response.

Senses.Explanation: Miss it face to face is a sharp encounter verdict: the requested matter is already present in the exchange, yet the questioner or audience passes it by at the very moment of meeting it. Jingshan Zhice answers the question why the Tiantai master is beneath his questioner's feet with the headword itself. Sanshan Denglai likewise gives it as the answer when a hypothetical interlocutor calls his reply worlds apart, while Yuanwu Keqin uses it as his answer for the Yunmen house. The phrase also warns an audience against losing the immediate event. Tianyin Yuanxiu says the monastery's timber, tiles, and stones are already turning the teaching wheel and tells the assembly not to miss it face to face; Liao'an Qingyu asks why half the audience still does so despite an overt explanation. In another Yuanwu address, even Yunmen and Muzhou are judged to have missed face to face, so the verdict is not reserved for novices.

SearchAliases: to let it pass right before one's face
to miss what is directly before one
Senses.Explanation: To miss something face-to-face is to fail to recognize what is directly present; speakers apply the warning to a person, ordinary sights, a staff, and an encounter before the assembly. The phrase occurs as a verdict, a warning, and an author's acknowledgment. Meixi Du pairs two kinds of people: those who stand out shoulder it directly, while those confused about the head and recognizing a shadow miss it face-to-face (超群拔萃的，直下荷擔；迷頭認影的，當面錯過). In a letter he says that on first meeting a correspondent he did not recognize the correspondent's freedom and literary quality, “truly what is called missing it face-to-face” (誠所謂當面錯過也); this is the corpus's only formula using “what is called” for the term. Boshan Wuyi says, after asking whether anyone can assess the value of what he has presented, “one still must not miss it face-to-face” (也不可當面錯過). Elsewhere Boshan lists “rice comes from grain, soup from water, and a nun is a woman,” then says “do not miss it face-to-face” (飯是米做底、湯是水做底、師姑是女人做底，切莫當面錯過). Yunxi's record places the warning after “kites fly and fish leap; mountains stand and water flows” (鳶飛魚躍，山峙水流，切莫當面錯過). Panlong calls on his staff to bring news to the assembly, warns them not to miss it face-to-face, raises the staff, and asks whether they understand. The exact phrase occurs 134 times in 67 allowlisted files.

Senses.Explanation: A mass of doubt is something cultivated until it becomes concentrated and then breaks open or is shattered at awakening. The Chan record makes doubt materially mass-like: a discourse says that inside and outside ‘roll into one mass of doubt’ (滾作一箇疑團), and other records speak of making the whole body, sitting, walking, dressing, eating, and even the encountered world into that mass. The same physical grammar governs its end: it is ‘broken through’ (打破疑團), or remains ‘unbroken’ (疑團不破). In an autobiographical public account, repeated blows make Gaofeng Yuanmiao's mass of doubt more acute (疑團愈切). Thus the phrase is not merely ordinary uncertainty; these later Chan records deploy it as the consolidated, bodily condition named around sustained investigation and its reported breaking. The corpus does not make the mass a separate object from the doubt or state a further gloss for the breaking.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a sustained, felt condition of doubt used in inquiry, not a passing uncertainty about a proposition. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly asks what this doubt is and describes it erupting, knotting at the brows, and becoming impossible to put down or drive off. Dahui Zonggao says that while it remains unbroken, life and death press in. Gaofeng Yuanmiao recounts it suddenly arising while he held the question where the one returns, leaving him unable to distinguish directions. Librarian Lai tells Xueyan Zuqin that investigating Chan requires raising it and connects small doubt with small awakening. Preface author Wang Xigun calls not knowing a parent's destination or one's own beginning and end the great doubt of life and death shared across time. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that even uninterrupted conjunction of saying and doubt can become a subtle stealing mind. The corpus thus presents a concentrated condition to be raised and broken, while also warning against treating its continuity as achievement.

Senses.Explanation: To make something clear or bring it to light. Chan biographies repeatedly say that someone brings “the great matter,” “the mind-ground,” or “the essentials of mind” to light. One record lists bringing the great matter to light alongside having one's mind-ground opened through mountains and waters and recognizing one's original face through things encountered; the text supplies these neighboring predicates without making them synonyms. A later address states its aim as having each person “directly bring to light one's own fundamental great matter” (直下發明自己本分大事), anchoring direct instruction rather than retrospective biography. Other biographies say “there will certainly be clarification” (必有發明) or that someone was “not greatly clarified” (不大發明). Those result and degree constructions name the outcome of the same bringing-to-light event, not another lexical referent.

Senses.Explanation: To swear an oath is to make an explicit pledge; the surviving witnesses record different oath contents and do not all describe a public performance. The Xuefeng Genxin row is compiler biography: it says he vowed to travel and then went to Gushan, not that he utters the headword. Another biography records a private vow to travel to China, a training text says one must vow in order to endure discipline, and Baozhi recalls a vow made with an Indian monk. The common element is an explicit pledge, while publicity is not established as defining.

Senses.Explanation: Broad daylight under a blue sky names an openly visible daytime setting. Chan records place it in rebukes against dream-talk, concealment, or extra business, and also retain it in verse; the phrase itself remains the literal daylight image. Zhongfeng Mingben asks why people sitting under broad daylight and blue sky are still bound by drowsiness and distraction. Wuzhun Shifan forbids dream-talk there, then calls his own report dream-talk. Chushi Fanqi joins the phrase to the room's undisguised blows and shouts. Other authors use the same daylight image in Buddha-day verse and case verse, so the entry reports a recurrent visible setting without adding an unattested significance.

Senses.Explanation: Baizhang’s wild fox names the canonical causality case and the fox-body at the center of its retelling. In the received account an old man says that his answer 'does not fall under cause and effect' led to five hundred lives as a wild fox. Baizhang answers the repeated question 'is not blind to cause and effect'; the old man reports release and asks for a monastic funeral. Guishan later responds to the raised story by shaking a door panel, and two monks dispute the easy fall-and-release opposition. Later masters repeatedly reopen the named case: Daxin raises it in the chamber, Wansong heads it as the eighth case, Foyan Qingyuan is tested on it, Shita Xuanmi Li comments on it in a hall address, Hongfu Ziwen versifies it, and Yunju Shuai'an Fancong gives another verse. A fox narrative thus becomes a stable public-case label; the entry reports its documentary parts and later testing without adjudicating cause and effect.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make the top of a hundred-foot pole the place where gaining entry is still insufficient and a further step is demanded, questioned, or refused. Changsha Jingcen’s verse says that even one who has gained entry is not yet genuine and must step forward from the pole-top, with the ten directions as the whole body. Wumen transmits Shishuang’s question asking how to advance, and Fojian Huiqin comments on the moment of advancement. An unnamed monastic puts the fixed question to Fadeng, while Yanguan Qi’an counters by asking what use advancement would have. These divergent responses preserve the pole-top as a public challenge rather than a fixed ladder stage.

a person who can feel pain
Zen have blood under the skin
Senses.Explanation: Blood under the skin is the records' bodily image for someone who registers pain and itching, unlike unresponsive earth and wood. It is consequently used by Gulin Qingmao as a qualification for people addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, Yu'an Zhiji asks the head cook, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.

Senses.Explanation: The whole earth names the maximal terrestrial field brought under a statement. Speakers use it in comparisons, declarations, and encounter formulas: the whole earth may be gathered, called a gate, treated as a person's eye, or included in an appraisal. The phrase supplies the scope of those claims; it does not by itself explain or endorse them.

Senses.Explanation: A paired saying that denies any object as an object before one while locating the meaning immediately there. Its fuller inherited form adds that it is not a presently objectified object and cannot be reached by ear or eye. Senses.Explanation: The records define straight mind against bends, twists, crookedness, and falseness: ‘straight mind means without bends or twists.’ Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，直心是淨土), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 24 times in 17 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a named Chan figure's meetings with people.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make this action a lineage banner for Bodhidharma’s coming while also turning it into a question and a claim that teachers qualify in their own words. Dahui Zonggao twice states the Bodhidharma formula and glosses direct pointing as what every person already has. Huitang Zuxin and Yuanwu Keqin place it in lineage discourse, while Yuanwu also says the branching lineage has no destination outside it. An unnamed monastic asks Juelang Daosheng what the paired formula means. Mengan Siyue compares it to an antelope hanging by its horns, resisting a flat explanatory capture. The evidence supports the recurring banner and its public testing without treating Bodhidharma as the grammatical speaker whenever he is named.

Senses.Explanation: Look-alike words are phrases that resemble an established Chan saying closely enough to be quoted, sought, or traded as if resemblance established understanding. Zhongfeng Mingben condemns pulling resembling language from books to answer the matter of birth and death, and elsewhere refuses to lead people into weeds with it. Foyan Qingyuan criticizes seekers who hunt similar phrases and use them to certify one another. Later speakers repeat the warning about storing, comparing, or testing with such language. The defect named by the corpus is resemblance used as borrowed proof, not ordinary verbal similarity.

Senses.Explanation: To deceive one another is a recurring accusation or warning in Chan address. Faxiu Yuantong, Baichi Xingyuan, and Hongzhi Zhengjue use it when a proposed understanding, an apparently obvious scene, or even lantern and pillar would collude in passing off an answer that has not been seen through. One hall address asks listeners not to blame Faxiu Yuantong for deceiving them if they cannot identify the color of wind. Baichi Xingyuan goes further: even lantern and exposed pillar ‘deceive one another,’ making reciprocal collusion part of the image. Hongzhi Zhengjue uses the negated assurance inside a compact assurance, while Dahui and Yunwai warn against mutual deception. The polarity changes—accusation, warning, or denial—but the reciprocal relation remains one thing.

Senses.Explanation: For two parties to deceive or lead each other astray. Frozen-corpus concordance: 207 exact hits in 111 storage files representing 109 independent works. Chan records repeatedly place this ordinary reciprocal act under negation in the assurance, ‘Only provide the assenting heart; we certainly will not deceive one another’ (但辦肯心。必不相賺), with graphic variants in the verb ‘provide’ and the adverb ‘certainly.’ Yuanwu Keqin closes an address with that formula. Dahui Zonggao uses it after answering an interlocutor's request about how to receive and keep a statement. Zhongfeng Mingben quotes the old formula and elsewhere tells a Chan student to trust his words because they will not deceive one another. Puan Yinsu repeats the assurance, but also asks whether an old worthy's saying amounts to mutual deception (古人恁麼道。莫是相賺麼). Affirmative, negative, and interrogative forms retain the same reciprocal act; the Zen-specific bend is the formula's recurring use as a public assurance tied to an assenting heart.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one's eyebrows fall out in these Chan records. Its wording is the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). Frozen-corpus concordance: 7 exact hits in 6 storage files representing 6 independent works. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 48 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.

SearchAliases: look at the word or saying
Senses.Explanation: To look at a saying is to direct attention to the word, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound often occurs in the longer phrase ‘look at the saying’s head’, where the local wording determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. One recorded questioner seeks written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. The records also criticize the activity: Mingben reports people calling it ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ contrasting this with looking around at one’s selected saying. The Chan bend is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in exchanges and itself subjected to public criticism.

Senses.Explanation: The true Buddha sits within is the final line of Zhaozhou's four-Buddha saying, after gold, wood, and clay Buddhas fail their respective ordeals. Senses.Explanation: The eye faculty is the capacity through which visible form is encountered, distinguished in the records from the object seen and from visual consciousness. Masters and compilers examine whether it is identical with seeing, how it returns to the source, and what remains when root, object, and consciousness are cut off. The Source-Mirror Record distinguishes eye faculty, visible object, and visual consciousness, and describes the faculty as freely observing form. Feiyin Tongrong says that leaving even the eye faculty uncut shows the decisive cut has not occurred. A lamp-record answer says returning to the source through the eye faculty is named Manjusri. Across these uses the faculty is examined as a functional capacity, not reduced to the eyeball or to whatever is seen.

Senses.Explanation: Sand getting into the eye is the stock image of something the eye cannot admit. The Chan record preserves Baishui Benren’s paired saying that the eye cannot take sand and the ear cannot take water, then sets it against the contrary image of an eye containing Mount Sumeru. Baishui Benren states the pair and answers a request for its meaning with “a worthy one without peer.” Hongzhi Zhengjue later quotes the complete exchange. Shending Yikui places “the eye cannot take sand” opposite “the eye contains Mount Sumeru,” making the incompatible capacities explicit in one address. Chushi Fanqi repeats both the exclusion and inclusion formulas and assigns them to contrasting ways of coming and going. Linye Qi invokes the sand-and-water pair after saying that even a displayed auspicious scene would still incur a beating. Daowu Wujin Wen turns the image transitively: if the assembly cannot name the incense burner’s color, he has put sand in their eyes and water in their ears.

Senses.Explanation: The many blind people feeling an elephant each encounter a part and mistake partial contact for the whole animal. Xiangtian Jinian explicitly reads the elephant comparison as exposing the illness of clinging to one's own view. Dahui Zonggao lists it among cases that must be met personally rather than settled in speech. Xutang Zhiyu says the blind know an elephant yet do not see the whole; an unnamed questioner asks Zhaozhou what the true elephant is when each gives a different account, and Zhaozhou answers that there is no reliance—one simply does not know. The Chan bend turns the comparison into a public test of whether partial descriptions are being promoted as complete seeing.

Senses.Explanation: A “blind fellow” is someone a named case participant or commentator charges with failing to see the live point of an exchange while still making claims about it. Puhua hurls the term directly at Linji when Linji calls his action crude, rejecting the distinction of coarse and fine. Linji turns it on listeners who seek elsewhere and 'put a head atop the head,' while Tianyin Yuanxiu uses it for running to other houses instead of seeing immediately. The rebuke also functions as retrospective appraisal. Donglin Changzong asks whether earlier commentators escape being two blind fellows, and later compilations preserve Puhua's insult as the pivot of the Linji encounter. Zen bends ordinary blindness into public failure of discernment. The word does not politely diagnose an error; it exposes a participant, listener, or commentator in the case and often sits next to a threatened beating, shout, or reversal.

Senses.Explanation: To deceive people is a recurring adverse judgement on words, conduct, or inherited interpretations. The phrase retains that ordinary act while Chan records put it under public pressure. Yunmen asks for a saying that does not deceive people, then supplies the substitute response, “Do not say this is the one that deceives people.” Miyun Yuanwu states that deceiving people is no good affair and that a good affair does not deceive people; Fushi Tongxian publicly raises the positive half. Shiyu Mingfang attacks people who deceive others for gain, while Wuzhun Shifan distinguishes deceiving people from deceiving oneself. In the Blue Cliff Record, Longya Judun denies that patriarchs and buddhas intend deception but says that, because people cannot pass through, they nevertheless become deceivers. The phrase therefore becomes a test of sayings, speakers, hearers, and self-deception without losing its transitive meaning or allowing the entry to infer intent where Longya denies it.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: 僧問 assigns “where does the person who knows there is go?” to an unnamed monk; Fachang Yiyu answers afterward.

Senses.Explanation: A person who knows there is is the record’s description of someone who has recognized the matter at issue and can act without borrowing a formula. Zhaozhou Congshen asks Nanquan Puyuan where such a person goes; Yunju Daoying says such a person protects what is known and usually refrains from speaking. Biographers say Kaiyuan Ziqi cuts through language like splitting bamboo. Dawei Zhe and Zhe’an Fan make the type itself a public question and description, while an unnamed monk asks Fachang Yiyu for that person’s destination. The phrase marks demonstrated recognition in conduct and speech, not possession of miscellaneous information.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2012A.xml). Essentials of Transmitting the Mind by Chan Master Duanji of Huangbo Mountain (黃檗山斷際禪師傳心法要): Huangbo Xiyun says undigested intellectual understanding is all poison.

Senses.Explanation: Intellectual understanding is knowing reached through interpreting or explanation. The corpus overwhelmingly uses the term as a rebuke or warning. Its flagship form is 'a follower of the intellectual-understanding lineage' (知解宗徒, 40 occurrences), a label applied to Shenhui and Guifeng Zongmi: even Shenhui and Guifeng were rejected as followers of intellectual understanding (神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒). In an origin case, a student names the matter 'Buddha-nature at the original source,' and Huineng says that even if this fellow later founds a place, he will become only a follower of intellectual understanding (此子已後設有把茅蓋頭，只成得箇知解宗徒). Another passage puts a whole list of teaching styles under the same verdict (此等見解盡屬知解宗徒). The common gate-entry warning 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) occurs 90 times in 65 files representing 63 works. Mi'an Xianjie continues by comparing its non-arising to the king's sword. Other records say people are deceived by intellectual understanding and conjecture (多被知解卜度瞞過), or that the matter is not an affair on the side of intellectual understanding (不是知解邊事). The headword occurs 1,186 times in 237 files representing 234 independent works. This entry reports the corpus's repeated pejorative deployment without turning it into a general theory of mind. Huangbo Xiyun extends the term through a food-and-digestion comparison: 'what is called intellectual understanding not digested is all poison' (所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥). Parallel witnesses preserve the same wording in two other collections.

Senses.Explanation: The stone woman is a stock impossible figure who bears a child, dances, sings, plays music, or acts beside a wooden man in Chan verse and public answers. Pumen Xibian groups her bearing a child with dust rising from a well bottom, waves rising on a mountaintop, and an empty flower bearing fruit. Dongshan Liangjie pairs the wooden figure singing with the stone woman dancing; Qingshan Shoulong places her playing a reed organ under water. Hongzhi Zhengjue, Baiyu Si, Yandang Wenji, and Shu'an Fancong retain the same impossible woman across answer, verse, and appraisal. No stored witness makes the headword a stone statue or named historical person.

Senses.Explanation: A stone ox barring the ancient road places an immovable animal across an inherited route. Chan masters use the line as a demand for a word beyond lip movement and pair it with impossible horse-birth formulas, making blockage and generative impossibility meet in one capping phrase. Yuejiang Zhengyin asks for a word that does not touch lips and answers with the stone ox barring the ancient road. Luoshan Daoxian gives the line after a companion fails to answer the staff thrust before his face, then adds “one horse, no paired foal.” Baoning Zhongfang pairs the old-road stone ox with one horse producing three tiger-cubs.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 上堂，舉世尊一日以兜羅綿手舉金色波羅華普示大眾，時迦葉破顏微笑，世尊云：吾有正法眼藏、涅槃妙心付囑於汝。師云：一盲引眾盲，相牽入火坑。

Senses.Explanation: Breaking into a smile is Kashyapa's recorded response when Shakyamuni Buddha raises a flower before the assembly. In the Chan record the action is not a settled badge of approval: masters repeatedly raise the same scene and then praise, question, or attack the reported exchange. Wanru Tongwei and Dahui Zonggao contrast Kashyapa's smile with the assembly's failure to respond; both place the reported charge immediately afterward. Yuansou Xingduan retells exactly that sequence and caps it with ‘one blind person leads a crowd of blind people’ (一盲引眾盲), while Juelang Daosheng asks whether the eye reportedly handed over was originally present or absent. The stable fact is the case action and its place in the exchange; the later verdicts do not supply a second meaning of the phrase.

Senses.Explanation: Polishing a tile to make a mirror names the impossible task Nanyue Huairang stages in his exchange with Mazu Daoyi. Huairang polishes a tile and says he is making a mirror; when Mazu objects, Huairang asks how sitting Chan could then make a buddha. Later records reuse the compact case-name as a comparison for wasted or over-solicitous effort. Fachang Yiyu compares private explanations and forced elaboration to the task; Shending Yikui groups it with striking the cart or ox and calls both children’s play; Tian’an Sheng includes it in a rapid list of ancestral demonstrations judged excessively solicitous; Luyan He pairs it with making a meal from steamed sand and angling for a fierce dragon with a straight hook. The records preserve Huairang’s public correction and repeatedly reopen its impossible action.

Senses.Explanation: The meaning or point of the patriarch's coming from the West, with the patriarch understood in these records as Bodhidharma coming to China. The words usually form a stock public question rather than a request for travel history. Named respondents answer with a cypress, washing feet, a Chan board, ripe plums, a fan, landscape lines, a refusal, or a demand that the questioner turn toward his own intent. Dahui Zonggao can also name it as a topic for which there is not yet time to speak, and Zhongfeng Mingben warns that interchangeable verbal explanations miss it. The phrase therefore names one recurring question whose Chan force lies in the publicly testable answer, not a fixed route or a single explanatory paraphrase.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan visitor is a monastic participant addressed or identified within the public life of a named master’s community. Linji points the hall toward two such visitors after their exchange; Foyin interprets visitors' bows before the assembly; Dazhu addresses arriving students by the title; Nanyang examines one from the south; and Yanguan challenges the visitors to supply a turning phrase. Verse writers also address this audience. The term therefore marks an active interview participant or visiting student, not simply any traveler.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan sickness is not an illness belonging to Chan itself but a diagnosed error in how people investigate, certify, imitate, teach, or seek recognition; Dahui states that distinction explicitly and later masters keep applying it publicly. Dahui Zonggao says Chan has no headache, leg pain, deafness, or dim sight: the sickness lies in practitioners' differences of investigation, certification, effort, and dependence on teachers. Yunwai Xingze quotes that diagnosis while addressing requests to expose contemporary faults. Hanyue Fazang's letter praises Dahui for exhausting the human sicknesses of Chan, and the receiving master punctuates the reading with shouts. Yingning Jing identifies cleverness, accumulated explanation, and imitation among contemporary illnesses; Tianran Hanshi attacks the pursuit of reputation by teachers and students.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan monastery is the named residential institution in which an abbot presides and a recorded teaching career is located. Lamp colophons identify Puming and Huirì Yunwen through the Chan monasteries where they serve as abbots. Transmission rosters attach named lineage figures to Baoing Chan Monastery, while collected-record contents organize successive bodies of sayings by Ciyun, Lianfeng, and Shousheng Chan Monasteries. A preface treats restoring Zhaojue Chan Monastery from overgrown ground as a major institutional act. The Chan bend is documentary and public: the monastery is not generic scenery but the named seat that locates a lineage figure, an abbacy, a body of sayings, and the restoration or transmission of the lineage.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。問：「海眾臨筵，側聆師誨。如何是燈節一句？」師云：「騰輝遍大千。」進云：「我見燈明佛，本光瑞如此。」師云：「如何是本光？」僧指燈，師云：「瞎。」進云：「爍破乾坤。」師云：「還見山僧麼？」僧喝，師云：「不得禮拜。」僧作禮，師云：「眼私鹽漢。」乃云：「天上月圓，人間月半。若道是月半，則違卻天上；道是月圓，則違卻人間。道得平等句子，許你天上人間；若道不得，萬古碧潭空界月，再三撈摝始應知。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB187.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Tian’an Sheng (天岸昇禪師語錄). Speaker: Tian'an Sheng.
Occurrences.VariantForm: 萬古碧潭空界月，再三撈摝始應知

Occurrences.Kwic: 結冬上堂，僧問：「一槌打就，固是好手；點著便來，不妨伶俐。紅爐上雪片即不問，堂裏聖僧道個甚麼？」師云：「西山有老虎。」進云：「恁麼則萬古碧潭空界月，再三撈摝始應知。」師乃云：「今朝十月十六，較之去歲前年，千足萬足。羅夢章居士為我新蓋法堂七間，權可安眾，寮房又添得幾間茅屋。監院知客直歲安單有序，上下內外雍雍肅肅。山田薄收得晚禾蚤穀，不用休糧方，人人俱飽腹。呵呵呵！好快活。知事頭首不肯安分，更要剋期結制，做瘡剜肉。眾中有個漢，聞山僧恁麼道，便出來大叫：『長老！長老！你與麼說話，與我置之高閣。我等出家，秪為不明生死，不遠千里百里而來，究竟佛法，一字不聞，終日普梆，忙忙碌碌，不是擔柴運土，便要磨磨舂穀，稍有遲回，便乃打罵如雷。及至今朝，又說恁麼話，教我晚輩後生如何棲泊？』山僧向你道：『上座！上座！與麼則老僧罪過。』」卓拄杖，下座。

Occurrences.Kwic: 開元寺大雄寶殿陞梁上堂，僧問：梵宇輪奐即不問，如何是接物利生底句？師云：空中書梵字。進云：恁麼即重重寶閣雲中現，萬象森羅盡點頭。師云：古殿正重興。僧禮拜，師乃云：插標建剎，充塞十方。剖塵出經，掘開寶藏。向無佛處作佛，五綵繪虗空；於無法處說法，萬竅鳴天籟。海底之泥牛駕浪，雲中之木馬嘶風。夜明簾外振家聲，無影樹頭布春色。正當恁麼時，開元古殿輪奐維新，林泉舊蹤徽猷不替。勇破四魔成佛，名曰大雄；廣闢華藏玄門，來者直入。若千林之互照，如兩鏡之含光。涉入重重，無壞無雜。嚴佛土於億劫，贊皇圖於永年。誘引諸子，推排出火宅之門；拯拔迷流，踊躍登菩提之岸。且道畢竟從甚麼處建立？良久，云：拈出紅爐一點雪，長作人間六月冰。復舉：開元瑩禪師上堂語云：有一面鏡，到處懸掛。凡聖不來，誰上誰下？拈拄杖，云：這箇是拄杖，那箇是鏡？良久，云：萬古碧潭空界月，再三撈摝始應知。師云：歷劫無名，彰為古鏡。只要諸人知有，不為他影子所惑。瑩禪師大有為人處，山僧今日亦有一偈，不免舉似大眾：有一面鏡，到處懸掛。凡聖普現，非內非外。豎拂子，云：這箇是鏡，喚甚麼作拂子？還委悉麼？分明覿面別無真，休更迷頭猶認影。下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1442.xml). Drafts from Chan Master Weilin’s Traveling Hermitage (為霖禪師旅泊菴稿). Speaker: Kaiyuan Ying. Selected for clean exact-turn ownership and a distinct deployment class.

Senses.Explanation: The couplet pictures the moon of open space reflected in a blue pool and says that repeated dredging is needed before one knows it. Jiangshan Faquan states the couplet after a pause at the close of his mirror-and-staff hall address. The “Zhaojue Qin said” marker assigns the closing couplet to Yuanwu Keqin after his two-person comparison.

Senses.Explanation: All things are consciousness-only is an inherited proposition that Chan records repeatedly put under pressure in face-to-face questioning. Yongming Yanshou presents it as a scriptural formula, but Huangbo Xiyun says the paired mind-only and consciousness-only wording was spoken against outside wrong views and refuses to make it a final resting place. Xitang Zhizang asks a purple-robed lecturer to state consciousness-only, then points to the door panel and asks what it is. In the Fayan case, Luohan Guichen invokes the same formula before asking whether a courtyard stone is inside or outside mind. Bie'an Xingtong retells Guichen’s test after rejecting the explicitly unnamed questioner’s conceptual explanation as ‘not yet’; Dahui Zonggao likewise describes Xiaonan as having mastered the formula before a separate encounter overturned that settled account. The entry therefore records both the proposition and its observable Chan deployment as material for testing. It does not adopt an outside systematic exposition as the definition of Zen.

Senses.Explanation: The myriad things return to one: the opening clause of a stock public question (萬法歸一). It most often forms the first clause of the stock question, 'The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一；一歸何處). In Zhaozhou Congshen's case the answer is: 'When I was in Qingzhou; I made a cloth shirt, weighing seven catties' (我在青州；作一領布衫，重七斤). The corpus preserves other answers without making any of them a dictionary gloss: Wenshu Yingzhen says, 'The Yellow River has nine bends' (黃河九曲); Baizhang Mingzhao An says, 'There has not been a single person who did not ask' (未有一箇人不問); Shending Yikui answers the first clause with 'rain comes, the mountain colors darken' (雨來山色暗), then answers the second with 'clouds clear, the moon is newer' (雲淨月彌新). The phrase is therefore not merely a proposition. Zen records bend it into the opening move of a portable public-interview case whose second clause and sharply speaker-specific answers must remain attached. Juelang Daosheng answers the inherited question by challenging who taught the monk to ask it; Zhean Fan raises the Zhaozhou version and comments on its pressure. Both keep the headword as the first clause of the same public question.

Senses.Explanation: Yazhou, ten thousand miles away names an extreme distance. Masters use the place formula as a spoken verdict: a proposed middle, a two-sided escape, a delayed answer, or another proposed position or verbal move is nowhere near. Shexian Guisheng answers the upward matter with the full departing-for-Yazhou couplet. Zhongfeng says trying to suppress motion and stillness is not yet even as near as Yazhou; Guanghui Lian rejects both having and lacking guest and host; Shanhui applies it when neither side nor middle remains; Yuan’an Liao answers one participant with a remade couplet; Yanxi Guangwen applies it to grasping “not mind, not buddha.”

Senses.Explanation: The scale weight is the dense iron counterweight used in weighing. Masters exploit that physical hardness and fixed weight in public answers: Mingjue Cong calls it seven catties; Guyin Yuncong and Quanan Qiji say that stepping on it is hard as iron. Tian’an Sheng and Qigang Zong deliberately force the impossible image further, pressing the iron weight for golden juice or oil. The corpus keeps the concrete implement visible while using its resistant material in replies and attached verses.

Senses.Explanation: The Mirror of Qin is a named mirror repeatedly brought into Chan verse and exchange as an instrument before which a form, a speaking participant, or the person himself is exposed and distinguished. In the Recorded Sayings of Master Baiyu, Baiyu Jingsi says that before the mirror a jackal has no way to hide its original form; in the Recorded Sayings of Konggu Daocheng, Konggu Daocheng hangs the mirror at the head of a staff and says that every dust-mote land becomes responsive. In direct questioning recorded in the Recorded Sayings of Master Hansong, Hansong Zhicao answers after the absence of the mirror prompts the question how one can distinguish the matter. The compilers Jing and Yun, narrating Xuefeng Yicun's biography in the Zutang Collection, place Xuefeng face-to-face with the mirror and tell him to inspect himself. These are observable deployments of the mirror in appraisal and exposure, not a claim that every mention carries one secret fixed meaning. The headword occurs 29 times in 25 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: Moving a step is ordinary bodily movement made diagnostic in Chan positional language. Masters demand it after sustained exertion, pair it with turning the body, or place it before a bright hall: the step tests whether a respondent can leave the position already occupied. Hansong Zhicao says that strenuous pressure still is not ‘moving a step’; when he asks whether the assembly knows the move, he shouts ‘put it down.’ Zhe'an Jingfan pairs moving a step with turning the body in the work of an effective teacher. Hongzhi Zhengjue places moving a step before the bright-moon hall beside turning the mechanism on a crystal ground. The repeated positional pair shows a demanded shift, while ordinary travel occurrences remain a falsification class.

Senses.Explanation: Before the empty aeon is a deliberately unreachable temporal boundary repeatedly posed as the topic of an interview, a claim of realization, or a Caodong case-position. Wuyi Yuanlai asks his summer assembly whether the matter before the empty aeon has yet corresponded with them and ties failure to continuing birth-and-death. Linquan Conglun’s commentary asks whether Dongshan’s silence means he understood before the empty aeon and then refuses an easy endorsement. The phrase functions less as chronology than as a public boundary at which present understanding is tested.

Senses.Explanation: Before the empty eon is the deliberately impossible position before differentiation from which masters demand an answer about oneself, one's parents, or the matter at hand. Across the stored cases, masters ask what one was before the empty eon, demand speech from there, warn that merely speculating there misses present functioning, and use the phrase as a test rather than as a historical date.

Senses.Explanation: A flower in empty space is an apparent flower where no external flower stands. The stored Chan witnesses call the three realms flowers in empty space, pair true speech and false speech with flowers in empty space and the moon in water, say dream-illusion flowers need not be grasped, and compare seeing and hearing to flowers in empty space. These uses consistently present an appearance or image as lacking the solid object a viewer might seize, but the present evidence does not store the diseased-eye formula that would explain its optical cause.

Senses.Explanation: a nest or mortar; in the Chan record, a fixed mould into which words and conduct settle. The corpus speaks of falling into another's rut (墮他窠臼, "fall into his fixed rut") as oil enters flour and cannot get out, and of both inherited gestures and current fashions as ruts: "killing buddhas and patriarchs" falls within the old people's enclosure, while wielding the staff and shout does not escape the present-day rut (殺佛殺祖，盡落古人圜繢；行棒行喝，不脫今時窠臼). One record pairs new and old while saying "jump out of the rut" (一新一舊，跳出窠臼). The decisive corpus warning is recursive: pupils may mistake Yuanwu Keqin’s refusal to establish a rut and thereby make "no rut" into a rut (以無窠臼為窠臼, "take having no rut as a rut"). Thus the Chan deviation is not merely an ordinary habit: the term names repeatable religious speech, gestures, formats, and even anti-formulas once followers preserve them as a template.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula “Where you stand is all genuine” is paired with acting as host wherever one is, then repeated as a Fayan-house characterization and as a predicate of immediate use. Literally, at the place of standing or taking one's position , all is genuine or real : "where you stand is all genuine." It occurs 35 times in 24 allowlisted texts. Linji's record supplies the governing formula twice: "act as host wherever you are; where you stand is all genuine; arriving circumstances cannot turn you around" . The second passage precedes it with "do not receive another person's delusion" and follows it by warning that a single doubtful thought gives an opening. Jingtu Huimin reverses its paired order as "where you stand is all genuine; act as host according to the place" . Zhongyan Huayan Zujue attaches it to "take it up and immediately use it" , while Zhenjing Kewen explicitly quotes Linji's wording as "bring it and immediately use it; where you stand is all genuine" . Chan bends the ordinary idea of a standing-place into a stable Linji roster phrase about taking the host position amid changing circumstances; the entry reports the formula and its transmitted predicates without adding a claim beyond those recorded predicates.

Senses.Explanation: Standing in the snow primarily recalls Huike’s vigil before Bodhidharma; a separate image compares a white heron standing in snow. Huike's vigil in the snow before Bodhidharma. Huike, still called Shenguang in the account, stands unmoving through a night of heavy snow until it rises above his knees, and Bodhidharma asks, “You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?” (汝久立雪中，當求何事). Retrospective formulas join “standing in the snow” with “cutting off the arm” (立雪斷臂), transmission of the robe and bowl, and Huike's request for the buddhas' essential way. Later masters preserve conflicting appraisals: Shuwei Tongxuan says, “standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing,” while Bailu Xianduan calls “the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind” unworthy. It also becomes a stock public question—“what is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?”—to which Jiangshan Faquan answers, “a leap month comes once in three years.” The ordinary weather action has thus become the compact name of a lineage encounter and a recurring interview prompt.

Senses.Note: The heron forms (鷺鶿 and 鷺鷥) are graphic variants within one physical-action family. The direct answer and the verse comparison are different deployments of the same bird-and-snow scene, not further senses.

Senses.Explanation: To raise or hold upright the whisk, the teaching-seat implement and emblem of authority. The action occurs as an answer, demonstration, and object of public questioning rather than as a gesture with one fixed message. Nanta Guangyong answers a question about Manjusri's teacher by raising the whisk. Zhaozhou Congshen raises it when asked whether he will receive the person who sets the realm in order. Yuanwu Keqin twice raises it and says, "Just this is it." Yunmen Wenyan reopens an older exchange in which a monk asks Zifu Zhensui the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk. Deshan Yuanming classifies raising a finger and raising the whisk as a dead phrase. In the dominant spelling, Baiyu Jingsi raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, while Yinyuan Longqi raises it as his answer to a new-command question and then tests the monk's shouts. The Zen bend is the action's institutional and interview setting: it is the presiding master's implement raised as an answer or challenge, while the corpus refuses a universal symbolic decoding. Xueyan Zuqin twice raises the whisk within hall addresses—once before calling unfreed affective dust blindness, and once before a moon verse. The surrounding sayings differ, but the referent remains the same public action with the teaching-seat implement.

Senses.Explanation: Raising a finger is the compact action-form used in records and verses of Juzhi's one-finger response. The corpus distinguishes the action's original transmission, a novice's imitation, later reenactment, and masters' explicit criticism of copied gestures. Lamp compilers use “Juzhi raises a finger” as a case label, and the Juzhi narrative separately reports Tianlong raising a finger, the novice imitating it, and Juzhi's response. Verse collections then compress the action into a case emblem. Zhongfeng Mingben and Xisou Shaotan explicitly criticize copied fist-raising and finger-raising. The shorter headword therefore includes the famous case but is not confined to approving reenactment.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 百尺竿頭坐底人。雖然得入。未為真。百尺竿頭須進步十方世界現全身。
ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2005.xml). The Gateless Barrier (無門關): Changsha Jingcen owns the exact quoted clause in the complete case.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 百尺竿頭坐底人。雖然得入。未為真。百尺竿頭須進步十方世界現全身。

Senses.Explanation: The step beyond the top of a hundred-foot pole, where the image leaves no footing for another step. The fixed phrase and case title are drawn from Changsha Jingcen's verse: the person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole, although having gained entry, is not yet real; the verse then requires a step forward and says that the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body (百尺竿頭坐底人，雖然得入，未為真；百尺竿頭須進步，十方世界現全身). Wumen Huikai's Case 46 titles the case Stepping Forward from the Pole-top and attributes the question “atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?” to Shishuang Qingzhu (石霜和尚云，百尺竿頭如何進步). Fojian Huiqin's later verse explicitly names Old Changsha at the time of the pole-top step (百尺竿頭進步時……老長沙). The phrase then circulates as a public question: Yexian Guixing answers “the southern continent, the northern continent” (南贍部洲，北欝單越), Linye Qi answers “then retreat” (退後即得), and Shanduo Zhenzai answers “a beheaded boatman goes down to Yangzhou” (斷頭船子下揚州). Langye Huijue places the pole-top step beside a saying with no intent in the phrase and no phrase in the intent, then asks how to breathe out. Zen bends the impossible ordinary action into a named case, a quoted verse-line, and a repeatedly answered public question; the records give different answers without changing the action denoted.

Senses.Explanation: A second moon is an apparent duplicate: visible or asserted beside the first, but not a second lunar object established in its own right. Masters challenge claims that add another position by asking which moon it is, call even refined sayings a second moon, and contrast first and second in direct questions; explanatory records also list it with reflections and optical appearances. In the broom case, an unnamed temple director asks where there could be a second moon, while Xuansha Shibei separately supplies, 'this is still a second moon,' as a substitute answer.

Senses.Explanation: “To take it as an answer about Buddha” marks a mistaken way of understanding a reply to “What is Buddha?”. The records do not name a gathering. One critic says that communities merely take the reply this way; in the repeated encounter, the reply is followed by an instruction not to understand it this way after the questioner offers thanks. The final graph functions as understanding or construing the reply, while the preceding words supply the Buddha-answer reading being refused.

Senses.Explanation: A reply is an answering turn treated as an object of request, thanks, criticism, or discrimination inside an exchange. An unnamed monk thanks Caoshan Baoji Xiong for one; other monks ask Mengxi and Shuangquan to provide one. Luohan Ji cites critics who call a particular reply an added fetter, Tiantai Deshao warns that fluent discrimination among replies can still produce inverted understanding, and Dongchan Qi asks whether another reply is still required. The term names the response-turn and the corpus's scrutiny of it, not proof that the response is adequate.

Senses.Explanation: Gruel-and-rice breath is the meal-fed breath behind speech, turned in Chan records into a cutting name for verbal display that does not itself settle the matter under question. Zhaozhou Congshen gives the phrase itself when asked for the true teaching eye. The answer makes ordinary meal-fed breath occupy the place where the questioner requests an elevated principle, without converting food into a hidden substance. Elsewhere the compound is explicitly critical. Jiufeng Shao says rehearsed material brought to the hall only smokes the community with gruel-and-rice breath; Tiebian Yunshao says even seamless question-and-answer can amount to empty drumming with it. Xuetang Daoxing applies the verdict to surplus commentary on Yunmen, while Zhongfeng Mingben and Baiyan Fu use the same drumming image when judging inherited encounter performance. The repeated job is to expose impressive talk as still powered by eating and breathing. The phrase can therefore be an answer or a criticism, but those are deployments of one image rather than different things. It does not mean gruel’s aroma, and it does not make ordinary meals contemptible.

Senses.Explanation: A refuse heap is where discarded filth is piled. Chan masters make it a place for burying pretension and rejected words, yet the same corpus pictures a full-sized golden body appearing on its top and a bright pearl found there; the heap does not itself fix the value of what appears on it. A question in the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps contrasts Yunmen’s threat to beat Shakyamuni with a threat to smother Yunmen on a refuse heap; the recorded reply is thirty blows. Zhenjing Kewen says ten or five muddy, indiscriminate fellows like Yunmen could be buried in the refuse heap without fault. Xuedou Chongxian says a full-sized golden body appears atop the refuse heap, then sets the line aside before pressing the case further. Dongshan Shouchu likens his joy to finding a bright pearl on a refuse heap. Shiyu Mingfang says he cast a worn-out whisk onto such a heap for more than ten years. These opposed predicates keep the literal locale stable.

Senses.Explanation: The top of a dung-sweepings heap is the refuse pile where discarded and filthy things collect. Chan masters repeatedly make it the unlikely place where a jewel, treasure, robe, shoe, or even a golden body is found, while also using the same heap for adding still more rubbish. Juelang Daosheng says the Buddha found a mud pellet on the heap and raised it before the assembly. Muting Pufu calls a display of pots, tiles, bamboo scraps, and bricks “adding more rubbish atop the dung heap.” Xuedou Chongxian places a sixteen-foot golden body on the heap before setting that proposition aside. Changling Zhuo’s verse says treasure is found there without seeking. Dongshan Liangjie compares joy after leaving holy truth undone to finding a bright pearl on the heap. Yehai Ziqing says he found a torn robe there and kept it for decades. Mi’an Xianjie uses the rubbish-adding frame after saying that even forgetting both delusion and awakening remains additional refuse.

Senses.Explanation: A dung basket is a coarse cleaning implement that Chan speakers repeatedly call for beside a broom as an answer, a dismissal, or a cap on an exchange. Chonghui answers praise comparing his assembly with Vulture Peak by calling for a dung basket and broom. Another interview gives 'dung basket and broom' as the third phrase. Later commentators repeat the call while criticizing displays involving a bright pearl. Shuangfeng Xinghui places the basket in Hanshan's hands, and Guanghui Yuanlian summons an attendant to bring it after an exchange.

Senses.Explanation: To submit a failed showing is to be publicly charged with, or made to concede, a particular failure in an encounter or address. Zhanran Yuancheng refuses another failed showing after the proclamation; Juelang Daosheng contrasts exposing ancestral failures with submitting one; Xutang Zhiyu charges Shakyamuni with submitting one at death; and Yuanwu Keqin applies the phrase to a clumsy public display. The lay official Feng Ji directs the accusation at Dahui Zonggao, while a genuinely unnamed monk directs it at Xutang Zhiyu. Each verdict remains limited to the showing under review.
