Senses.Explanation: Dafang Xinghai's mountain verse is the corpus's direct plant action: he is too indolent to gather purple fungus beside the stream (懶去溪邊採紫芝). The plant-name circulates much more widely in the compound Purple Fungus Song. Tiantong Shanxin is publicly asked what that song is and answers by clapping; Fahua Quanju answers an independent transmission of the question by saying that it is not a Wu sound but must be Han speech (不是吳音，切湏漢語). Yongjue Yuanxian asks who will join a solitary recluse in singing it (中有幽人守貞獨，誰來同唱紫芝歌), Xisou Shaotan places groups of two and three singing it on stones under pine roots (三三兩兩松根石上唱紫芝歌), and Yuanwu Keqin asks who can sing it in the season of high mountains, autumn wind, and a single goose (誰當此時節，解唱紫芝歌). Wuwen Daocan separately invokes the Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang and their heart of withdrawal, but his verse does not contain the headword. Zen bends the plant-name into a song asked about in public interviews and sung in mountain-retreat verse. The evidence does not make the bare word itself the title of a second thing.

Records use the term both as an institutional event heading and as an action in Xueguang’s biography: Xueguang winters at Jingde, while the records of Shiqi Tongyun and Hanxiu Ruqian mark the winter opening immediately before a hall address. The event can be formally sponsored. Muchen Daomin’s Northern Journey Collection records an imperial command to open the hall and winter assembly, with court officers carrying incense before Muchen Daomin takes the seat. Yulin Tongxiu asks the gathered community what will keep this winter from betraying their lives; Ruibai Mingxue says a general tea was prepared because of the winter assembly and asks what the monastery will offer its arrivals. The term names the institutional opening, not a weather description and not a private exercise. Closely related opening and closing formulas remain separate entries or cross-references.

Senses.Explanation: To revive after being cut off: the records use a death-and-revival image in a recurrent teaching-seat formula and in explicit criticism of that formula. Its dominant fixed formula is ‘let go at the cliff and personally assent and undertake it; revive after being cut off, and you cannot deceive anyone’ (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再甦，欺君不得). Records also place it after ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), beside ‘shed skin and exchange bones’ (去皮換骨), and compare it with a cold ember flaming and a withered tree flourishing again. Tianqi Benrui explicitly departs from the inherited formula: ‘the former sages all wanted to revive after being cut off; I am not like that.’ The entry reports this recurrent sequence and its criticism without deciding what state the phrase denotes.

Senses.Explanation: The term names an observable walking circuit or action, with records specifying its timing, direction, companions, and coordination with rest. Literally, to 'go along walking' or 'walk about.' The term occurs 1,022 times in 273 allowed texts and names an observable bodily action. A late biography makes the direction explicit: at night a recluse goes outside the crag to walk about, the visiting master follows, and 'each walks east and west' (隱者出巖外經行，師亦隨之，第東西各步). A Five Lamps address pairs physical condition and action: 'when well, walk about; when tired, rest' (健即經行困即歇). The same collection records Layman Feng Ji walking about the teaching hall with Foyan when a child recites a line, and records another unnamed questioner 'walking under the pines one evening' when he hears a mountain spring (一夕，松下經行，聞巖泉聲). In the collected old cases, Sudhana searches in all four directions for seven days and finds Meghashri 'walking slowly on another peak' (在別峰上徐步經行). Daily timing is also explicit: a biography says an unnamed questioner ate only after serving the assembly, while Bingseng watched him 'walk about after each meal' (每飯罷經行時). The term is frequently coordinated with sitting and lying as one of the body's recorded activities. These places, times, directions, companions, and contrasts support the plain action word.

Senses.Explanation: Vimalakirti is the pre-Zen householder whom Chan masters repeatedly raise in public interviews and comments. His exact name occurs 263 times in 116 allowlisted texts. Linquan Conglun directly notes that the Sanskrit Vimalakirti means 'Stainless Renown' and is also rendered Jingming (梵語維摩詰，此云無垢稱，亦云淨名). The dominant Chan deployment is his sickroom and silence: Manjusri asks him about entry into the gate of not-two, Vimalakirti remains silent, and later masters test that silence rather than merely repeat it. Yuanwu raises the exchange as a case; Dahui cites both Vimalakirti's account of illness and his silence; Weilin Daopei invokes the empty sickroom while addressing illness. Xuedou asks what Vimalakirti said, Fenyang would give Vimalakirti and Manjusri thirty blows, and Yun'e Xi calls his closing his mouth 'eating salt to stop thirst.' The Zen Vimalakirti is therefore the seated, sick, silent figure whom masters question, rebuke, praise, and reuse—not an imported life story.

Senses.Explanation: The organizing framework by which a lineage's inherited sayings and distinctions are arranged and identified. The image joins a net's main cord (綱) to an ancestral line or school (宗). Huiyan Zhizhao's preface to the Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) places 'the key outlines of the five houses' (五宗綱要) beside 'the terms of the lineage framework' (綱宗語句), including the names and decisive details that an abbot is expected to know. Named-house compounds show the same category applied to particular lineages: Lin Xuan speaks of 'the Linji lineage framework' (臨濟綱宗), while Lin Zhifan writes of 'the Caodong lineage framework' (曹洞綱宗) being restored after confusion. Zhean Jingfan quotes Yantou Quanhuo: 'Only recognize the lineage framework; originally there is no actual thing' (但識綱宗，本無實法). Juelang Daosheng raises Yantou's other formula: 'For the great governing lineage framework, first one must recognize the phrase' (大統綱宗，先須識句). The term travels with verbs such as establish, uphold, display, grasp, and restore. Zen bends the net's main cord into the named structural vocabulary by which a teaching house recognizes, transmits, and publicly tests its inherited distinctions. Tianyin Yuanxiu says one must first reach the root and then know the lineage framework; Chaozong Tongren speaks of establishing that framework while distinguishing deviant alternatives. The added uses preserve an institutional-discursive framework rather than a new object.

Senses.Explanation: Close-woven, tightly knit, and allowing no gap; by extension, continuously and meticulously joined. Wuyi Yuanlai gives the clearest in-record definition: the brows knit with empty space, a needle cannot enter, water cannot wet it, and no hairbreadth gap is allowed. Dahui Zonggao critically reports respondents who stick an answer directly to a student's question and call that close-woven and free of affective dust; he also reports one-sentence answers called close-woven and not running away. An unnamed monk asks Yongjue Yuanxian for the close-woven house style and receives, "The golden needle does not permit knowing." Cizhou Fangnian appraises Zhanran Yuancheng's phrases as close-woven and not falling into beginning or end. Yuanwu Keqin uses the reduplicated form for what is continuous and close when set down. Yinyuan Longqi says a single mystery has three essentials, layered and close-woven so that no wind passes. The Zen bend is the qualitative transfer from textile closeness to public speech, house style, and lineage phrases: a saying or presentation is judged by whether any seam, temporal edge, or opening remains, while Dahui's reports preserve the possibility that this label itself is being criticized.

Senses.Explanation: Continuous and close-woven describes something carried without a break or seam. Masters apply it to sustained inquiry, conduct, a line of words, and the manner ascribed to the Caodong house; the shared force is continuity without an opening, not one prescribed activity. Ruibai Mingxue instructs the assembly to hold one question continuously and closely without discursive searching. Dufeng Shan says that when doubt is weighty, the question naturally remains present and pure attention continues close-woven without interruption. Shixi Xinyue contrasts flawless speech with conduct that continues without the smallest break, warning that either alone may fail to reach the other. Yuanwu Keqin applies the pair to what happens when something is put down; Baichi Xingyuan answers ‘Caodong school’ with the same phrase. These uses widen the predicate without producing a second object.

Senses.Explanation: To climb a tree seeking fish is to pursue a goal by a route whose direction cannot reach it. Zhongfeng Mingben pairs the phrase with guarding a stump when inherited sayings are treated as certificates. Kaifu Daoning applies it to seeking the subtle point through conceptual knowledge; Yuejiang Zhengyin joins it to rigidly waiting for verification. Tianyin Yuanxiu contrasts it with the unobstructed movement of skilled encounter, and Foyan Qingyuan warns students not to wait for it. The records use the impossible search as a procedural criticism: effort continues, but the chosen means and sought result do not meet.

Senses.Explanation: A donkey-tethering stake is a post to which a donkey is fastened. Chan speakers call bodhi and nirvana, teaching collections, and fixed formulations donkey-tethering stakes. Boatman Decheng makes the verbal deployment explicit: “one phrase that fits the head—ten thousand aeons a donkey-tethering stake.” The stake remains the concrete tethering object; Zen bends it into a name for words or teachings at which someone stays tied.

Senses.Explanation: Continue the flame is the records' fire image for carrying a house's succession forward, but public exchanges can question, strike, or refuse a claimant who asserts that continuation too easily. Konggu Daocheng says lamp after lamp continues the flame as patriarch follows patriarch to his own teacher and present seat. Zizhou Chuan quotes Baozang Puchi's succession verse, then comments that Baozang continued the flame and spread its fragrance. In encounters the image remains contestable. An unnamed questioner tells Guxue Zhenzhe that lamp after lamp will continue for a long time, and Guxue answers that he has not arrived. A second unnamed questioner claims that the Linji purport thereby continues; Chaozong Tongren strikes him and immediately turns 'the matter of continuing the flame' back into a question. Jizong Che likewise receives a direct question about lamp after lamp continuing the flame.

Senses.Explanation: To be at a loss: unable to answer or know what move to make in an encounter. The records use the term for an unnamed monk after Hangzhou Wenxi remains silent, Emperor Daizong after Nanyang Huizhong remains silent, Li Ao after the named respondent’s silence, and another unnamed monk after Muzhou Daozong laughs. Miyun Yuanwu's hall officer, Later Baoshou, Censor Wang, and the still-studying Yaoshan Weiyan are likewise described as at a loss when a question or response leaves them with no answer. These cases ground the plain meaning in observable interview turns; they do not turn the word into an imported diagnosis of an unseen inner condition.

SearchAliases: an antelope hanging by its horns
Zen an antelope hanging by its horns
Senses.Explanation: An antelope hanging by its horns is a recurrent Chan image defined inside the corpus by the absence of anything a hunter can follow. One instruction says that when the antelope hangs by its horns, not only its tracks but even its scent cannot be found. The phrase is then moved into several public forms. Yunju is asked what it is like at that time and answers “six times six is thirty-six,” adding that there are no tracks. Buhui answers a question about taking the person but not the surroundings with “the antelope hangs by its horns without a trace; the mountain is naturally high and the water naturally deep.” A later instruction applies the comparison directly to a lineage teacher's speaking, saying that it has a small measure of correspondence only when it is like the horn-hanging antelope. Thus the corpus does not leave the image as animal lore: it makes the missing track and scent a question, numerical answer, position answer, verse line, and appraisal of teaching-seat speech. The exact phrase occurs 77 times in 38 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase ‘Old monk’ is both an ordinary designation for an elderly monk and the conventional first-person self-reference used by named teachers such as Baizhang Huaihai, Linji Yixuan, Zhaozhou Congshen, and Yunju Daoqi. The human role remains the same across narration, address, and self-reference; those grammatical settings do not create separate senses. Its characteristic Chan deployment is humble first-person self-reference in monastic speech, conventionally translated ‘this old monk’ and grammatically serving as ‘I’ or ‘me.’ Baizhang Huaihai recalls receiving Mazu Daoyi’s shout; Linji Yixuan says he sits securely and distinguishes the visitors who come; Zhaozhou Congshen redirects a public interview by saying, ‘this old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly’; and Yunju Daoqi addresses the assembly at his final meeting. The same noun phrase also refers in narration to an old monk: Wuzhuo meets one, a raised case begins with an old monk carried by two disciples, and a record introduces ‘an old monk named Puhui.’ Speaker self-reference, third-person reference, and definiteness are contextual readings of the same human-role noun, not different things.

Senses.Explanation: This old monk’s fault is a compact turning reply, not necessarily a confession with a named offense. Masters use it to return another person’s blame, answer an accusation, supply a requested turning phrase, or cap a hypothetical challenge. Mazu Daoyi returns Baizhang’s “my fault” by making the fault his own; Damei Faying similarly answers an accusation that he deceives people. Nanyang Huizhong supplies the words as the requested turning phrase for the stone lion, after which Danyuan reopens whether the emperor understood. Dahui Zonggao proposes it as a hypothetical reply, and Xinghua Cuyuan uses it in live sparring with Linji, who says Xinghua’s words conceal a blade.

Senses.Note: The phrase is neither automatically praise nor a guarantee that the action described is harmless. A commentary reports that people call Jinniu's carrying rice and dancing "pressing old-woman concern," then rejects their reading: it is "arsenic soaked in honey to entice people to put it in their mouths" (以蜜浸砒霜誘人下口). Elsewhere the location of Yaoshan's pressing concern is itself made the next interview question: "where is the place of his pressing old-woman concern?" (那裏是他老婆心切處). It can also enter verse, as in "pressing old-woman concern, laughing ha-ha, letting bystanders say long or short" (老婆心切呵呵笑，一任傍人說短長). Common frames include "only because" (the “only because” form, 24 occurrences; variant 祇為, 7) and "so very" (得恁麼老婆心切, 18). These uses support a forceful relational appraisal while preserving the possibility of criticism.

SearchAliases: an old woman's concern is pressing
Senses.Explanation: The phrase appraises urgently solicitous intervention: records sometimes praise it and sometimes compare it to poisoned honey. Literally, "an old woman's concern is pressing": old woman or granny (老婆) plus the concern being urgent or pressed hard (心切). The phrase occurs 270 times in 129 allowlisted texts. It is a predicate applied to an unnamed interlocutor's insistent words or actions toward someone else, not the name of an inner state or a sentimental ideal. In the Linji–Huangbo–Dayu case, Dayu says Huangbo's old-woman concern was so pressing that "for you he exhausted himself completely" (為汝得徹困); when Linji returns, he says it was "only because the old-woman concern was pressing" (祇為老婆心切). In another exchange, a layman calls Huitang's concern pressing and Huitang replies, "I only want you to arrive home" (秖要公到家耳). The records thus show the idiom through predicates, agents, and replies rather than through a modern emotional gloss.

Senses.Explanation: Old-woman Chan is an appraisal label for talk or handling compared in the records with an old woman's solicitous speech. Masters apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to sayings and encounters; it is not the name of a separate lineage. Dahui Zonggao asks whether the National Teacher's three calls may be called 'speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water' (說老婆禪，拕泥帶水, ‘speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water’), and elsewhere says that if he had initially explained everything this way, the student would later have cursed him. Huang Yuangong's letter contrasts Miyun Yuanwu's 'pungent handling' (手段辛辣) with people elsewhere who speak old-woman Chan. The label is also attached to actual old-woman encounters in the Floating Cup and Mount Wutai cases. Dahui Zonggao calls a line 'old-woman Chan in the great Tang country' (大唐國裏老婆禪), and Wansong Xingxiu asks whether someone with firm heels would consent to learn old-woman Chan. The term is therefore an attested appraisal label rather than the name of a separate lineage: records apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to different sayings and encounters.

Senses.Explanation: Laozi is the pre-Chan Chinese figure whom Chan records quote and place beside Confucius, Zhuangzi, and Gautama. Yongming Yanshou assigns Laozi to the ‘empty mystery’ in a threefold comparison; Fushi Tongxian and Guxue Zhe juxtapose his ‘holding to the one’ with sayings of Confucius and Gautama. Yanxi Guangwen turns the story that Laozi transformed the foreigners into buddhas into a public question: why did he not transform them into Daoists? The Chan bend is not a new biography of Laozi but his deployment as a named voice and case figure within comparative instruction and teaching-seat questioning.

Nanyue Jiqi calls Xuefeng ‘this old fellow’ after raising his words; Dahui uses the same form for the named teaching figure in a self-narrated confrontation. Zen a rat entering an ox horn
Senses.Explanation: A rat entering an ox horn is a narrowing image whose endpoints are stated differently in different passages. Dahui says to press inquiry until there is no further place to investigate, “like a rat entering an ox horn,” when the stealing mind suddenly ends. In a winter-solstice exchange, an unnamed monk asks how a patch-robed monk turns around when the yin forces are exhausted and one yang returns; Xutang Zhiyu answers with the phrase. Another instruction says to press forward day after day and month after month like the rat in the horn, and explicitly says that then a living road appears. The image can also be used as criticism: one record says that a declining lineage becomes narrower and narrower like the rat in the horn, while Ciming scolds an answer consisting of the phrase. These attested contrasts prevent the dictionary from turning the image into a fixed declaration of either hopeless dead end or guaranteed success. Chan makes the narrowing horn a public answer, an instruction, a rebuked reply, and an appraisal of a lineage's contraction. The exact phrase occurs 30 times in 24 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: Water getting into the ear is the auditory half of a paired bodily obstruction: the eye cannot take sand and the ear cannot take water. Chan speakers preserve Baishui Benren’s saying, question each half in public, and also reverse it with the image of an ear containing the ocean. Baishui Benren states the paired formula and answers the question about the ear with “pure and undefiled.” Shending Yikui sets the exclusion formula against its opposite: the eye contains Mount Sumeru and the ear contains the four seas. Wanru Tongwei applies the water image to Xiangyan’s hearing bamboo strike, alongside dust entering Lingyun’s eye. Linye Qi cites the paired saying while warning that a displayed auspicious scene still does not settle the address.

Senses.Explanation: To hear a sound and awaken to the Way is a recurrent formula paired with seeing a form and clarifying mind. Yunmen raises the paired formula as a question rather than a procedure. Other masters repeat it in hall addresses and public exchanges. The corpus also refuses automatic endorsement: Tian’an Sheng compares it to quenching thirst by imagining plums, and Fuyan Baozong says it loses Guanyin’s eye. Zen bends the formula into something to test, challenge, or reject in encounter. Hearing a sound is not presented here as a guaranteed staged procedure.

Senses.Explanation: To continue the lineage lamps is to carry Chan succession from predecessor to successor and from generation to generation. Yongjue Yuanxian defines the governing lamp image in the Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian: successive transmission is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and reveals things, and because its illumination can continue without end. His histories then call more than seventy generations an unbroken chain of linked lamps and describe them as linking the lamps while continuing the flame. Hanxiu Ruqian uses the phrase in memorial verses for succession after receiving his predecessor's blows and for two named lineage holders carrying the line in different regions. Zefeng Yue applies it to an ancestral portrait during a teaching-seat address. These uses concern public lineage continuity, not ordinary lamps physically fastened together.

Senses.Explanation: The book Linked-Lamp Essentials is a specific Chan compilation, not the act of continuing a lineage. In his self-preface, Huiweng Wuming says that he selected material from more than six hundred teachers, arranged encounters, questions and answers, comments on old and recent cases, and essential statements under each person's chapter, divided the work into thirty fascicles, and gave it this title. Li Yong's preface says the title was placed on the work and the blocks were carved for circulation. Yongjue Yuanxian later places Wuming's compilation among the five lamp records. A lineage biography records Wuming as its compiler, while Sichong's republication preface calls it the Linked-Lamp Record and recounts its printing history.

Senses.Explanation: Before sound marks the point at which a Chan exchange is tested before an utterance has become an audible phrase. Senses.Explanation: Asked “what is the phrase before sound?” Xuanquan Yan answers with the vocalization “un” (吽), and Heyushan Guanghui says, “it is just like not saying” (恰似不道). Huanglian directly answers, “before sound there is no phrase; after the sound, bring your question” (聲前無句，聲後問將來). Later addresses make contrary predicates within the same public record: one says “everyone originally has” the phrase, while the Blue Cliff Record says “the thousand sages do not transmit” it. These are attested answers and claims, not grounds for choosing an ineffable reading. Zen bends the temporal phrase into a recurrent interview prompt whose answers may themselves be spoken sounds; this entry preserves that observable deployment and the corpus’s own disagreement.

Senses.Explanation: The paired sensory objects of ear and eye: sound (聲) and visible form or color (色). Chan records do more than repeat the pair abstractly. Yongjia's exchange explicitly assigns them to the faculties — 'when eyes and ears meet sound and form' (眼耳緣聲色時) — and asks what is the substance of sound and form. Dahui makes the pair demonstrable during a public address: he raises the whisk and says, 'this is form,' strikes the Chan seat and says, 'this is sound' (這箇是色／這箇是聲). Another record gives ordinary audible examples: wind in pine trees, frogs, and crows are all sound, while saying that what one discriminates is sound and form. The corpus also predicates 'pass through all sound and form without obstruction' (透一切聲色，無有滯礙) and draws its own distinction between function 'together with sound and form' and 'the affairs of sound and form' (用同聲色而不是聲色之事). The Zen deviation is this repeated use as a named field of public testing and concrete demonstration; the graphs still denote what is heard and seen.

Senses.Note: The phrase 'cast off sensual attractions' (擯去聲色) occurs in nine allowlist texts, chiefly recensions of the same Zhao Bian biography; 'indulge in sensual attractions' (耽聲色) supplies a structurally independent witness. No distinctively Chan lexical bend was found for this ordinary sense. Frozen-corpus concordance: 2545 exact hits in 339 storage files representing 334 independent works.

Senses.Explanation: To have the feet planted on solid ground is to answer or investigate from firm, firsthand footing instead of relying on verbal display. Chan masters use the bodily image for an actual place to stand and for inquiry that does not float in borrowed explanation. Caoshan Baoji Xiong gives the phrase as the student’s place for settling life. Tianmu Mingben tells an inquirer to discard memorized sayings and investigate with feet on solid ground. Yuanwu Keqin contrasts such a person with an interlocutor left speechless by Muzhou. Dahui Zonggao uses the phrase for entering a demanding gate that uproots birth and death.

Senses.Explanation: Through-and-through. Shangfeng Bencai's formula contrasts the relative ease of emerging from one's situation with the difficulty of speaking through-and-through. Feiyin Tongrong applies the same force to conduct after former valuables have been dropped, and Yinyuan Longqi to taking the matter up completely. Chaozong Tongren joins the term to completion, Yushan Shangsi to accord, Guishan Zhe to departing free, and Miyun Yuanwu to full disclosure. The changing predicates preserve one intensifying job rather than seven separate things. Zen bends a bodily image into a demand with no protected remainder. The corpus tests whether speech, accord, responsibility, or manifestation is complete in the whole person, not merely asserted in part.

Senses.Explanation: Seeing the cheeks from behind the head pictures an impossible exposure: a person’s face is visible from the side that should conceal it. Chan speakers use the formula as a terse answer and, most often, pair it with “do not associate with him,” making the impossible visibility a warning-sign appraisal. Huqiu Shaolong asks what caused his laugh and answers with the full formula followed by “do not associate with him.” Miyun Yuanwu gives the phrase as his direct answer to “what is originally pure?” Sanshan Lai’s praise expands the cheeks to eight feet and pairs them with a crown eye three fathoms long. Hanyu Xian answers an approving follow-up with the same four graphs. Minshu sets the phrase against possessing the crown eye in his comment on Bodhidharma and Emperor Wu. Yulin Tongxiu repeats the warning formula in an independent record.

Senses.Explanation: The recorded formula 'right under your heels' locates what is immediately beneath one's stance and recurs in demands to inspect or recognize what lies there, in questions about it, and in appraisals and reversals. Chan interviews repeatedly turn this ordinary location back upon the person questioned. Poshan Haiming gives the appraisal 'right under your heels, thirty blows would be fitting.' Wuyi Yuanlai asks 'how deep is the water under your heels?', Sanshan Denglai directs a questioner to 'recognize it right under your heels,' and Juelang Daosheng answers a request for direct pointing with 'look clearly right under your heels.' The phrase also marks relative position in a public comparison: if the unnamed monastic can distinguish the kinds of leakage, Dongshan is under his heels; if not, he is under Dongshan's heels. A stock question asks about 'the matter under your heels' and receives 'putting a head atop your head.' The Chan-specific bend is consistent and observable: the spatial phrase becomes the immediate locus of an interviewer's demand, appraisal, or reversal, often contrasted with what the questioner seeks elsewhere or above. The texts do not supply a further object hidden beneath the feet, and neither does this entry.

Three independent case collections assign the answer directly to Xianglin Chengyuan and preserve the unnamed questioning monk's question about the matter beneath the patch robe. The article records the stable case line and its later quotation without assigning the impossible seasonal image an external interpretation.

Chan usage refuses a single romantic valuation: Ruibai strikes the questioner who proposes it, Weian Ran contrasts it with raising dust at the crossroads, and Erzhan Zun places a tended water buffalo among those same peaks. Senses.Explanation: Linji's Three Mysteries and Three Essentials are the paired threefold terms attributed to Linji's house and repeatedly raised as a named classification. Hall speakers list them beside Caodong's Five Ranks, Yunmen's three barriers, Guiyang's circles, and Fayan's nothing-outside-mind. Others ask where they are seen, what remains if they perish together, or quote Fenyang Shanzhao's verse that one clear phrase contains the myriad forms. Their public deployment is therefore interrogative and comparative as well as classificatory; the entry does not invent definitions the selected lines do not supply.

Senses.Explanation: Linji’s shout is a named Chan device, repeatedly paired or contrasted with Deshan’s staff and tested in later encounters. Device lists pair 'Linji's shout' with 'Deshan's staff,' and later sermons compare the shout to rushing thunder. The phrase is not merely a historical label: masters publicly ask what its purport is, demand that an unnamed monastic produce it, or declare that they have no use for it today. The corpus also polices the inherited emblem. In a later Fushi exchange, the presiding teacher strikes after being asked what indication lies beyond Deshan's staff and Linji's shout, then says that calling it 'staff-and-shout' sends one to hell like an arrow. Thus Zen bends an ordinary shout into a named lineage implement and object of later interview, imitation, comparison, and criticism; the entry reports only those recorded deployments.

Senses.Explanation: Able to act, come and go, or respond without constraint: free and at ease, at liberty, or freely. The word is attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. Foyan Qingyuan closes an address by telling everyone to drink tea in the hall, free and at ease (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Yunmen Wenyan says that only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired (卷舒自在，應用無虧). The Yongzheng Emperor uses the result phrase “obtain great freedom” (獲大自在), while Zhean Jingfan says “unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time” (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui Zonggao says that one then enters birth and death and obtains great freedom (出生入死得大自在). Other records pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. Zen bends an everyday freedom word into public tests about response, movement, birth, and death, while Baizhang Huaihai warns against casually declaring a buddha free or not free. Adjective, adverb, result noun, and the repeated form “free and at ease” remain grammatical deployments of the same condition.

Senses.Explanation: One’s own nature is the nature attributed to the person or mind itself. The records place it in public questions, explanations of what it contains, compound names such as ‘the naturally true buddha of one’s own nature,’ and claims about what does or does not depart from it. The expression occurs 2,091 times in 260 allowlisted texts. The Platform Record says that one's own nature is originally clean, contains the ten thousand things, and is not apart from them; another recension lists it as originally clean, not arising or perishing, complete in itself, unmoving, and able to produce the ten thousand things. These are the record's predicates, not an imported definition. Other Chan records use the term in questions about seeing, clarifying, or being unaware of one's own nature. Tianru Weize says that what is reluctantly named the naturally true buddha of one's own nature is also called one's own householder. Direct answers do not settle into a single formula: asked 'What is one's own nature?' Huanyou Zhengchuan says, 'I will not say'; asked about the naturally true buddha of one's own nature while tending a fire, the respondent tells the unnamed questioner to bring a bundle of firewood.

Senses.Explanation: Unable to save oneself is an adverse verdict on a position that cannot carry its holder through the present test. Chaozong Huifang applies it to resting in “not obscuring causality,” Linji Yixuan makes it the result of attaining only the third phrase, and Deshan Xuanjian applies it to conventional holy ranks. Later commentators use it against readings of the cat case and against inherited verse.

Senses.Explanation: To know for oneself is to recognize or judge without another person supplying the recognition. Yongming Yanshou says recognition is already present before a gesture. Tianran Hanshi says a genuine person knows and decides for himself; Zhenjing Kewen says the buddhas can only know for themselves. Baizhang Huaihai warns against clinging to self-knowing as a fixed cure; Juelang Dasheng and Hansong Zhicao use the phrase for personally knowing measure or an intimate matter.

Senses.Explanation: As a figure for speech, the tongue is said to lack bones, be cut off, or be restrained from moving in public exchange. A person's capacity to speak is what Chan verdicts test, trust, disable, or demand under the image of the tongue. Yungai Jipeng and Chengtian Weijian each answer a public question by saying that the tongue has no bone. Guanghui Yuanlian says that he no longer doubts the tongues of old masters, and Shoushan Xingnian immediately asks him to state his understanding. Huangbo Xiyun predicts that Linji Yixuan will cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. Longyuan Fa says that a demon king has cut off the Buddha's tongue and offers to redress the wrong. Huiyun Benchong Sheng orders a respondent to produce a statement without moving the tongue, then says the respondent's shout still involves lips and mouth. These are speech acts and verdicts, not reports of bodily injury, so they establish a Zen-loaded referent separate from the organ that can be bitten.

Senses.Note: Two independent bodily witnesses establish the ordinary anatomical referent. No special Zen deviation is asserted for it.

Senses.Explanation: A tongue dragging on the ground is speech made bodily excessive: the organ extends so far that it trails along the earth. Chan masters deploy the image as an answer about a saying, as Zhongfeng Mingben’s capping comment on a visitor’s words, and as a cost of choosing one side of a comparison. Wuzhun Shifan answers a question about Zhaozhou’s saying of no guest and host with “the tongue drags on the ground,” then answers the follow-up with “words fill the world.” Zhongfeng Mingben inserts the phrase after replaying a visitor’s answer “I came for the teaching.” Juelang Daosheng gives it as the answer requested before birth, then follows it with “eyebrows propping up heaven.” Mingjue Cong says that choosing Yunmen in his comparison would wrong himself until his tongue dragged on the ground.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X81/X81n1568.xml). Strict Lineage of the Five Lamps (Vols. 10–25) (五燈嚴統(第10卷-第25卷)): Yungai Jipeng answers a direct question about the main point of the teaching with 'the tongue has no bone.'

Senses.Explanation: The tongue has no bone is a Chan appraisal of speech as able to turn without a rigid support: masters use it for agile wording, unreliable verbal flexibility, or a line that can be extended and reversed, so the saying can praise responsiveness or expose talk that bends too easily. Hongzhi Zhengjue pairs Shitou's boneless tongue with Yunmen's sinewed eyes while discussing reciprocal and nonreciprocal language. Wuyi Yuanlai places the boneless tongue beside eyes without sinews after telling the assembly that the displayed world is present yet still unseen. Tianru Weize answers by opposing sinews in the eyes to a tongue without bone, setting visual steadiness against verbal flexibility. Zhangxue Zui gives 'the tongue has no bone' as an answer to the third of Linji's four selections, then answers the fourth with the mouth as the gate of calamity. Xisou Shaotan admits his own boneless tongue while adding words to earlier teachers and calls the move a dog's tail joined to sable. Chushi Fanqi offers the phrase as one of several substitute answers. The saying therefore describes a capacity whose value depends on its use, not a fixed compliment.

The allowlisted corpus has 507 hits in 163 files representing 160 independent works. Its small size supplies the comparison ‘mustard-seed-sized’ (芥子許, 76 hits in 54 files representing 54 independent works), as when a named record subject speaks of a doubt as small as a mustard seed. The corpus also repeatedly pairs the seed with Mount Sumeru in both directions: ‘Sumeru contains a mustard seed’ (須彌納芥子, 57 hits in 40 files representing 38 works) and ‘a mustard seed contains Sumeru’ (芥子納須彌, 71 hits in 56 files representing 54 works). In the Guizong encounter, Li Bo accepts the first statement but asks whether the second is false; Guizong asks where Li Bo’s ten thousand books are held in a body the size of a coconut. In another exchange, the two directions receive the one-word answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’ A later address records mountains, earth, trees, monastics, laypeople, sages, and ordinary people placed inside a mustard seed without the seed becoming narrow. These are the corpus’s recorded scale constructions; the entry does not turn them into a symbolic meaning for the seed.

Senses.Explanation: If you do not climb the tower and look, how could you know the ocean is deep? In Zhenjing Kewen's record an unnamed monk twice uses the line as an advance inside a public exchange, making the proverb an offered response rather than scenery. In the first exchange the questioner asks about the ancestral import, receives Kewen's terse answer, advances the tower-and-ocean line, and is told ‘passed’ before Kewen says one move is still lacking. In the second exchange Kewen answers ‘pour out your heart and bare your gall’; the questioner advances the same line, and Kewen immediately asks him again about what remains constantly clear. Both witnesses belong to Zhenjing Kewen's record and one independent work. The entry is therefore provisional despite the phrase's repeated public use.

Senses.Explanation: To be blankly at a loss. In Chan encounter narratives it is an observable failure to answer or proceed: after being asked "who observes, and what is quiet?" the recorded questioner is at a loss; after being seized and ordered "speak! speak!" the recorded questioner is at a loss and is pushed away. The record makes the absence of an answer explicit in "the narrator records that Wenshu Zhengdao was at a loss and did not know how to reply" (師茫然不知對). It also applies collectively: after the answer "clear conversation face to face—if not buddha, then who?" the assembly is all at a loss (眾皆茫然). A training biography records a student being required to give one fitting word and withdrawing at a loss (師茫然退). The Zen deviation lies in this recurring public-interview function: the adjective marks the recorded point where a participant or assembly has no response, not a mystical state and not an explanation of why the exchange defeated them.

Senses.Explanation: Straw sandals remain literal footwear while serving as the ordinary equipment and expense of traveling on foot through the Chan record. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. The object also enters named encounters: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his sandals, and leaves; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head after Nanquan recounts cutting the cat. Jiashan Shanhui compares ‘the patriarchs’ dark purport’ to worn-out straw sandals and says bare feet would be better. The corpus records these concrete actions and comparisons without supplying a symbolic gloss for the sandals.

Senses.Explanation: A thorn thicket is dense, catching growth through which ordinary passage is painful and difficult. Chan masters make entering, leaving, or crossing it a measure in public address: Yunmen says the level ground kills countless people but one who gets through the thicket is skilled, while later speakers can point to a whisk or the encounter itself as the thicket still to cross. Cijue Zongze describes people boring their heads into the thicket while believing only living beings suffer. Liao’an Qingyu repeats the level-ground and thorn-thicket formula in a memorial hall address. Foyan Qingyuan raises Yunmen’s formula, then declares that the whisk itself is the thorn thicket and asks how anyone crosses it. An unnamed monk asks Yunju Daoqi to clear a road through the thicket; Yunju asks where he intends to go. Yaoshan Weiyan places the questioner’s red and ulcerated parents lying in the thicket. Xiatang Huiyuan describes pulling one’s feet free of the thicket while wearing the inherited robe. Liao’an Qingyu says the chief seat strides within the thicket and pulls out the stakes rooted by others. Shending Yikui later raises Yunmen’s old thorn-thicket formula in a release-day address.

Senses.Explanation: The estate steward is the monastery officer responsible for an outlying estate or farm and its material business. The office can therefore identify both an institutional post and its holder, but these are the same role rather than separate senses.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB286.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yingning Jing (攖寧靜禪師語錄): Yingning Jing utters the exact quoted wording in the complete source unit.

HeadwordSpanReview.GrammarEvidence: Both exact spans are irreducible because the dream formula names Zhuang Zhou twice inside one uninterrupted quotation by Yingning Jing; splitting them would erase the attested contrast.

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.

SearchAliases: Zen do not get it wrong
Senses.Explanation: An imperative: do not (莫) understand or take it (會) wrongly (錯). Its distinct Chan deployment is as warnings that named speakers attach directly to a saying or answer in public discourse. Asked the intention of the coming from the West, Anguo Hongtao answers 'it is so, but do not get it wrong.' An extended address says not to infer 'not round and not sudden' from the preceding words and not to present borrowed, similar, or calculated phrases as one's own understanding, repeating 'do not get it wrong.' Elsewhere Bao’en Huiming warns an assembly not to say that speech, silence, movement, and stillness are all buddha-affairs. The formula can also follow an unexplained seasonal statement — 'yesterday snow, today it melts' — leaving the warning itself as the only explicit appraisal. These contexts establish the public-interview function without supplying an interpretation of what the preceding words secretly mean.

Senses.Explanation: In case collections and recorded sayings, an interjected comment (著語) is compact wording inserted against a cited exchange, often immediately after one of its lines and introduced by “appends a comment and says” (著語云). The Blue Cliff Record preserves Xuedou Chongxian's repeated comments such as “seen through,” and Yuanwu Keqin's recorded sayings insert “wrong” after successive turns of an older case. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly quotes comments by Yuanwu and then answers them from his own position. Tianyin Yuanxiu and Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise interrupt cited exchanges with short verdicts. A reviewed unnamed monastic questioner asks Langting Ting for a comment on a named case, while Xiangtian Jinian says he will place a comment against each line. The form can therefore name either the inserted wording or the act of adding it; it does not denote ordinary authorship where the verb authored merely precedes the noun recorded sayings.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1998A.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue (大慧普覺禪師語錄): Dahui Zonggao is the exact headword speaker. Dahui describes the fear and responds by questioning whether the one who fears falling into blankness is itself empty. The exact headword-bearing actor is Dahui Zonggao. This exact quoted claim is anchored in the reviewed source unit.

Senses.Explanation: The records warn against collapsing into blank nothing, then answer that blankness itself is absent or is not blank. Literally, 'fall into emptiness,' but in these records the observable warning is against falling into a blank nothing. The term occurs 325 times in 128 allowed texts; the expanded form 'fall into blank annihilation' (落空亡) occurs 75 times in 43 texts. Dahui reports people who hear 'a teaching in which nothing is obtained' (無所得法) and become afraid that they will fall into blankness; he answers by asking whether the very one who fears falling into blankness is empty. A lamp dialogue answers the charge that Chan teachers mostly fall into blankness by saying that letters and other things arise from wisdom and that, when 'great function appears before one' (大用現前), there can be no falling into blankness. Another exchange dismantles the spatial wording itself: asked whether 'originally there is nothing' falls into blankness, the reply asks, 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立). The same collection says that people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). There are 6 occurrences of 'not fall into blankness' (不落空) and 21 of the warning 'do not fall into blankness' (莫落空).

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Five Lamps (Vols. 34–120) (五燈全書(第34卷-第120卷)): Tianbo Chongyuan is the exact hall speaker, saying that only by treading the ground step after step does one know the landing place and otherwise must step back and look underfoot.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase asks or states the place where something comes down, settles, or finds its point of application. Chan exchanges use that ordinary landing-place relation to press where a saying, action, or person’s understanding actually comes to rest. Chan records apply it to words, answers, cases, actions, people, and one's life: 'know where it lands' (知落處) occurs 897 times in 226 files representing 223 independent works, while 'not know where it lands' (不知落處) occurs 209 times in 103 files representing 101 independent works. Yuanwu says that as soon as Danxia raised it, he knew where it landed (才方舉起便知落處), and his Blue Cliff prose twice contrasts knowing and not knowing where Mazu's public case lands. Dahui asks whether the assembly knows where his teacher's words land and says that knowing it identifies the top graduate (還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元). Changqing asks, 'Do you understand where it lands?' (還委落處麼). A lamp record joins origin and destination: 'if you know where it arises, then you know where life lands' (若知起處。便知身命落處). Xiuyelin gives the richest explicit relation found: 'the fundamental matter is precisely where the person's own life-source lands' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). The article therefore keeps the verbal image and reports what the texts assign a landing point; it does not replace that image with an imported abstraction.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan records, the image of intertwining vines denotes language that proliferates, entangles, or demands cutting through. Yuanwu Keqin directly joins the tangle to the need to cut off words, calls old cases vine-tangle cases, and elsewhere praises action that cuts the tangle straight off. Zhongfeng Mingben lists vine-Chan among defective labels and describes later students caught where vines spread everywhere. Qingshan Puning self-deprecatingly calls his unavoidable address tangling with the assembly. Dahui Zonggao says Wushang had already entered mud and water for the assembly and produced no little tangle. Lingyao Liang offers a vine-entangled proclamation for the community to disentangle together. The metaphor can criticize interpretive or case language, describe a named speaker's own speech, or name material deliberately presented for disentangling; it is not a flat synonym for every use of words. A literal-plant control searched plant predicates and collocations such as sprouting, spreading, branching, rooting, binding, covering the ground, and filling the ground. In the retained Chan uses these extend the same speech-and-case tangle—lineage talk sprouts, sayings branch, cases cover the ground, or words bind a participant—rather than describing cultivated or botanical vines. The selected evidence therefore supports one loaded tangle referent, not a hidden second plant article.

Senses.Explanation: In these records, medicine and illness are a reciprocal pair: a saying functions as medicine only against a corresponding illness, and medicine retained after the illness is gone becomes illness itself. Yunmen Wenyan raises the formula and asks, when the whole earth is medicine, what cures oneself. Baizhang Huaihai calls language about form and emptiness medicine-and-illness counter-treatment. Linji Yixuan says his own speaking is only a temporary counter-treatment and contains no fixed thing. Fayan Wenyi calls splitting a statement into two pieces something like medicine and illness treating one another. The surrounding corpus passage also states directly that medicine left after illness is gone becomes illness, which bounds the reciprocal image without supplying another sense.

Senses.Explanation: Empty space is the open expanse in which things can be located or compared. The term is attested 5,943 times in 279 allowlisted texts. Chan records also make that ordinary expanse measurable, containable, breakable, and fillable. Productive forms include "in empty space" (虛空中, 91 occurrences), "inside empty space" (虛空裏, 136), and "like empty space" (如虛空, 364). They also record impossible or emphatic actions: "empty space shattered" (虛空粉碎, 167), "break empty space" (打破虛空, 85), and "empty space burst apart" (虛空迸裂). Zhongfeng says of an incense offering, "empty space cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it" (虛空包不住，大地載不起). Zhe'an Fan says that if one understands at a stated point, "empty space can be measured" (虛空可量). A memorial narrative describes one who raised his head and suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, "lucid like empty space, impossible to approach or lodge in" (如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊). The corpus also says "empty space has no inside or outside" (虛空無內外, 9), while a formal address says that the Chan lineage's defining feature "fills empty space, with nowhere to evade it" (充塞虛空，無處回避). These are literal comparisons and recorded predicates; no single further sense is imposed on all 5,943 occurrences.

Senses.Explanation: A mosquito on an iron ox meets a surface on which its mouth has nowhere to enter. The stock completion repeatedly says “there is nowhere for you to put down your mouth.” Masters deploy it as an answer, a blocking verdict, and a description of an encounter in which verbal purchase is unavailable; one lineage story contrasts being like the mosquito at Shitou with a later breakthrough under Mazu.

Senses.Explanation: A clam containing the bright moon is Zhimen Guangzuo's fixed answer when asked for the body of complete discernment; later comments and verses preserve that answer beside the rabbit bearing a fetus. In the Zhimen case, the first question concerns the body of complete discernment and Zhimen answers with this clause, then answers the question about its use with 'the rabbit bears a fetus.' Senses.Explanation: The animal appears both in ordinary lists and in striking Chan sayings. Baima Ai answers a question about the pure teaching-body with a toad at the bottom of a well swallowing the moon (井底蝦蟆吞却月). Sanyi Mingyu pairs a monkey accustomed to climbing a tree with a toad jumping into a well (猢猻慣上樹，蝦蟆跳入井). In an exchange with Xinghua Cuyuan, Yang Yi says that a three-legged toad jumps into the sky (三脚蝦蟆跳上天), and Xinghua lets it jump as it pleases. Dongshan Xiaocong lists the variant-written toad with earthworms as creatures having holes. The animal also enters the named appraisal Toad Chan. Tian'an Sheng explicitly asks what Toad Chan is and describes a toad croaking like a drum in the rain and crying, “what suffering?” (蝦蟆遇天雨，叫喚聲如鼓……何苦？何苦？). Juelang Dasheng applies the same label in a public exchange. Zen bends the ordinary animal-name into answers, impossible animal actions, and a named Chan appraisal, while the records continue to use it for the creature itself.

Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hanxiu (憨休禪師語錄): A hall address sets the passing traveler's worldly labor over snail-horn and fly-head matters beside a great treasure, bright across heaven and earth, hidden in the bodily mountain. Senses.Explanation: A snail's horn supplies the minute ground for two recurrent corpus families. In prose and verse, people contend for “the minuteness of a snail's horn,” and profit and fame on a fly's head and snail's horn become an empty battle. A discussion explicitly recalls the Zhuangzi story of Chu and Man fighting over territory and leaving corpses for ten thousand miles, then places even the yielding of Yao and Shun and the conquests of Tang and Wu in “the waste of the snail's horn.” Chan verses also reverse the scale: one puts the universe on the tip of a snail's horn, while a hall address opposes the passing traveler's labor over fly-head and snail-horn matters to a great treasure hidden in the body. The minute object, its contest language, and the vast things placed on it are one image under different predicates. The Chan deviation lies in bringing the horn into hall speech and scale-reversal verse, not in assigning it a hidden meaning. The exact phrase occurs 36 times in 26 allowlist texts.

Orthodox Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統): Orthodox Continuation of the Lamp (續燈正統), section on Zhongfang Tianlun: after a thunderclap, Zhongfang Tianlun says that the minute insect swallows five Mount Sumerus. Zhongfang Tianlun is not yet represented in the local roster.

Senses.Explanation: The minute jiaoming insect is an extremely small creature. In the Collected Guidelines of the Lineage Masters, Yuejiang Yin makes the scale explicit by saying that it builds its nest on a mosquito's eyelash, hence the descriptive alternate “mosquito-eyelash insect.” Chan verses and addresses repeatedly reverse that scale: Dahui Zonggao puts a giant turtle inside its eye; Mengshan Yi has it drain the ocean; Lia'an Qingyu is asked about its swallowing a tiger; Yinshan Can puts a night market in its eye; and Zhongfang Tianlun says it swallows five Mount Sumerus. In the Surviving Draft of the Continued Lamp, Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that such an insect has blundered into his sky-spanning net; the line occurs inside Duanya Liaoyi's biography because Gaofeng is speaking about Duanya. These are distinct large-in-small actions and comparisons involving the same tiny creature, not evidence that the headword itself means the cosmos or carries one fixed interpretation. The headword occurs 394 times in 166 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: A transmission line is the continuity that Chan records locate through cases, question-and-answer, sentences, and succession. Caoshan Benji answers the withered-tree dragon-hum question by saying that the line is unbroken. Yuanwu Keqin says that the ancients' line is unbroken because the question is in the answer and the answer in the question; elsewhere he says that differing speakers do not lose it sentence by sentence. Yunxi Langting Ting directly names precise question-and-answer as the line unbroken. Xueguan Zhiyin passes what he received onward as the continuation of Shouchang's line and the extension of Boshan's house style. Zen thus bends hereditary and bodily continuity into a documented connective line through public speech and teacher-successor transmission.

Senses.Explanation: Travel on foot means to journey from place to place on one's own feet. Chan records use the expression for departing an instructor or monastery, crossing the various regions, and seeking other teachers. Dongshan Liangjie asks permission to travel and is directed toward Nanquan; Yaoshan Weiyan asks whether a visitor has travelled through the regions seeking what is hard to obtain. Later records speak of travelling a thousand miles to seek a lineage teacher and of a 'person travelling on foot' (行腳人) or 'patch-robed monk travelling on foot' (衲僧行腳). The walking journey is literal; whom the traveller visits and what is asked belong to each encounter.

Senses.Explanation: A patch-robed monk is the Chan participant marked by the patched robe and repeatedly addressed, questioned, and appraised in public encounters. The robe-word becomes a public standard in compounds asking after the patch-robed monk's eye, conduct, own affair, house, and manner. Asked “what is a patch-robed monk?” (如何是衲僧), one reviewed exchange answers, “investigating, seeking, and visiting the Way” (參尋訪道). Another exchange asks for “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧分上事) and answers, “when you want to walk, walk; when you want to sit, sit” (要行即行，要坐即坐). The corpus also asks directly about “the patch-robed monk's eye” (衲僧眼) and “the patch-robed monk's place of conduct” (衲僧行履處). It speaks institutionally of what can be used “under the patch-robed monk's gate” (衲僧門下), and appraises an assembly as lacking anyone with “the air of a patch-robed monk” (衲僧氣息). The Chan deviation lies in this public standard: the robe-word names the person expected to answer within the encounter record, while the compounds test that person's eye, conduct, handle, own affair, and house. These are attested compound deployments, not claims about an inner state.

Senses.Explanation: A patch-robed monk’s proper business is what remains when accomplishment, verbal display, and borrowed devices are set aside. Masters ask for it directly, deny that spectacular feats amount to it, and answer the question with words or blows that must themselves be met in the interview. Yuanwu Keqin says even extraordinary accomplishments are not yet the patch-robed monk’s proper business, then asks for a statement outside accomplishment. Tianyin Yuanxiu says that even overwhelming shouts and blows are not it, asks what it is, and answers with a verse whose standing peaks do not turn the label into a generic achievement. Poshan Haiming calls ordinary travel and attendance the patch-robed monk’s proper business, but immediately says that this still is not the ancestral visitor’s meaning. Xueqiao Yuanxin answers the direct question with repeated blows. Dahui Zonggao likewise raises the question after listing feats and refers the hearer to the two appointed seats.

Senses.Explanation: The wearer of patched monastic robes: a patch-robed monk or monk in patched robes. The term occurs 2,174 times in 317 allowed texts and names monks whom Chan teachers address, question, appraise, and describe through their clothing, livelihood, daily activity, and house style. Pin Jixiang gives a direct naming formula: 'Each wears a hat and waist-pack and is named a patch-robed monk; name and reality should match' (箇箇都是頂笠腰包，名為衲子，要當名實相稱). Nanquan Puyuan says, 'Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; patch-robed monks are hard to fool' (龍蛇易辨衲子難謾). Yushan Shangsi calls an astute patch-robed monk difficult to find (伶俐衲子難得), while Jingqing Daofu twice praises Fengxue Yanzhao as 'a fine patch-robed monk' (衲子俊哉). Zhufeng Zhenxu says, 'The patch-robed monk's eyebrows leap' (衲子眉毛𨁝跳), in an end-of-retreat hall verse. Minshu names a snow hat and cloud gourd as 'the patch-robed monk's livelihood' (雪笠雲瓢，為衲子之活計). Haizhuang Azi Jinwu says that the patch-robed monk's daily activity already has a great treasury of light and requires being such a person. Hansong Zhicao contrasts 'keeping to poverty and quiet, the patch-robed monk's house style' with 'pursuing warmth and bustle, the ordinary person's livelihood' (固窮守寂，衲子家風；附熱趨喧，常人活計). Asked directly, 'What is a patch-robed monk?' (如何是衲子), Shanhui answers, 'Bare-bodied atop Mount Sumeru; do not go toward the northern continent' (赤身須彌頂，莫向越單行). Zen bends a clothing label into an institutional and interpersonal name for the monks addressed and tested in the teaching community; it does not make praise, clothing, or house style into separate person-senses.

Senses.Explanation: To pull the patchwork quilt over one’s head is to withdraw completely from claims, schemes, and public business. Chan masters use monastic bedding as an image of radical non-involvement: ten thousand matters stop, even claims to understand are set aside. Yunfeng joins the covered head to letting all matters rest; Yuanwu quotes the same line when asking how to raise the guestless-hostless saying at the hearth; Hongjue includes it among proposed escapes from mental binding and rejects treating it as an automatic solution; and Poshan’s farewell verse sends a practitioner into the mountains with the quilt over his head even if a thousand Buddhas appear.

Senses.Explanation: The “meaning from the West” is the shortened public-interview form of the question about the patriarch’s coming from the West; the records answer it with fresh words and actions rather than one explanatory definition. Direct abbreviated questions ask simply “what is the meaning from the West?” Tianzhu Chonghui answers with a white ape carrying its young and butterflies holding flowers; Helin Xuansu answers that understanding is not understanding and doubt is not doubt. Yunfeng Zudeng answers with striking the forehead and nose, an unnamed monk asks Mazu Daoyi and Mazu answers “what meaning is present now?”, Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang says “three years carrying one boat,” Longya asks Linji and Linji demands the Chan board, Zhaozhou descends from the seat, and Shitou sends the questioner to ask the exposed pillar. The Chan bend is the abbreviation’s life as a public test whose many incompatible replies are preserved rather than harmonized into a hidden proposition.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Chan records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: The faculty or nature of seeing, a noun phrase rather than the action of seeing one's own nature. Hanyue Fazang and Bore Gulin each quote an outside claimant who treats this seeing faculty as an unchanging witness that survives the destruction of a visible tile or stove; both speakers identify that claim as an error. Huanyou Zhengchuan groups the phrase with the nature of hearing and the nature of awareness, then says seeing and nature are not two separately visible things. This distinct segmentation matters because translating these passages as an achievement of seeing one's nature would reverse their grammar and hide the criticism.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this paired action as a banner for direct recognition and as a proposition that teachers immediately unpack, question, or test. Yunju Zhi equates nature with Buddha and says this is why the phrase is used; Huineng voices it as the wished-for result of hearing his words; Guizong Huicheng says the ancestral teacher came from the west only to state it. The records thus retain both its compact banner form and explicit internal explanations.

Senses.Explanation: The four ordinary functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, named together as a fixed sequence. Chan texts warn against constructing an additional understanding from them or treating some separate entity as standing behind them. The same functions can be described as the cause of birth and death and, without changing the wording, as the root of release. Other passages say that they neither obstruct complete command nor bind a person in themselves. Translate the four actions directly; do not replace them with an imported technical noun such as 'awareness.'

Senses.Explanation: Seeing form, clarify the mind is a compact encounter formula that joins visible form to immediate recognition. Yunmen raises the paired formula as a question; later masters quote and test it in public addresses. The records do not treat it as automatically valid. Tian’an Sheng compares clarifying mind by seeing form to filling hunger with a painted cake, and Zhengfang asks why one would need it at all. Zen bends the formula into tested encounter language, not a prescribed inner procedure.

Senses.Explanation: Seeing the tracks is the second oxherding stage: the seeker has found signs of the ox but has not yet caught it. Oxherding sequences place it after seeking the ox and before seeing or catching the ox. Their headings, prefaces, and verses describe tracks beside water or in wild country as an initial but incomplete disclosure. The stage explanations explicitly call it provisional and distinguish seeing traces from direct possession. The corpus's own sequence fixes the stage's observable job.

Senses.Note: Two exact works use seeing traces outside the oxherding-stage title, once for traces appearing with mental turning and once for traces that remain after knowing where to return.

Senses.Explanation: Huike's fixed reply in the mind-settling case: ‘having sought the mind, I could not find it. Huike says his mind is not at ease; Bodhidharma tells him to bring the mind so it can be set at ease; Huike answers with this phrase; Bodhidharma replies that the mind has now been set at ease. Subsequent records repeatedly examine the quoted sentence. Yuanwu asks why Huike answered only this. Juelang distinguishes Huike's utterance from later students repeating the same words. Zhuanyu Heng explicitly judges Huike's reply as falling into conceptual understanding when comparing it with the flower sermon, while Wanfeng asks how the sentence should be understood and comments on it in another register. Daxiu Zhu redeploys the wording in a first-person public question and is immediately asked where he is now. Huigong Xiong presses the abbreviated grammar: if it is altogether unobtainable, what remains to regulate? These disagreements and questions concern the force of one fixed quoted reply; they do not create a second referent.

Senses.Explanation: The records use this transitive appraisal for seeing through a saying, case, person, condition, or position before or after it is presented. Literally, 'look through' or 'look and break through.' The compound occurs 509 times in 154 allowed texts. It is used transitively of a saying, case, person, condition, or distinction; in passive clauses someone or something is 'seen through.' Hongzhi asks, 'What is the eye with which you can see through it?'. Comments on earlier cases say that someone saw through Lingyun and Mahakasyapa, that Tianning saw through Dahui, or that an interlocutor should see through an action before it occurs. The passive form appears in a warning about being seen through by someone at a later time (他時異日被人覷破). The fuller form 'be able to see through' occurs 40 times in 25 texts, while the emphatic 'with one look, see through' (一覷覷破) occurs 19 times in 17. The texts do not supply a separate technical definition beyond these observable objects, contrasts, questions, and active/passive constructions.

Senses.Explanation: Inspect mind or look at mind. The compound occurs 474 times in 84 allowed texts, but 257 hits are concentrated in the Record of the Source-Mirror, and the corpus does not give the action one uniform set of predicates. In the Daoxin–Niutou Farong encounter, Farong answers ‘inspecting mind’ when asked what he is doing; Daoxin asks, ‘Who is doing the inspecting, and what thing is mind?’ (觀是何人，心是何物), and Farong gives no answer. The Treatise on Breaking Appearances says, ‘Only inspecting mind, this one thing, gathers all things’ (唯觀心一法，總攝諸法), then asks, ‘How does inspecting mind count as understanding?’ (云何觀心稱之為了). Its reply distinguishes a clean mind and a soiled mind and later says, ‘Inspecting mind in this way may be called understanding’ (如是觀心可名為了). The Record of the Source-Mirror quotes a different direct formula: ‘Inspect mind as no mind; things do not dwell on things; my mind is itself empty; fault and fortune have no owner—this is called correct inspection’ (觀心無心，法不住法，我心自空，罪福無主，即是無心無數，名為正觀). Other Chan witnesses criticize particular deployments. The Yongzheng Emperor says that making silence final and ‘then devoting oneself to quietly inspecting mind’ is ‘escaping a pit and falling into a ditch’ (便務靜觀心，又所謂逃坑落塹). Layman Xuri says, ‘closing the eyes, vainly seek seeing; inspecting mind, mistakenly seek penetration’ (閉目妄求見，觀心誤覓通). Zhang Tingyu, Layman Chenghuai, writes that ‘holding mind and inspecting mind divide guest and host’ (持心觀心紛主客). Chaoding Yuxuan writes, ‘if inspecting mind here is clear, the undivided single flavor is itself alert’ (於此觀心若了了，混然一味自惺惺). These are text-drawn assertions and criticisms by different named voices; they do not supply a single imported category for the headword.

Senses.Explanation: Understanding-realization names realization grounded in comprehension, but the retained records distinguish and evaluate it in more than one way. Yongming Yanshou conditionally commends such understanding as entry into an inconceivable means, while Guting Shanjian warns that making a view of understanding-realization and adaptability becomes an obstruction. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly contrasts understanding-realization gained through words with stronger penetrating realization reached through personal investigation, comparing the two to hearing about an object and seeing it directly. Guifeng Zongmi supplies a second exact contrast: sudden understanding followed by gradual cultivation is understanding-realization, whereas cultivation culminating in realization is verification-realization.

Senses.Explanation: To form an intellectual understanding is regularly rejected as construing or calculating from words rather than meeting the cited exchange. In Chan records the word commonly names understanding made from discriminations, words, or received knowledge rather than a neutral success at understanding. Yuanwu reports that many people make an emotionally conditioned construction of a public case and then explain Huichao's answer as simply meaning that Huichao himself is buddha. A record warns that seeking words and pursuing phrases in order to find such understanding produces proliferating differences and verbal facility. Huangbo's record says that construing the way as seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing leaves one far from it. The observable Chan bend is therefore critical: the ordinary verb 'understand' repeatedly labels the very explanatory grasp that masters reject. The term can still occur neutrally in a question such as 'how should this be understood'; this is the same act under different appraisal, not a different referent or word class.

Senses.Explanation: To unstick attachments and remove restraints is a corpus-defined teaching job: masters use it for freeing people where words, explanations, or inherited handling have adhered and bound. The records make the job observable by pairing it with pulling nails and wedges, breaking cangues, and prescribing medicine according to illness. Zhenjing Kewen says this, together with prescribing medicine to illness, is the one thing the Shengshou elder knows how to do. Yuanwu Keqin applies it to Bodhidharma in the Blue Cliff Record and uses it again in his own formal address after demanding the end of calculation. Feiyin Tongrong places it among the uses of a fully displayed mechanism; Gaofeng Yuanmiao says his counter in the goose-in-a-bottle case would enable patch-robed monks to do it.

Senses.Explanation: The records call a settled place of release a deep pit: fearsome, like dead water, and not a place in which to sit fast. Dahui Zonggao says that the buddha rebukes a person who remains in extinguished stillness as fallen into the deep pit of release, a fearsome place. Dongchan Guan says that Shariputra rests on great extinction and sits in this pit. Yunmen Wenyan raises his staff, calls it the deep pit of release leaping, and supplies 'out' as the substitute response. Hanyue Fazang places it beside a body filled with dead water and directly warns that one must not sit attached there. These predicates establish a pit or trap within the corpus's own language; they do not authorize a general account of release.

Senses.Explanation: to touch or meet the eye; in context, whatever meets the eye. It forms public questions—'what is the affair that meets the eye?' and 'what is awakening that meets the eye?'—to which Xuefeng answers with a question, 'what is it?', with 'heavens!', by lifting the whisk, or by pointing out a bare pillar. Yunmen's statement 'even if whatever meets the eye is unobstructed' becomes a repeatedly quoted and tested formula. One later master raises a whisk and says that calling it a whisk leaves obstruction in what meets the eye, while not calling it a whisk does too. Linji's record says 'whatever meets the eye is it,' and immediately supplies its own stated obstruction: feelings arise, knowledge separates, and thought changes the object. The ordinary visual phrase is thus heavily loaded as interview and teaching-seat vocabulary.

Senses.Explanation: Masters raise ‘awakening wherever the eye lands’ as a public question, then enact or redirect the answer through an immediately visible object or action without making one response universal. The graphs say “meet or strike the eye” and “awakening”: “awakening wherever the eye meets.” The exact question “What is awakening wherever the eye meets?” accounts for 69 of the headword’s 127 occurrences. The answers and follow-up actions vary. When Shishuang Qingzhu asks Daowu, Daowu calls a novice, tells him to add water to the clean-water jar, later asks Shishuang what he had just asked, and leaves as Shishuang begins to repeat it; the narrative then says Shishuang woke up. Another exchange answers, “All things constantly abide”; when asked what that means, the named record subject answers with the headword again. Elsewhere the answer is “the buddha hall before you,” a named record subject kicks a dog so that it runs off making a sound, or Xuansha says, “Before a dead monk is precisely awakening wherever the eye meets.” Linquan’s later comment on the Daowu case says that it has “no empty gap.” The records preserve these named exchanges and different predicates; this entry gives no single explanation in place of their different answers.

Senses.Explanation: To become obstructed along every route or at every turn. The phrase diagnoses fixation, conceptual impurity, mishandled teaching formulas, or ongoing course that converts whatever it meets into an impediment. Huanglong says an object lodged in the chest remains before the eyes and produces obstruction at every turn. Dahui says mixed poison entering the mind makes one obstructed wherever one turns. Linquan warns that inadequate grounding in Caodong teaching repeatedly meets obstruction. Yunju contrasts realization’s unimpeded function with loss, which produces obstruction everywhere.

Senses.Explanation: A narrative formula reporting that someone was greatly awakened immediately at or under spoken words. It marks the event's position in an exchange; it does not itself state what was understood. The recorded words differ in every case. Daoxin is reported awakened after Sengcan asks who binds him and why he seeks release. Damei Fachang follows Mazu Daoyi's answer "mind itself is buddha." Wuxie Lingmo follows Shitou Xiqian's challenge about turning his head away from "only this." Yanyang follows Zhaozhou Congshen's answer to carry away what he cannot put down. Fenyang Shanzhao follows Shoushan Xingnian's two answers concerning Baizhang's rolled mat, and Huanglong Huinan follows Ciming Chuyuan's question whether he takes the rebuke as scolding. Huiming is reported awakened after Huineng asks for his original face at the moment of thinking neither good nor evil. The Zen bend lies in the strict attribution chain: a named speaker's precise turn precedes a named person's reported awakening, while the narrative formula belongs to the compiler and never turns the awakening into a free-floating event without a case.

Senses.Explanation: The temporal phrase places discernment before words, or ahead of speech, in a recurrent Chan contrast with responding after a phrase. Its visible deployment is the paired formula 'discern before the words' and 'accord after the phrase.' Multiple records immediately refuse both positions: discerning before the words fails one's whole life, while according after the phrase departs from the body of the Way; Yuanwu similarly quotes discernment before words as still confined by a shell. A preface also says the mind seal may be discerned before words. These passages establish a stock temporal axis for examining an answer's relation to spoken words, not a named realm.
